To address this complex challenge, a new approach is proposed, in which the processes for classifying the activity and estimating the entities work in tandem and complement each other. This collaborative method is realized through the Collaborative Glance-Gaze TransFormer (CoFormer) model, consisting of two components: the Glance transformer, which classifies the activity, and the Gaze transformer, which identifies entities and their relationships. As the Gaze transformer analyzes entities, it relies on the Glance transformer's activity classification. Conversely, the Gaze transformer focuses solely on entities relevant to the activity predicted by the Glance transformer, thus estimating the grounded entities. The proposed CoFormer model achieves state-of-the-art performance on all evaluation metrics using the SWiG dataset. Training code and model weights are available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/jhcho99/CoFormer.

Inverse problems in wave propagation can be reformulated into computationally manageable source extension methods in certain scenarios. A fundamental aspect of these methods is solving a linear inverse problem, which entails minimizing data discrepancies using the least squares approach while softly imposing physical constraints on the source via a quadratic penalty term. A modified time reversal approach from photoacoustic tomography can generate an approximate solution that serves as an efficient preconditioner, allowing Krylov space iteration to rapidly converge towards the subproblem solution. The efficacy of this preconditioner can be demonstrated through a 2D acoustic example, specifically with surface-supported sources and a constraint enforcing point support.

We introduce a novel test-time adaptation technique for cross-domain image segmentation tasks. Our approach is straightforward: at test time, we modify a pre-trained model by recalibrating its instance-specific BatchNorm statistics. It consists of two main components: 1) we substitute the pre-defined BatchNorm calibration rule with a trainable module and 2) utilize aggressive data augmentation to simulate random domain shifts, thus learning an adaptive rule. Unlike traditional domain adaptation methods, our technique doesn't need access to the target domain data during training or expensive model fine-tuning at test time. By incorporating our method into models trained with conventional protocols, substantial performance gains can be achieved, outperforming multiple state-of-the-art domain generalization and one-shot unsupervised domain adaptation methods. Moreover, when combined with existing domain generalization techniques, our approach can even surpass current state-of-the-art results.

The orbital angular momentum of light is considered a valuable resource in quantum technology, including applications in quantum communication and sensing. Unfortunately, the OAM state of light is vulnerable to unwanted factors such as distance and phase distortion, limiting the practical application of related technologies. This study leverages an advanced deep learning algorithm to detect various OAM modes at different distances and under phase distortion. Our model can accurately identify the topological charge and propagation distance of a vortex beam with 97% precision, offering significant implications for OAM-based communication and sensing methods.

Minor mergers in galaxy clusters can generate sloshing cold fronts, but the impact of subsequent mergers on these formations remains uncertain. We analyzed the resilience of cold fronts in galaxy clusters after a subsequent minor merger using simulations of triple cluster mergers with varied approaches and parameters. Our simulations revealed that cold fronts persist in all scenarios, except briefly after the initial collision. Notably, minor mergers that directly collide with the cluster significantly reduce cold fronts, whereas off-axis mergers have a more moderate effect, and outer cold fronts prove particularly resilient. Our findings suggest that cold fronts are common in galaxy clusters, but determining a cluster's merger history from observed cold fronts might be more intricate than expected.

To improve the accuracy and robustness of reduced-order models for the compressible Euler equations based on proper orthogonal decomposition and Galerkin methods, researchers have been examining alternative inner product spaces for dimensionality reduction and norm measurement. Currently, the widely used L2 space results in models that lack robustness and dimensional consistency. To address this limitation, a new study focuses on the potential benefits of using dimensionally-consistent inner products, starting with the exploration of non-dimensional inner products, followed by the investigation of physics-based inner products grounded in entropy principles. This study aims to enhance the reliability and accuracy of reduced-order models for three complex fluid dynamics problems: the one-dimensional Sod shock tube, the two-dimensional Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, and two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence.

Reduced order models derived from full order solutions can still have computational complexity issues due to scaled terms.  To mitigate this problem, sampling-based methods known as hyper-reduction techniques can be applied to approximate the scaled terms, thus significantly reducing the computational dimension. A hyper-reduction approach based on the S-OPT algorithm, which was originally proposed for uncertainty quantification, aims to select points that maximize a quantity representing both orthogonality and determinant properties.  Numerical experiments show that using S-OPT for hyper-reduction yields higher accuracy in predicting full order solutions compared to over-sampled Discrete Empirical Interpolation methods, especially when using a limited number of indices.

Researchers have proposed the existence of compact, exotic stellar objects known as boson stars, which could potentially be detected through gravitational wave signals from binary coalescence events in current and future observatories. Our analysis reveals a universal relationship among the moment of inertia, angular momentum, and quadrupole moment of rotating boson stars, which holds true across various models. This relationship is distinct from its counterpart in neutron stars and offers a reliable method for identifying boson stars and distinguishing them from other celestial objects through gravitational wave observations. Furthermore, this universal connection can serve as a valuable tool for studying the strong gravity effects of general relativity and constraining the properties of matter within compact stars.

Advanced coreference resolution models typically rely on local decisions made
for individual mention pairs. Our proposed method, however, takes a more
comprehensive document-level approach by making global decisions. To do this,
we utilize a graph structure, with words in the text as nodes and the
connections between them as edges, to represent coreference links. Our model
predicts the graph in a non-autoregressive fashion, and subsequently refines
it based on its previous predictions, allowing for the incorporation of global
dependencies between decisions. The experimental findings indicate that this
approach yields better results compared to established baselines, thereby
validating our hypothesis that incorporating document-level information leads
to improved coreference resolution.

The second public dataset from the DECam Local Volume Exploration survey is now available, incorporating both new and previously collected data. The DELVE dataset, consisting of over 160,000 exposures across more than 21,000 square degrees of the high-latitude sky, offers detailed optical and near-infrared observations of approximately 2.5 billion celestial objects. This dataset provides photometric data for these objects with high sensitivity, and a significant portion of the data covers all four observation bands. Compared to the previous release, this dataset spans nearly four times the area and contains roughly five times as many celestial bodies. The dataset is accessible through the NOIRLab Astro Data Lab platform for public use.

Current galaxy simulations can model individual molecular clouds, the precursors to massive star clusters. The fate of young massive clusters and whether they evolve into old globular clusters is influenced by a combination of internal processes and external galactic forces. Our research involves the first detailed star-by-star models of massive star clusters formed in a simulation of a galaxy similar to the Milky Way, taking into account various initial conditions and galactic effects. By selecting and integrating data from a previous study, we found that a simulated Milky Way-like system would likely have around 148 globular clusters, most of which formed early in the galaxy's history. However, our simulated globular clusters differ from observed ones in the Milky Way and Andromeda Galaxy, as they are younger, less massive, and more collapsed. This difference can be attributed to the specific history of their host galaxy, including factors such as galactic tidal forces and the presence of black holes, which can influence a cluster's mass and size. Our findings highlight the importance of detailed simulations and realistic stellar physics in understanding the evolution of globular clusters in galaxies.

The rise of digital technology has led to a renewed interest in "dark mode" (DM) design in everyday applications and professional software. In this paper, we make a case for introducing DM themes in astronomical journals, including a customizable class file for implementation. DM themes come with numerous benefits for users, including reduced energy consumption, minimized OLED screen damage, improved figure navigation, and better compatibility with colorblind-friendly designs. Our analysis of iPoster trends from AAS conferences 237 and 238 suggests that at least 35%, and possibly up to 42%, of the community would appreciate this feature in journals. However, there are some drawbacks to consider, such as increased ink usage when printed and decreased readability in low-light environments. Nevertheless, these issues can be mitigated by offering a dual submission option featuring both DM and traditional themes. Ultimately, incorporating DM into journals may enhance astronomers' productivity and expertise.

Discovering accurate constitutive models for solid materials under large deformation has long been a complex problem, particularly for those undergoing significant strain. Our research offers a novel physics-guided artificial intelligence framework that utilizes full-field displacement data and global force-displacement measurements to identify constitutive model parameterizations. Unlike many current studies, we base our approach on the weak form of the underlying equations to impose realistic physical limitations on neural network predictions. This method is computationally efficient, suitable for irregular shapes, and can directly process displacement data without grid interpolation. We evaluate our approach using well-known hyperelastic models such as the Neo-Hookean, Gent, and Blatz-Ko models to represent general, polymer, and foam material behaviors, respectively. Our findings demonstrate the potential of physics-informed machine learning to revolutionize the utilization of full-field experimental data in constitutive model calibration under finite deformation conditions.

We present dGSLM, a pioneering "textless" model capable of creating audio samples 
of authentic, spoken conversations. It leverages advancements in spoken unit discovery 
alongside a dual-tower transformer framework with cross-attention trained on 2000 hours 
of two-channel, untranscribed conversational audio (the Fisher dataset). Our model demonstrates 
the ability to simultaneously produce spoken words, laughter, and other paralinguistic 
sounds in both channels, while also replicating more lifelike and smooth turn-taking dynamics, 
outperforming text-driven cascaded models.

Our research focuses on solving Partial Differential Equation (PDE) based Data Assimilation problems through variational methods and Kalman filter techniques. Recently, we introduced a Domain Decomposition framework called DD-DA, which partitions a physical domain across both spatial and temporal dimensions, combining Schwarz' methods and parallel-in-time approaches. To optimize DD-DA parallelization, subdomains' computational loads must be evenly distributed. Typically, this requires effective partitioning to minimize computational costs and communication overhead. In this work, we address the challenges posed by non-uniformly distributed and sparse observation data by developing a parallel load-balancing algorithm called DyDD. This algorithm dynamically adjusts Domain Decomposition boundaries to balance workload according to data location. We will apply this framework to constrained least-squares state estimation problems and validate its performance across various scenarios.

Time crystals with discrete Floquet properties are distinguished by the spontaneous
breaking of time-translational symmetry in periodically driven systems. Similar to equilibrium phase transitions, time-crystalline phases exhibit distinct critical behaviors characterized by oscillations whose period exceeds two times that of the driving period. We've introduced a novel order parameter that can unambiguously identify crystalline phases across all possible periods and serve as a tool for diagnosing chaotic behavior. This new perspective has allowed us to delve deeply into the phase diagram of the long-range kicked Ising model, revealing a complex landscape of self-similar boundaries. Our comprehensive theoretical framework describes the emergence of DFTC phases in terms of Floquet drive strength and period, capturing the inherent Zp symmetry within Floquet-Bloch waves.

To accurately determine the Cabbibo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix element $|V_{cb}|$ from inclusive data, it's essential to have a precise measurement of the semileptonic $b \to c$ decay rate. However, this quantity exhibits poor convergence properties when expressed in terms of on-shell or $\overline{\text{MS}}$ quark masses. Therefore, recent studies have focused on the kinetic mass scheme, where a precise understanding of the inter-scheme relations is also crucial. In this paper, we present our calculations that have significantly improved both the decay rate and inter-scheme relation to $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^3)$ accuracy, enabling a refined inclusive determination of $|V_{cb}|$.

Astronomers use photon counting to analyze low-signal targets observed with an electron multiplying CCD (EMCCD). This method involves amplifying the signal and filtering it using thresholding to reduce noise, resulting in a more precise measurement of photo-electrons. To further improve accuracy, photometric corrections have been developed. The Nancy Grace Roman Telescope will leverage these corrections and a noise model to optimize its coronagraph instrument's observations. We have established mathematical formulas describing the signal-to-noise ratio for photon counting with and without the photometric corrections in place.

This study examines a discrete-time Stackelberg mean field game featuring multiple strategic leaders, several major followers, and an infinite number of minor followers. Leaders have exclusive knowledge of their private types, which evolve according to conditional independence and controlled Markov processes. These leaders, adopting a "Stackelberg" approach, implement a dynamic strategy to optimize their reward. In contrast, followers, comprising major and minor groups with distinct private types, react optimally to both the Stackelberg leaders' strategies and each other's. Each leader anticipates the mean field outcome resulting from the followers' game, then selects a policy that maximizes their reward, leading to a Stackelberg mean field equilibrium with multiple leaders (SMFE-ML). This paper derives a master equation to determine SMFE-ML, and further expands the model to include an infinite number of leaders.

Automatic detection of vulnerability-fixing commits is now crucial due to the growing number of discovered open-source software vulnerabilities over time. Monitoring commit updates to prevent exploitation is part of standard vulnerability management. However, manually reviewing the large volume of commits for vulnerability fixes is laborious. To address this challenge, various machine learning-based techniques have been developed, but they either lack deep learning capabilities or rely on limited data sources. This study introduces VulCurator, a tool that utilizes deep learning to analyze a broader range of data, including commit messages, code modifications, and issue reports to classify vulnerability-fixing commits accurately. Our results demonstrate that VulCurator significantly outperforms existing approaches by up to 16.1% in F1-score accuracy. For further information and a demo, please visit VulCurator's public repository at https://github.com/ntgiang71096/VFDetector, https://zenodo.org/record/7034132#.Yw3MN-xBzDI, and https://youtu.be/uMlFmWSJYOE.

The flavoured anti-$k_{\text{T}}$ jet algorithm, introduced recently, is applied to the analysis of $Wb\bar{b}$ production at the 8 TeV Large Hadron Collider. Our research yields the total cross-section and various differential distributions for this process, calculated at the next-to-next-to-leading order of QCD. We examine the impact of the remaining adjustable parameters within this jet algorithm, and contrast it with the conventional flavour-$k_{\text{T}}$ approach. Our findings show good correlation with the CMS data, which further strengthens once the NNLO QCD corrections are integrated.

Relativistic magnetic reconnections are widespread in celestial systems, where the plasma is often cooled significantly by synchrotron radiation. In systems with intense synchrotron cooling and high magnetic compactness, the production of electron-positron pairs from photons is inevitable, regulating the system's magnetic fields. We've derived an analytical solution that reveals a stable, self-consistent state for these systems, contingent on their magnetic compactness and initial magnetization. This finding allows for more accurate estimates of the upstream magnetic field strength in scenarios where the plasma density is difficult to determine, offering a valuable tool for understanding various celestial phenomena. Notably, this concept can be applied to study specific systems, such as the M87 supermassive black hole and the Crab pulsar's equatorial current sheet.

We studied the internal movement patterns of young stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud's region NGC 346 using two sets of Hubble Space Telescope observations taken over a period of 11 years. By tracking the movement of different groups of stars based on their colors and spatial distribution, we observed complex motion patterns in young stars of the region, including both outward and inward flows in the outer areas. The inner parts of the cluster showed a combination of rotational and inward motion. Inflow and rotation speeds reached up to 3 km/s and 1 km/s respectively in the inner 10 parsecs of the cluster. Changes in motion coherence were observed near massive young stars and sub-clusters, indicating turbulence played a key role in this region's star formation. Notably, similar movement patterns were observed in metal-poor NGC 346 and Milky Way star-forming regions, suggesting metallicity and dust differences did not significantly impact star cluster assembly. Our findings align with various models of star cluster formation.

Code element names vary greatly in style and wording, hindering effective comparison, as identical meanings are represented by different words or words with varying meanings. To accurately compare these names, a library of functions has been developed that can account for spelling errors, synonyms, word reordering, and other variations, allowing researchers to choose the most suitable comparison method for their needs, which may involve trade-offs between lexical precision and human-like similarity assessments.

This paper offers a general formula for the $n$th term of the $k$-generalized
Fibonacci sequence, a broadened Fibonacci sequence with $k$ arbitrary starting
values, where subsequent terms are calculated by summing the previous $k$ terms.
By analyzing patterns in derived formulas for specific sequences, we established
the general formula for the $k$-generalized Fibonacci-like sequence and applied
it in the proof of our paper's main finding.

Graph artificial intelligence has made significant breakthroughs in modeling intricate systems, encompassing biological networks, physical particle interactions and more. The growing diversity of graph datasets necessitates novel multimodal approaches, which can integrate disparate inductive biases. Multimodal graph AI encounters core challenges due to varying inductive biases across data modalities and often lacking explicit graph inputs. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have begun to merge multiple data types, utilizing cross-modal relationships to facilitate predictions. Our comprehensive review of 145 studies in graph AI reveals an increasing trend of combining diverse datasets and applying advanced multimodal techniques, categorized into image-rich, knowledge-based, and language-driven models. This classification framework serves as a guide to analyze existing methods and inform the development of future multimodal graph AI solutions.

Nonlinear conservation laws pose significant difficulties in adjoint-based optimization due to concerns about the direct and adjoint solutions' existence and uniqueness, as well as the problem's well-posedness for sensitivity analysis and gradient-based optimization algorithms. This paper explores the convergence of adjoint equations towards exact solutions of the inviscid Burgers' equation under different numerical methods, examining the impact of non-differentiable approximate Riemann solvers and inconsistencies in time-stepping methods on the results of complete versus incomplete scheme differentiation.

An object that moves and settles in a stationary fluid undergoes an inertial torque that causes it to align its broad side when settling downward, similar to a stationary particle. For a self-propelled spherical object, this torque is given by $\boldsymbol{T}^\prime = -{\tfrac{9}{8}} m_f (\boldsymbol{v}_s^{(0)} \wedge \boldsymbol{v}_g^{(0)})$, where $\boldsymbol{v}_s^{(0)}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_g^{(0)}$ are the swimming and settling velocities respectively, and $m_f$ is the equivalent fluid mass. This torque causes the swimming direction to oppose gravity, resulting in stable upward movement and unstable downward movement.

This research investigates the current stability of cosmic strings that exhibit bosonic superconductivity, specifically when they possess a non-zero curvature, which can induce quantum instability in the particles they carry. Various decay rates and models are examined in detail to determine the impact of different parameters and curved shapes on particle stability. The research also applies cosmological principles to the stability of superconducting strings within cosmic networks and vortons, evaluating their evolution to identify patterns and limitations. Ultimately, the findings suggest that vortons are unstable under certain conditions, such as significant mass differences between the string and its particles, or substantial particle couplings to lighter species like those in the Standard Model.

In a study of a single-twist trilayer graphene, the researchers utilized circularly polarized and longitudinal light emanating from a waveguide to examine the magnetic field-generated Hofstadter butterfly. They found two distinct chiral states within the equilibrium and an increased visibility of the butterfly. The use of circularly polarized light resulted in significant energy gap creation within the butterfly and the Landau levels, showing clear asymmetry around zero energy. Notably, right-handed light shifted the central band downward, while left-handed light caused it to rise. Furthermore, investigations into the effect of longitudinally polarized light demonstrated a unique symmetry breakdown for low driving forces, only restored at stronger forces, a phenomenon contrasting with twisted bilayer graphene.

Compounds with non-centrosymmetric structures have garnered significant attention for their potential to host unconventional superconductivity, and a newly discovered compound, NbIr$_2$B$_2$, has proven to possess this property below a critical temperature of approximately 7.3 Kelvin. Characterized by its exceptionally high upper critical field, this compound presents a fascinating case for researchers. Recent muon spin rotation experiments conducted to investigate its properties suggest a fully gapped s-wave superconducting state. The compound's upper critical field is also confirmed by transport measurements, with its ratio of critical temperature to magnetic penetration depth being comparable to those of other unconventional superconductors. Interestingly, the compound's behavior above and below its critical temperature, as revealed by zero-field muon spin relaxation measurements, indicates that time-reversal symmetry is preserved in its superconducting state. These findings are expected to prompt theoretical investigations aiming to provide insight into the underlying microscopic mechanisms of this intriguing non-centrosymmetric system.

We're driven by applications in distributed storage and computing to develop communication-efficient methods for computing linear combinations of encoded data. Our focus is on a specific problem: given a set of coded symbols, evaluate the weighted sum of $\ell$ symbols when we can access $d$ of the remaining components. We consider codewords in Reed-Solomon codes over field extensions of $\mathbb{B}$, where the task is to compute the weighted sum of $\ell$ symbols by downloading sub-symbols in $\mathbb{B}$ from $d$ available nodes under certain conditions. Our scheme surpasses existing methods in many scenarios, and we derive a lower bound for the evaluation bandwidth of Reed-Solomon codes.

High-entropy alloys have garnered considerable interest due to their remarkable mechanical properties and vast compositional possibilities. However, studying their innovative physical properties is hindered by their intricate chemical nature, which poses significant challenges to theoretical modeling and the development of reliable large-scale models for evaluating numerous potential alloys. The application of machine learning has shed new light on these obstacles by enabling the representation of extremely complex relationships. This review explores the effectiveness of machine learning in addressing these challenges and its promising potential for future applications. We initially introduce the fundamental concepts of machine learning and its application areas, followed by a summary of the latest machine learning models describing atomic interactions and atomistic simulations of thermal and mechanical properties. Special attention is given to phase predictions, defect calculations, and plastic deformation simulations. Subsequently, we review machine learning models for large-scale properties, including lattice structures, phase formations, and mechanical properties. Examples of machine-learned phase-formation rules and order parameters are provided to illustrate the workflow. Lastly, we discuss the remaining challenges and outline potential research directions, including uncertainty quantification and machine learning-guided inverse materials design.

The root-mean-square velocity of non-relativistic warm dark matter particles is inversely proportional to the expansion parameter of the universe. This dispersion leads to a cut-off in the power spectrum of density fluctuations, caused by dark matter free-streaming. Estimates derived from observed galaxy distributions yield a $0.41$ km/s uncertainty range for this velocity at the current time, and a corresponding $2$ Mpc^-1 cut-off wavenumber at the era of radiation-matter equality, both at 68% confidence. This result aligns with the process of reionization. Considering the velocity cut-off provides further constraints: a velocity of less than $0.54$ km/s and a wavenumber exceeding $1.5$ Mpc^-1. These findings are consistent with previous measurements based on spiral galaxies, the formation of the first galaxies, and reionization. These parameters determine the temperature-to-mass ratio of warm dark matter. This ratio agrees with a specific warm dark matter scenario featuring decoupled, spin 0 particles, while other scenarios, including spin 1/2 and spin 1 particles, are disfavored. An extension of the standard model incorporating scalar dark matter is proposed to reconcile all existing measurements, addressing discrepancies with dark matter particle mass limits from the literature.

We establish a fluctuation algebra for fermions in a nearly free state and 
investigate its time-evolution under quasifree dynamics. We also discover a 
Bose-Einstein condensate and analyze its stability under interacting conditions.

In various scientific computations, linear algebra expressions are frequently calculated through a series of library calls, with a sequence representing a specific computational strategy, or algorithm. For one expression, numerous equivalent algorithms often exist, but their performance can differ significantly despite mathematical equivalence. Several high-level languages and tools optimize algorithm choices to minimize floating-point operations (FLOPs), but multiple algorithms may have the same or nearly identical FLOP counts with varying execution times. Moreover, the algorithm minimizing FLOPs might not necessarily minimize execution time. To address this, a new methodology is developed to evaluate the reliability of FLOPs as a performance discriminator for linear algebra algorithms. Given a set of algorithms for a specific expression, the approach ranks them into performance classes, allowing algorithms with similar performance to share the same rank. By iteratively measuring algorithms until changes in ranks become negligible, FLOPs are deemed a valid discriminator if the best-ranked algorithms all have the minimum FLOPs, otherwise, the instance is flagged as an anomaly to be further investigated.

We provide a comprehensive analysis of how backscattering is influenced by acceptor holes or Mn spins in mercury telluride and mercury-manganese telluride quantum wells, specifically within the context of the quantum spin Hall regime. Our study systematically evaluates the impact of anisotropic s-p and sp-d exchange interactions, Kondo coupling, Luttinger liquid effects, precessional dephasing, and bound magnetic polarons. Our numerical findings and the resulting temperature dependence of conductivity are consistent with experimental data from HgTe and (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells.

Our research focuses on the contextual bandit problem, a theoretically supported framework with broad real-world applications. Unlike traditional studies that assume noise independence from contexts, we consider a more realistic scenario where noise affects both contexts and rewards. This confounded setting is more practical and has the potential to expand into various fields, but also introduces a bias in estimating the reward function, leading to a significant regret. To overcome these challenges, we utilize dual instrumental variable regression, which enables the accurate identification of the true reward function. We demonstrate that this method achieves a near-optimal convergence rate in specific reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, providing the basis for designing computationally efficient and regret-optimal algorithms for confounded bandit problems. Furthermore, our numerical results show that our proposed algorithms excel in the confounded bandit setting.

In a previous study, we demonstrated the possibility of obtaining any minimal symplectic filling of an oriented lens space by applying a sequence of symplectic rational blowdowns along linear graphs, derived from the minimal resolution of a cyclic quotient singularity with its canonical contact structure. Here, we present a significantly simplified representation of our algorithm using convex polygon triangulations, allowing us to organize minimal symplectic fillings into a structured graph with a root representing the minimal resolution and directed edges representing symplectic blowdowns. Additionally, we establish an upper limit for the complexity of each minimal symplectic filling.

The challenge of efficiently generating trajectories in complex dynamic environments still exists in the field of unmanned surface vehicles (USVs). A new algorithm for a USV-UAV cooperative system is proposed, allowing the USV to navigate safely and smoothly through maps with multiple obstacles in autonomous mode. The UAV acts as a flight sensor, providing real-time global maps and obstacle information. The algorithm generates an initial trajectory using a graph-based search method and then refines it using numerical optimization, taking into account the USV's unique kinematic characteristics and motion constraints. To minimize energy consumption during execution, a novel motion control method based on NMPC is developed. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system, resulting in a locally optimal trajectory for the USV with high tracking accuracy.

In ocean exploration and environmental protection, Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) require advanced technologies to successfully complete their missions. This paper introduces a cutting-edge trajectory generation and tracking method for USVs, based on optimization techniques to ensure precise navigation. By applying dynamic flatness to the USV model and utilizing dynamic RRT* for linear trajectory generation, the proposed approach optimizes the boundary conditions to create a realistic and efficient trajectory. To further enhance performance, a local optimization process refines the trajectory while respecting the USV's kinematic characteristics. Finally, model predictive control with sequential quadratic programming is incorporated for motion tracking, resulting in more accurate and reliable navigation as demonstrated by experimental results.

Financial transactions in developing countries, particularly in Africa, largely rely on physical currency. In Ethiopia, a country with one of the highest rates of blindness and low vision, approximately 4 million people live with visual impairments, including 1.7 million who are completely blind. This population faces significant challenges in situations requiring cash exchange. To address this issue, we propose an AI-driven solution. Our mobile application, compatible with both Android and IOS platforms, achieved 98.9% accuracy in identifying currencies using machine learning models. It also features a voice assistant that announces currency types in Amharic, Ethiopia's native language, providing users with easy access and alleviating the difficulties faced by visually impaired individuals.

The role of vortices in planetary formation, where they gather dust in the pressure centers of protoplanetary discs, has been extensively studied, with researchers seeking to understand when vortices remain stable and when they break apart. By running high-resolution simulations of dust-laden vortices within a protoplanetary disc, the study found that vortex stability depends on its size in relation to the disc's height and the degree of dust interaction. The research demonstrated that smaller vortices remain stable, while larger ones are subject to a drag instability that causes them to contract and eventually break apart due to the presence of dust grains, particularly larger ones. The study's findings imply that dust in a protoplanetary disc influences the stability of vortices formed through shear and zombie vortex instabilities or the disruption of larger vortices through hydrodynamic instabilities, with dust accumulation occurring in vortex cores despite the reduced lifespan.

In recent years, machine learning models for simulating individual atoms have garnered significant interest within the fields of chemistry and materials science, where researchers have developed several new approaches with the goal of replicating the accuracy of electronic structure calculations on large-scale systems comprising thousands of atoms. Despite these advances, the reliability of these models in capturing the intricate details of complex potential-energy landscapes remains challenging to determine for such large systems. Conversely, investigations into smaller systems where quality-control assessments can be rigorously performed have become less frequent. In this study, we employ high-precision harmonic and anharmonic vibrational frequencies as a sensitive validation tool for high-dimensional neural network models. For the formic acid dimer, a well-studied model system, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art calculations can yield high-quality frequencies that align with coupled cluster theory and experimental data.

The study of human anatomy and diseases can be significantly hindered by restricted access to medical imaging data, due to governance concerns, data ownership issues, and high costs. To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored the development of synthetic imaging models. Building on existing deep learning techniques used for generating synthetic 2D images, a novel approach has been proposed to create high-resolution, 3D volumetric images of the human body, specifically the brain. By providing an abundance of anatomically accurate data, this model has the potential to greatly enhance our understanding of human anatomy, facilitate large-scale studies, and contribute to breakthroughs in AI research areas such as anomaly detection and fairness.

Remote hacking attacks on laptop computers have increased significantly, often utilizing malware to gain unauthorized access to webcams and microphones, enabling users to be secretly spied on. Although commercial webcam covers offer a degree of protection against such webcam attacks, the same can't be said for microphone attacks. Given this issue, a new system called TickTock is being proposed to help protect against mic hacking by detecting when the microphone is in use. This is possible because microphones emit detectable electromagnetic signals when in use, which TickTock can identify from outside the laptop. To test the effectiveness of TickTock, a proof-of-concept system was created, which demonstrated that it can accurately detect microphone status on a variety of laptops. Evaluations conducted on 30 laptops showed that TickTock successfully identified the microphone's on or off status with high accuracy in 27 of the laptops.

We broaden the application of Krasnoselskii's fixed point theorem to a broader category of functions. Our new method yields a straightforward proof for a previously known outcome attributed to Hillam. Notably, our proof doesn't rely on the mapping's image being compact or bounded. By doing so, we expand the applicability of Hillam's result to self-mappings on the real numbers. Furthermore, we develop an alternative proof for the global convergence of the Newton-Raphson method.

Iron chalcogenides, with their distinct electronic structures, have been proven to be inherent topological superconductors and are a promising material for quantum computing. Studies on FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$ had already predicted and verified its non-trivial surface states via high-resolution photoemission and scanning tunneling experiments. However, there has been a lack of conclusive electrical transport evidence for these surface states. Recent experiments revealed a topological transition characterized by non-linear Hall conductivity and linear magnetoresistance near the superconducting transition temperature. Additionally, a sign reversal of the Hall coefficient along with concurrent softening of the ${A}_{1g}$ phonon mode at approximately 40 K, indicating nematicity, was observed. This synchronized phonon softening further highlights the role of spin-phonon interaction in creating an enhanced fluctuation state. The obtained results conclusively confirm the existence of topological surface states in FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$ and provide a clear understanding of the underlying superconductivity mechanism in iron chalcogenides.

Two-dimensional arrays of subwavelength quantum emitters can be used to create efficient optical components in the linear regime when exposed to normally incident light. By exploiting the cooperative optical response between emitters, which arises from dipole interactions, the array's transmission properties, resonance frequency, and bandwidth can be precisely controlled. The optical properties of fully polarized incident light can also be manipulated using various polarization devices, including linear and circular polarizers, as well as phase retarders, and can be mathematically described using Jones matrices. Analytical and numerical simulations have revealed the optimal conditions for such optical operations, highlighting the need to carefully adjust the array's geometry and the external magnetic fields in terms of both amplitude and direction.

Understanding the mechanisms behind SARS-CoV-2's evolution and transmission is a significant issue of our time. Researchers utilized AI combined with genetic information from patients, large datasets of mutations, and advanced computational techniques like algebraic topology to uncover that SARS-CoV-2's evolution is influenced by an infectivity-based form of natural selection. Through the use of AI, researchers accurately forecasted key mutations at positions L452 and N501 on the virus's receptor-binding domain, long before these mutations became prominent in dominant variants like Alpha and Omicron. A new form of natural selection, where the virus develops resistance to antibodies, has been discovered, and AI models successfully predicted Omicron's characteristics, including its ability to evade vaccines and antibodies. These predictions were later validated through experiments. Topological AI models also accurately forecasted how specific mutations could impact the effectiveness of monoclonal antibodies.

Classical mechanics incorporates position and momentum variables, where specific coordinates must be selected to enable corresponding quantum operators. It's essential to choose unique variables to ensure valid quantization, as various options can sometimes lead to incorrect interpretations of physics. Selecting the most suitable variables and their associated quantum operators is crucial to guarantee a genuine and accurate quantization. Failing to do so might result in misinterpreting valid or invalid quantizations, which in turn can yield incorrect physical conclusions. The treatment will cover both particle and field examples, including gravity.

Rotating neutron stars with non-axisymmetrical crust deformations are a key area of research for continuous gravitational wave detection. The maximum allowable ellipticity, reflecting the difference in moments of inertia caused by'mountain' deformations, sets a crucial upper limit on the intensity of these gravitational waves. By adapting the model introduced by Gittins et al in 2021 and applying a transverse force, we have estimated a maximum ellipticity of 7.4 x 10^-6, which surpasses their original finding but is consistent with earlier studies by Ushomirsky et al in 2000. This implies that neutron stars undergoing rotation may be substantial emitters of continuous gravitational waves.

In today's deep learning model development, protecting sensitive information in crowd-sourced training data is crucial, adhering to strict privacy-preservation rules. To ensure models' privacy, the prevalent approach relies on differential privacy, achieved through optimization techniques. These methods effectively counter privacy threats but often compromise models' performance. This study compares the effectiveness of differential privacy's stochastic gradient descent with standard optimization methods, incorporating regularization techniques, and evaluates the trade-offs in models' utility, training performance, and vulnerability to membership inference and model inversion attacks. Furthermore, we examine the limitations of differential privacy and empirically show that techniques like dropout and l2-regularization can offer superior privacy preservation capabilities.

A new type of optomechanical sensor for detecting low-frequency vibrations and measuring acceleration has been developed. It features a resonant frequency of approximately 4.7 Hz, an exceptionally high quality factor of 476k, a tiny mass of 2.6 grams, and a projected detection limit of about 5E-11 m s^-2 per root-Hz at 1 Hz. This technology's compact size, low power consumption, and resistance to environmental influences make it an ideal candidate for geodesy missions. This paper showcases the experimental demonstration of low-frequency ground seismic noise detection using direct comparison with a commercial seismometer and also presents data analysis techniques for identifying, characterizing, and mitigating noise sources.

The objective of this brief note is that for any two sequences of positive real numbers, $\{ a_{n}\}$ and $\{ b_{n}\}$, where $a_{n}$ grows indefinitely and $b_n$ follows the approximate formula $b_n \approx k \cdot a_{n}$, with $k$ being a positive constant, it can be concluded that as $n$ approaches infinity, $\left(1+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right)^{b_{n}}$ converges to $e^{k}$.

To ensure reliable object detection in highly dynamic, safety-critical settings like autonomous driving and robotics, verifying the robustness of the detection against unexpected hardware faults like soft errors is crucial. Standard metrics used to evaluate object detection models often underestimate the severity of safety risks associated with silent data corruption caused by memory bit flips. This issue is addressed by proposing a novel metric called IVMOD, which assesses vulnerability based on incorrect image-level object detection and severity analysis. Evaluating multiple object detection models reveals that even single-bit flips can have severe safety implications, resulting in excessive false positives, lost true positives, and persistent ghost detections in sequences of images. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the safety-related vulnerability of critical workloads against hardware faults.

Deep Learning has significant potential to enhance the accuracy of Hyperspectral Imaging classification. However, training on the relatively limited hyperspectral datasets is complex, mainly due to the high channel dimensionality of the data and inter-manufacturer camera incompatibilities. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel 2D convolution model, which is optimized for Hyperspectral Imaging and incorporates a model bias and adaptive channel dimension. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness in two distinct hyperspectral applications - inline inspection and remote sensing - and find that the modification not only improves performance but also provides additional interpretability and enables data-driven camera filter design.

Research has demonstrated that observed potentials can be produced through quantum mechanics by utilizing an appropriate wavefunction. In this study, we focus on a tangible example, where we investigate the wavefunction responsible for generating the gravitational potential experienced by a test particle across various length scales, ranging from planetary to cosmological distances. Essentially, our findings suggest that the observed gravitational interaction at all scales can be explained by an underlying wavefunction, and we examine the significant implications arising from this discovery.

The atomic energy level shifts resulting from hadronic vacuum polarization are estimated in a semi-empirical method for hydrogen-like ions and muonic hydrogen atoms. By applying a parametric hadronic polarization function obtained from the experimental cross-sections of $e^-e^+$ annihilation into hadrons, an effective relativistic Uehling potential is derived to calculate the energy corrections due to hadronic vacuum polarization. These corrections are computed for low-lying levels using analytical Dirac-Coulomb wave functions and bound wave functions that account for the nuclear size. Furthermore, closed expressions are obtained for the hadronic Uehling potential of an extended nucleus as well as the relativistic energy shift for a point-like nucleus. These results are also compared to existing analytic formulas from non-relativistic theory.

Using data from proton-proton collisions collected at 13 TeV with the LHCb detector, the overall $C\!P$ asymmetry in the suppressed decay of $D^0$ mesons to $K^-K^+$ is measured. $D^0$ mesons must originate from decays involving a promptly produced $D^{*+}\to D^0\pi^+$, and the charge of the accompanying pion is used to determine the charm meson's initial state. A result for the overall $C\!P$ asymmetry of $\mathcal{A}_{C\!P}(K^-K^+)$ is $6.8 \times 10^{-4}$, which includes a significant uncertainty due to statistical and systematic effects. Direct $C\!P$ asymmetries for the decays of $D^0$ mesons to $K^-K^+$ and $\pi^-\pi^+$ can be derived by comparing the time-integrated $C\!P$ asymmetry of these decays. This yields direct $C\!P$ asymmetry values for these decays of $a_{K^-K^+}^{d}$ and $a_{\pi^-\pi^+}^{d}$, with the former indicating a $C\!P$ asymmetry of $(7.7 \pm 5.7) \times 10^{-4}$ and the latter of $(23.2 \pm 6.1) \times 10^{-4}$. These values indicate the presence of direct $C\!P$ violation in specific $D^0$ decays, with the former result showing a 1.4 standard deviation discrepancy from $C\!P$ symmetry and the latter showing a 3.8 standard deviation discrepancy.

Our research demonstrates that the first-order logical framework for binary overlap-free words, as well as a broader category of ${\alpha}$-free words, has a computationally solvable theory, provided that ${\alpha}$ falls within the rational range between $2$ and $7/3$. This breakthrough enables the application of an automated decision procedure, significantly simplifying the verification process for a variety of previously laboriously proved results in this domain.

A specific configuration of the Swapped Dragonfly network, denoted D3(K;M), is characterized by having K global ports per router and M routers per group, resulting in n=K*M*M routers. This paper investigates a restricted Swapped Dragonfly with the same parameters, K and M. Four distinct communication scenarios are analyzed: matrix multiplication, all-to-all exchange, broadcasting, and ascend-descend operations. For matrix multiplication, K being a perfect square enables an n-round matrix product. In the case of all-to-all exchange, if K and M share a common factor, it can be achieved in n/s rounds. A Swapped Dragonfly with a synchronized source-vector header can perform x broadcasts in 3x/M rounds. For ascend-descend operations, if K and M are powers of 2, the cost is twice that of the Boolean hypercube. Each algorithm on the Swapped Dragonfly eliminates link conflicts and is compared to its hypercube and fully populated Dragonfly counterparts. Since the Swapped Dragonfly encompasses emulations of every network with parameters J <= K and/or L <= M, the findings are more broadly applicable.

On finite networks, we study Activated Random Walks with particles entering randomly and exiting at the boundary. We find the relaxation time for this non-reversible process, despite limited knowledge about the equilibrium distribution. We prove the equivalence of separation cutoff to the product condition and establish precise bounds on the cutoff interval. Furthermore, we use these results to demonstrate specific separation cutoffs for specific networks, including subgraphs of large, infinite non-amenable graphs and large, finite, vertex-transitive graphs with absorption at a single vertex. This work resolves a long-standing conjecture by Levine and Liang. Our analysis is based on a refined study of a stationary time discovered by Levine and Liang, which involves the IDLA process.

The supersymmetry breaking mechanism typically predicts the existence of sgoldstinos, which can function as wave-like dark matter. Due to its universal interaction with electromagnetic fields, the light scalar sgoldstino dark matter can result in variations of the fine-structure constant. Utilizing precise atomic clock data, we have determined that the SUSY breaking scale $\sqrt{F}$ can be tested up to the grand unified theory scale within a sgoldstino mass range of $4\times10^{-7}$ eV $> m_\phi > 10^{-22}$ eV.

A novel approach to deriving the tunneling action for vacuum decay based on the tunneling potential has been proposed. This new method was initially derived by requiring that its variation leads to accurate equations of motion and results in the same action as obtained on the Euclidean bounce. We provide an alternative derivation of the tunneling potential action through canonical transformations. We examine both single-field and multi-field models as well as models involving gravity. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the new approach to calculating the prefactor in the tunneling rate.

At the AWAKE CERN experiment, novel automation methods leveraging unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) techniques were implemented to enhance the performance-critical stability and luminosity of the electron bunch at injection into the proton-driven plasma wakefield. To eliminate bias, various reinforcement learning agents were trained using model-free approaches and unsupervised state encoding through auto-encoders. For facilitating hyper-parameter tuning, a comprehensive synthetic model of the beamline was developed using a variational auto-encoder that generated surrogate data from equipment settings. This paper details ML-based approaches to automate setup configurations for low-energy beam delivery lines, like the one used for the AWAKE facility, and presents outcomes achieved with different ML strategies, including computer vision for image-based feature extraction. The potential for practical deployment and broader applicability is explored.

Revenue in freemium games comes from in-app purchases and ad exposure. As a player spends more time playing, the likelihood of generating revenue increases. Detecting impending player departure (churn) promptly is crucial to retain them, extending their in-game duration. This study examines how combining sequential and aggregate data through various neural network architectures can improve churn prediction accuracy. The comparative analysis demonstrates that combining both data types yields better prediction results than using either sequential or aggregated data alone.

The PSF knowledge benefits various astronomical applications, and we've developed a PSF Reconstruction algorithm for the LBT LUCI instrument, which is aided by the SOUL SCAO module. This algorithm uses real-time wavefront sensor data and some calibration measurements to generate a series of wavefront maps and their corresponding instantaneous PSFs. The reconstruction process is based on a straightforward approach, where each wavefront sensor reading is linked directly to a specific PSF, and we refer to this algorithm as "BRUTE" due to its one-to-one method of processing.

One of the biggest enigmas in modern physics is the minuscule, non-zero value of the cosmological constant. According to theoretical predictions based on quantum field theory, the actual value of the cosmological constant should be drastically larger, approximately 10^120 times greater than what is observed. The development of a complete theory of quantum gravity is expected to reconcile the significant disparity between theoretical expectations and empirical findings. In this research, we investigate the capacity of generalized uncertainty principle (GUP) models, which are grounded in phenomenological representations of quantum gravity, to resolve the cosmological constant anomaly. Specifically, we examine how these GUP models modify the phase space of quantum field theory and, in turn, influence the integration of zero-point energies in momentum space. Unfortunately, several issues suggest that the current forms of GUP models are unlikely to provide an adequate solution to the cosmological constant problem.

The interaction between the dark $U(1)_d$ sector and the Standard Model occurs via kinetic mixing between the dark photon field $Z_d^\mu$ and the SM's $U(1)_Y$ gauge field $B_\mu$. After symmetry breaking, the dark photon gains mass and mixes with the SM's neutral vector boson, resulting in parity-violating coupling with the Standard Model. This coupling is observable in both low-energy phenomenology and collider experiments, particularly in future high-energy Large Hadron-electron collider studies. A statistical analysis was performed using $\chi^2$ to compare variables associated with charge- and neutral-current processes. As a result, 90% confidence level contours were determined for the mixing parameter $\epsilon$, the dark photon mass $m_{Z_d}$, and its coupling strength $g_V$, effectively constraining these values up to $100$ GeV and $1.3$ TeV, respectively.

This research introduces MBURST, a groundbreaking multimodal system for enhancing audio-visual speech quality, grounded in the latest scientific findings on pyramidal cells in the prefrontal cortex and other brain regions. A key component, burst propagation, uses multiple strategies to address the credit assignment problem in a biologically inspired way: leveraging feedback to guide plasticity, combining forward and backward information across layers, approximating the strength of connections, and adjusting feedback signals. By learning the relationships between the distorted audio signal and visual cues, MBURST can effectively interpret and amplify meaningful speech components while suppressing noise. Trials conducted on the Grid Corpus and CHiME3 dataset demonstrate that MBURST produces comparable speech masking results to a benchmark model while exhibiting exceptional energy efficiency, achieving neuron firing rates up to 70% lower than the baseline. This energy-efficient capability makes MBURST a promising candidate for hearing aids and other embedded systems with sustainability concerns.

In autonomous driving, extreme weather conditions pose a significant threat to public safety due to their unpredictable nature, and climate change only exacerbates the issue by increasing the frequency of severe weather events such as heavy snowstorms. Despite efforts to enhance navigation in adverse conditions, there remains a need for standard metrics to assess the impact of precipitation on lidar sensor visibility, particularly in real-time. This chapter addresses this gap by introducing a novel metric, drawing on meteorological principles, to quantify lidar visibility loss in real-world scenarios. We validate this metric on the Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions dataset, investigating its correlation with the performance of a cutting-edge lidar-based localization algorithm, and examine the benefits of preprocessing point clouds prior to the localization process. The Iterative Closest Point algorithm surprisingly demonstrates robustness against snowfall, but sudden snow gusts can cause significant accuracy issues, highlighting the necessity for datasets focused on extreme weather events to understand their effects.

The area of a black hole's event horizon is considered to be quantized in terms of $l_P^2 \, (4 \ln 2) \, N$ and the degrees of freedom associated with this are limited and of a fermionic nature. The focus is on the black-hole entropy, $S_{BH}$, specifically examining its self-similar nature. By identifying a two-to-one correspondence between the black hole's states and the ordered partitions of $N$, a composition rule can be developed between the sub-states that constitute the entire configuration space. This leads to a unified understanding of black-hole self-similarity as a manifestation of the intrinsic self-similarity inherent in the ordered partitions of $N$. This is contrasted with the existing knowledge on quantum corrections that necessitate different statistical weights for various configurations.

MICADO, a key component of the ESO ELT, enables initial operation capabilities for high-definition imaging and multi-slit spectroscopy at near-infrared frequencies. The MICADO's PSF Reconstruction Team is pioneering the integration of a novel software solution, the first of its kind in the ESO telescope family, which reconstructs Point Spread Function (PSF) independently without relying on science data. Leveraging telemetry data from the MORFEO module, this tool accommodates both Single Conjugate and Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics systems. The PSF-R service will facilitate cutting-edge analysis for MICADO's imaging and spectroscopic data, providing essential updates on its current status following successful completion of the Final Design Review and presenting recent outcomes from simulated and real-world data acquired from analogous instruments.

We will utilize commutators to express $3\times 3$ matrices as the sum of terms that fulfill certain polynomial equations, and then apply this method to linear operators and module endomorphisms of infinite rank. Specifically, it has been shown that any bounded operator of an infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space can be represented as the sum of four automorphisms with a 3rd-order identity, and that every simple ring derived from the quotient of the endomorphism ring of an infinite-dimensional vector space by its maximal ideal is equivalent to the sum of three nilpotent subrings.

In the context of massless particle states, we identify the stabilizer group of the four-vector, also known as Wigner's little group, as the maximal solvable subgroup of the four-dimensional proper orthochronous Lorentz group, which is referred to as the Borel subgroup. For massless particles, states can be decomposed into distinct left- and right-handed chiral states, each controlled by specific maximal solvable subgroups of order two, denoted as ${\rm sol}_2^\pm$. By applying general representations of particle states, induced Lorentz transformations are established and utilized. The spin-flip contribution is demonstrated to be intimately connected with the presence of nonphysical spin operators.

To create a reliable static call graph, a balance must be struck between precision and soundness. However, most analysis methods used for call graph construction are not precise, resulting in inaccuracies. Researchers have introduced a new approach to address this issue by combining static analysis with machine learning-based call graph pruning. This involves training a model to capture structural features, which are then used to remove predicted false positives. Although machine learning has improved the process, these models are limited by their inability to consider source code semantics, making it difficult for them to accurately identify true and false positives. A novel approach, AutoPruner, uses both statistical and structural analysis to remove false positives in call graphs. AutoPruner employs a Transformer-based model to understand the semantic relationships between caller and callee functions. By fine-tuning a pre-trained model and extracting semantic features, AutoPruner can classify edges in the call graph more accurately than previous methods. Our evaluation on a benchmark dataset shows that AutoPruner significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches, achieving an improvement of up to 13% in F-measure when identifying false-positive edges.

This study focuses on examining the underlying structures of a particular subset of self-replicating graphs in the context of the sandpile group. Specifically, it examines Abelian sandpiles within Sierpinski gasket graphs under specific boundary conditions, leading to identification of the group's identity element and a recursive explanation of the group. Additionally, we analyze the behavior of Markov chains representing the sandpile process on these graphs and establish enhanced bounds on the rate at which these systems converge to equilibrium.

This paper employs local projections in high-dimensional settings to calculate impulse responses. We utilize a modified lasso technique, known as desparsified lasso, to estimate the local projections in high dimensions while excluding the target impulse response from penalties. We prove that the proposed estimator follows an asymptotic normal distribution under broad assumptions. Furthermore, we showcase the performance of our method in finite samples via a simulation study, as well as applying it to two significant case studies in the context of macroeconomic research, specifically focusing on monetary policy and the effects of government spending.

Real-time object detection on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles is a pressing challenge due to the processing limitations of edge computing devices such as Internet of Things nodes with integrated GPU. This paper introduces FasterX, a novel, lightweight deep learning architecture for real-time object detection on edge GPUs, based on the YOLOX model. We introduce a custom-designed PixSF head to improve detection of small objects, which can be further optimized using depthwise separable convolution. A SlimFPN layer is also developed to reduce network parameters while maintaining accuracy and speed. Additionally, an attention module is integrated into the head layer to enhance feature extraction, and label assignment and loss function improvements are made to mitigate category imbalance and box optimization issues on UAV datasets. Auxiliary heads are also introduced to facilitate online knowledge distillation and improve PixSF's position embedding and feature extraction capabilities. Experimental validation on NVIDIA's Jetson NX and Jetson Nano embedded platforms demonstrates that FasterX models strike a superior balance between accuracy and latency on the VisDrone2021 dataset compared to state-of-the-art models.

The current best adaptive optics systems have reached ground-based, diffraction-limited observation capabilities with high Strehl ratios, but utilizing this potential to its fullest extent necessitates a thorough understanding of the observed point spread function. The next-generation telescopes with 30-meter class sizes further highlight the importance of accurately characterizing this function. Consequently, researchers are now developing tools to accurately reconstruct the observed point spread function of AO systems, specifically known as point spread function reconstruction. In this context, our team has taken the lead in developing a point spread function-reconstruction service for the MICADO@ELT instrument, with the goal of making it universally applicable to various science cases. The proposed approach relies solely on the available telemetry and calibrations, bypassing the need for any data from science observations. Our reconstruction algorithm has now advanced to the point where we can test its performance on actual observations, and this presentation will focus on the reliability of our reconstructed point spread functions and the resulting uncertainties in scientific measurements for bright, on-axis observations. The application of our algorithm to real-world data taken from the SOUL+LUCI instrument on the LBT represents its first test case and serves as a benchmark for further testing. Notably, our point spread function-reconstruction algorithm has demonstrated the ability to accurately reconstruct the Strehl ratio and full-width at half maximum of the observed point spread functions with minimal errors of less than 2% and 4.5%, respectively. To further validate our results, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation using simulated data from an idealized science scenario.

In various applications such as plasma physics, astrophysics, chemistry and domain decomposition solvers, numerous independent and sparse linear system solves are commonly encountered. While it's possible to treat these as a single global linear system and utilize existing general-purpose solvers, this approach fails to exploit the systems' independent nature, resulting in suboptimal performance from Krylov solvers. Given the abundant number of independent processing elements present in modern accelerators such as GPUs, an efficient method involves tackling each system separately, allowing for optimal Krylov subspace utilization, reduced kernel launches, and minimized global communication. To this end, this research focuses on developing a portable linear system solver within PETSc that can execute the entire solution on a single processing element in a single kernel launch.

Bispectrum multipole moments can be used to quantify redshift space anisotropy, but their measurability depends on the level of statistical fluctuations present in galaxy surveys. We have developed a method to calculate the statistical fluctuations associated with measuring these bispectrum multipoles. Our study focuses on the specifications of a Euclid-style galaxy survey, evaluating two key parameters: the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which assesses the detectability of a multipole, and the rank correlation, which evaluates the degree of correlation between the measurement errors of different multipoles. Our analysis suggests that a Euclid-like survey has the potential to measure bispectrum multipoles up to a certain level of $\ell$, primarily for linear triangles and varying observation scales and redshifts. For the lower $\ell$ multipoles, a high SNR of over five can be achieved at larger scales, while higher $\ell$ values necessitate either smaller scales or increased bin sizes. Moreover, our findings indicate that error correlations are relatively weak for most multipole pairs across various triangle shapes, with a few exceptions, allowing for the potential combination of multiple multipole measurements to enhance the overall signal-to-noise ratio.

This research focuses on employing Reinforcement Learning in partially observable systems. It utilizes the Predictive State Representations model, a comprehensive framework that encapsulates other established models, such as Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. By representing states with future observation predictions and relying solely on observable data, the PSR model enables the development of novel model-based algorithms. One such algorithm is designed to learn a near-optimal policy, achieving a sample complexity that scales polynomially with the system's parameters, without explicitly depending on the size of the state and observation spaces. This algorithm's effectiveness is further enhanced by its compatibility with function approximation, allowing for efficient adaptation to systems with large state and observation spaces. The research demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves polynomial sample complexities comparable to the globally optimal policy in Predictive State Representations, marking a significant milestone. Furthermore, it demonstrates the versatility of the general theorem by applying it to derive sample complexity bounds for specific models, including POMDPs with various characteristics, such as low-rank latent transition and linear emission.

Improving fast matrix multiplication approximations holds great promise in reducing the cost of neural network inference. To enhance previous research, which suggested using table lookups by fitting a hash function from training data to replace costly multiplications, we introduce modifications tailored to deep learning inference, where training data and model weight matrices are accessible. We propose a fine-tuning procedure to speed up entire neural networks with minimal loss of accuracy. Furthermore, our approach is tested on a simple image classification task, demonstrating improvements over existing methods but acknowledging a significant drop in accuracy when compared to exact matrix multiplication. This work serves as a starting point for future investigations into accelerating inner products with faster nonlinear hashing techniques.

Explicit computations of Vafa-Witten invariants for 3-manifolds are conducted, paralleling Floer groups within Donaldson theory. Notably, the Vafa-Witten invariants are computed in specific instances of surgery procedures (Gluck twists, knot surgeries, log-transformations). Furthermore, the general structural properties of Vafa-Witten invariants for 3-manifolds are discussed, including the impact of the modular group, connections to Floer homology, infinite dimensionality, and the non-existence of instantons.

In models that expand on the Standard Model, specifically Two-Higgs-Doublet-Model-like extensions,  the heavy Higgs bosons that are expected are prime targets for analysis at high-energy colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider. For Higgs states that are sufficiently heavy, the  $SU(2)_{\mathrm{L}}$ symmetry has a significant impact on how these new scalars decay. Models with only additional Higgs doublets are expected to have fermionic decay channels dominate, but in some cases bosonic modes can produce clearer signals. However, if these models include singlet states and the singlet-dominated scalars are accessible, then Higgs-to-Higgs widths may end up being dominant. To interpret experimental data in a specific model, it's crucial to consider the impact of radiative corrections in the model. This paper looks into the bosonic decays of the heavy Higgs states that are dominated by doublets in the MSSM and the NMSSM at a full one-loop order, and how the  $SU(2)_{\mathrm{L}}$ symmetry affects these decays.

Even in a suspension of low to moderate density, where the particles are soft and don't experience friction, our findings show that discontinuous shear thickening can occur. We found that this phenomenon can be characterized as a switch-like transition in the behavior of the suspension under inertial conditions. Our kinetic theory model, which doesn't require any adjusted parameters, closely matches the results obtained from simulations based on the Langevin dynamics, and this agreement holds true across a broad range of particle volume fractions.

Small dam reservoirs contribute to sustainable development goals and climate targets, but lack consistent data on their locations. To fill this knowledge gap, an innovative approach involves automating dam reservoir extraction from globally accessible satellite images. This process can be considered a precise task of identifying water bodies in images and distinguishing dam reservoirs from natural water areas. We introduce a cutting-edge deep learning framework that breaks down dam reservoir extraction into two stages: segmenting water bodies from background terrain and identifying dam reservoirs among natural water bodies. Initially, a segmentation model separates water areas from land, and then a classification model predicts each water body as either a dam reservoir or a natural water body. To improve the first stage, we incorporate a learning method that uses triplets across images to address ambiguities between water areas and land regions. For the second stage, we employ a learning method that uses triplets from clusters to optimize the image representation space based on reservoir clusters. To facilitate further research, we create a benchmark dataset with earth imagery data and human-labelled reservoirs from river basins in West Africa and India. Extensive experiments were conducted on this benchmark, demonstrating superior performance of our method over existing approaches in water body segmentation, dam reservoir recognition, and joint dam reservoir extraction tasks.

Residual stress and elastic strain concentrations within microelectronic devices can impact their performance, durability, and radiation resistance. Characterizing these localized stress concentrations is challenging, as they occur on sub-micrometer scales, making traditional stress measurement techniques unsuitable. We present a non-destructive method utilizing synchrotron X-ray based differential aperture X-ray microscopy to analyze these stress concentrations in a depth-resolved manner. By applying this method, we mapped two-dimensional strain fields in a gallium nitride layer of high electron mobility transistors with high spatial resolution. Our analysis of strain fields in both pristine and irradiated HEMTs and a preliminary stress analysis show the distribution of stress components within the GaN layer. We observed that $\gamma$-irradiation leads to a notable decrease in the lattice plane spacing of GaN, which is attributed to radiation damage caused by components bonded to the GaN during irradiation.

Determining the performance of software AI-based medical devices under real-world variations is vital for ensuring their safety, efficiency, and usability before clinical implementation. Since medical device software is strictly regulated, and obtaining extensive medical data is challenging, we are developing a method to forecast the test accuracy of any given black-box model on an unlabeled dataset without modifying the original training process or making assumptions about the data source. We are proposing an innovative 'black-box' test estimation technique using conformal prediction and testing its efficacy on three medical imaging datasets under various clinical scenarios of data changes. Our goal is to help medical device manufacturers establish more consistent and practical evaluation methods, which in turn, can enhance the reliability and trustworthiness of AI-powered clinical tools.

We introduce a forward modeling technique for predicting galaxy redshift
distributions from photometric surveys without the need for spectroscopic data.
This framework consists of interconnected models that simulate galaxy evolution,
translate physical properties to photometry, and account for survey observation
processes, while explicitly addressing selection biases and redshift binning.
This method offers several benefits, including direct control over modeling
assumptions and a straightforward connection between photometric redshift
inference and galaxy evolution physics. Beyond redshift distributions, forward
modeling enables robust inference of galaxy population properties in general.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by estimating the redshift
distributions for GAMA and VVDS surveys and validate our results against
spectroscopic redshifts, achieving a bias of less than 0.003 in redshift
estimation for both surveys. Our baseline model accurately predicts redshift
distributions for GAMA and VVDS without hyper-parameter tuning, suggesting
that forward modeling can provide reliable redshift distribution inference for
future cosmological surveys, including those of Stage IV, with further
refinements.
