A biped walking robot model based on an inverted pendulum has been developed. It features two slender, hinged legs that enable stable movement on varied terrain. The robot's stride is generated through the pendulum motion of one leg standing upright, while the trailing leg moves in an articulated motion. The gait is feasible due to the legs alternating roles and the conservation of pendulum motion energy. By maintaining a consistent maximum leg angle during transitions and adjusting stride duration, the robot can navigate uneven surfaces and slopes. This solvable model accurately represents various bipedal motions and its closed-form solution is reversible in time. Furthermore, optimisation results have been obtained for the robot's gait speed as a function of its parameters.

Our investigation focuses on how insoluble surfactants affect the spatial and temporal changes of turbulent jets. Three-dimensional computer simulations are conducted, incorporating an interface-tracking method that accounts for Marangoni stresses resulting from surfactant concentrations. This study builds on our previous research examining vortex-surface interactions in surfactant-free conditions. The current analysis considers a broad range of Weber and elasticity numbers where vorticity is generated through surface deformation and surfactant-induced stresses. For the first time, we show the pivotal impact of Marangoni stresses, stemming from surfactant gradients, in the formation of three-dimensional, coherent vortex structures. These structures significantly influence the development of interfacial dynamics. Additionally, we provide theoretical equations explaining the factors influencing circulation production in three-dimensional, two-phase flows with surfactants and highlight the major contribution of Marangoni stresses.

To assess the effects of radiation on globular cluster formation, two turbulent giant molecular clouds are simulated colliding head-on. A sequence of idealized radiation-hydrodynamic simulations are carried out with and without radiation from stars or supernovae. We discover that a gravitationally bound cluster of approximately $10^5 M_\odot$ emerges within about three million years after a collision between giant molecular clouds weighing around $3.6 \times 10^5 M_\odot$. The cluster doesn't form from a single collapsing event but rather from the merger of local gas clumps and ongoing gas accretion. Ionizing radiation's momentum transfer suppresses gas collapse, while photoionization becomes effective as a sufficient number of stars form. In comparison, neglecting radiation feedback results in the cluster being roughly double in mass. Including extreme $\rm Ly\alpha$ feedback further increases this difference. When radiation feedback is included, supernovae explode after star-forming gas has dispersed, preventing the instant recycling of metal ejecta into new stars.

On considère une variété projective lisse définie sur un corps de nombres et $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0$. En conséquence, le groupe de Chow en codimension $2$ possède un sous-groupe de torsion fini, que Colliot-Thélène et Raskind ont déjà prouvé. Nous établissons des limites uniformes pour ce groupe fini lorsqu'il varie au sein d'une famille. 

Let K be a number field and X a smooth projective variety defined over K with H^2(X,Ω^1)=0. Colliot-Thelene and Raskind have previously shown that this results in a finite torsion subgroup in the codimension 2 Chow group. We establish uniform bounds for this finite subgroup as it varies over a family of varieties.

The presence of excess quasiparticles significantly impacts superconducting quantum devices, including qubits and quantum sensors. This study explores their behavior within phase-biased weak links, which feature multiple Andreev subgap states. By leveraging microwave resonators for parity state measurement, our theoretical analysis reveals a method to achieve nearly complete dynamical alignment within a specific parity state by delivering a tailored microwave pulse targeting a transition in the opposing parity state. Our findings are in line with recent research involving hybrid semiconducting nanowire Josephson junctions and offer practical advice for efficiently managing the parity state of Andreev qubits.

In this research, we broaden the applicability of established findings on $q$-solitons to encompass non-compact cases, thereby establishing their stationary and $q$-flat nature under specific constraints on the vector field and the curvature of the manifold. The paper's conclusions are exemplified by its application to various types of solitons, including obstruction solitons, Cotton solitons, and Bach solitons, highlighting the versatility of our theoretical framework.

Most binary star systems hosting exoplanets begin life within a densely populated star-forming environment that may induce significant changes to the binary-planet system's dynamics. We conducted computer simulations modeling gas giants orbiting within the gravitational influence of a low-mass binary companion, integrating the binary-planet system alongside a nearby cluster of stars. Approximately 10% of our simulated planetary systems experience instability due to cluster-induced perturbations that cause the binary's closest approach to collide with planets, resulting in planet-planet scattering and the loss of lower mass planets despite initially stable configurations. The chaos triggered by the cluster environment often leads to the loss of binary companions, causing these systems to resemble isolated stars hosting eccentric exoplanets. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrate how the cluster-driven evolution of binary orbits can give rise to planetary systems with misaligned axes, typically resulting from the planetary system's precession as a rigid disk under the influence of an inclined binary. Systems with the greatest spin-orbit angles are more likely to retain their binary companion and harbor multiple surviving planets.

Neural networks can approximate non-linear systems with great flexibility, whether these systems are represented explicitly through mathematical equations or as a black box. The Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) pioneered this concept in 2019 using rigorous mathematical theory. Following this breakthrough, researchers have developed a few other operators based on different approaches such as graph neural networks or Fourier transforms. When the governing equations of a system are unknown, neural operators rely on data-driven training, but if these equations are known, they can be incorporated into the training process to create more accurate physics-informed neural operators. Neural operators have a wide range of applications, including design problems, uncertainty quantification, and real-time inference, and can be used in complex systems by combining multiple pre-trained models. This review focuses on the DeepONet, the Fourier neural operator, the graph neural operator, and their variants, highlighting their utility in various computational mechanics applications like porous media, fluid mechanics, and solid mechanics.

Predicting emotions is crucial in mental health and emotion-driven computing, but it's a challenging task due to the complex interplay of factors such as physical health, mental well-being, and environmental influences. In this research, we exploit mobile sensing data to forecast happiness and stress, incorporating both individual physiological characteristics and external factors like weather and social connections. By leveraging phone data to create social networks and developing a machine learning framework that aggregates data from interconnected users, we can predict emotions for all network members. Our proposed architecture allows for seamless integration of social network affect prediction, efficiently handles dynamic social networks, and is scalable to large datasets. Our thorough evaluation demonstrates the benefits of incorporating social networks, and we also examine how graph topology affects the model's performance.

The irregular movement of a gas-liquid interface, such as during splashing or atomization, often creates intricate liquid structures within surrounding fluid. We investigate the application of skeletonization to determine the minimum amount of data required to describe the geometric features of these structures. By modifying a previously developed technique for coarsening multiphase flows while maintaining a sharp interface, we skeletonize a periodic liquid jet. This process involves spreading a numerical index and simultaneously moving the interfaces with it until they converge into a skeleton. The resulting skeleton represents the fundamental topology of the jet and we also track the extent to which the interface shifts (or the volume accumulated) during the process, which can be used to approximately reconstruct the jet. We examine various quantitative metrics to characterize and differentiate the skeletons, including standard morphometric analysis, such as branch length distribution, and a more complex representation called the Topology Morphology Descriptor (TMD), to achieve a compact description of the skeletons while retaining topological information.

The intricacy of Recommender Systems stems from their integration into larger applications and varied interfaces influencing user experience. Despite this, research primarily focuses on item ranking accuracy with inadequate assessment of RS performance in real-world settings. This narrow approach restricts RS long-term impact and renders them susceptible to unintended behavior like amplifying data prejudices. To address these issues, we introduce the EvalRS challenge, encouraging the development of open methodologies for evaluating RSs in practical environments.

Identifying interactions between people and objects is crucial for a comprehensive analysis of visual scenes. Notably, the spatial relationships between individuals and objects serve as vital clues for understanding their interactions. To this end, we present a novel graph convolutional network, SGCN4HOI, designed specifically for human-object interaction detection. This network leverages spatial connections between human and object keypoints to capture intricate interactions via graph convolutions. By integrating geometric, visual, and spatial features from human-object pairs, SGCN4HOI provides a richer understanding of their relationships. Moreover, to maintain the object's structural integrity and facilitate interaction detection, we introduce a skeleton-based object representation. Experimental evaluations on the V-COCO dataset demonstrate that SGCN4HOI outperforms existing pose-based methods and competes favorably with other approaches.

In Europe, the recent decades have witnessed a significant delay in electricity transmission expansion, despite its pivotal role in incorporating renewable energy sources into the energy system. A repurposed hydrogen network, built upon the existing fossil gas network, would address the demand for low-emission fuels and facilitate the balancing of wind and solar energy fluctuations across the continent, ultimately circumventing the necessity for power grid expansion. To examine this concept, we conducted a study on sector-coupled European energy systems with substantial renewable energy contributions and self-sufficient supply. Our simulations, spanning 181 regions and accounting for every third hour of a year, highlighted the benefits of a pan-continental hydrogen backbone. This infrastructure, connecting high-yield regions with demand centers and storage facilities, would result in up to 6% system cost reductions. Furthermore, up to 66% of this hydrogen network could be constructed using repurposed natural gas pipelines. Notably, the findings indicate that while hydrogen networks can partially substitute for power grid expansion, the two combined would yield the strongest cost savings of 12%.

Using the Dark Energy Survey's observations over three years along with external data, we constrain various extensions of the $\Lambda$CDM model, which involves the two-point correlation functions of weak gravitational lensing, galaxy clustering, and their cross-correlation. Our analysis is validated by simulated data and blind analysis of real data to ensure the robustness of our results. However, the constraining power is limited by the absence of accurate, non-linear predictions at our required precision level. We investigate the following models: dark energy with a time-dependent equation of state, non-zero spatial curvature, sterile neutrinos, modifications of gravitational physics, and a binned $\sigma_8(z)$ model to analyze structure growth. The results show that the dark energy equation of state is $(w_{\rm p}, w_a)= (-0.99^{+0.28}_{-0.17},-0.9\pm 1.2)$ at 68% confidence for the DES measurements alone and $(w_{\rm p}, w_a)= (-1.03^{+0.04}_{-0.03},-0.4^{+0.4}_{-0.3})$ for the combination of all data, indicating no significant evidence for physics beyond $\Lambda$CDM. In addition, we obtained constraints on curvature ($\Omega_k=0.0009\pm 0.0017$) and effective relativistic species ($N_{\rm eff}=3.10^{+0.15}_{-0.16}$) from external data. We also improved the upper bound on the mass of massive sterile neutrinos by a factor of three, resulting in 95% limits of $(\Delta N_{\rm eff},m_{\rm eff})\leq (0.28, 0.20\, {\rm eV})$. Furthermore, we constrained the changes to the lensing and Poisson equations, which are controlled by functions $\Sigma(k,z)$ and $\mu(k,z)$ respectively, to $\Sigma_0=0.6^{+0.4}_{-0.5}$ and $(\Sigma_0,\mu_0)=(0.04\pm 0.05,0.08^{+0.21}_{-0.19})$. Overall, our analysis shows that there is no significant evidence for physics beyond the $\Lambda$CDM model.

Schmidt's recent survey mapped equivalences between generalized bent functions, 
group-invariant Butson Hadamard matrices, and abelian splitting relative difference 
sets. We extend this equivalence network by exploring Butson matrices with cocyclic properties 
instead of strict group invariance, which has multiple practical uses, such as designing Boolean 
functions with expansions based on generalized partially bent functions, including scenarios 
where traditional bent functions cannot be constructed.

High-energy electron beams, which are extremely brief, with pulse lengths ranging from femtoseconds to picoseconds, provide a unique platform to investigate multiple active areas, including the dynamic behavior of molecules on an ultra-fast timescale and the effects of intense radiation on living tissues. This report outlines a simple approach for generating electron beams of the MeV class in ambient air by tightly focusing a high-powered infrared laser that emits in femtosecond bursts. The highest dose rate measured, which is 0.15 Gy per second, is greater than the annual radiation limit for any person and would cause significant harm in less than a second, necessitating strict radiation safety measures. Computer simulations of this phenomenon support the idea that the acceleration of electrons is caused by a powerful force that arises due to relativistic effects and confirm that the energy of the accelerated electrons aligns with experimental measurements. Additionally, this report explores the potential scalability of this method with improvements in high-powered lasers and suggests a possible path forward for developing radiation therapy techniques that involve brief pulses of high-intensity radiation.

We explore the concept of quantum speed limits to determine fundamental time scales governing the evolution of physical processes, establishing lower bounds for the rate of change in quantum states or the measurement of certain properties. Our work generalizes QSLs to describe the behavior of essential operator flows in physics, impacting both quantum and classical systems. We develop two types of quantum speed limits and investigate the transition point between them, demonstrating our findings with examples using a qubit and a random matrix Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we extend our research to analyze the time evolution of correlations and apply our results to provide calculable constraints on the dynamic response and precision of quantum systems operating outside equilibrium and the information used in quantum parameter estimation.

This research introduces a three-dimensional, cube-based robot that can be
reconfigured through pivoting with the aid of an electromagnet-based
mechanism. The development of actuation frameworks for self-reconfigurable
robots has been hindered by factors including cost, complexity, and assembly
requirements. To address this issue, the proposed actuation mechanism relies on
embedded electromagnets in each cube, generating repulsive and attractive forces
by creating oppositely or identically polarized pairs. Leveraging attraction and
repulsion enables the formation of hinges and pivoting maneuvers to voxelize the
robot's constituent modules, termed Electrovoxels. This concept is demonstrated
by creating fully untethered, three-dimensional self-reconfigurable robots that
demonstrate reconfiguration in both two and three dimensions. A thorough
description of the hardware design, pivoting framework, and reconfiguration
planning software is provided, along with an evaluation of the system's
electrical and dynamical characteristics to inform the development of scalable,
self-reconfigurable robots.

This paper focuses on the task of matrix recovery from noisy and incomplete data. Under specific assumptions, it demonstrates that a novel estimator, square-root matrix completion, attains optimal results in this task without requiring the noise variance as a parameter. The analysis of square-root matrix completion is linked to its connection with a nonconvex estimation method that constrains the rank of the matrix.

This article examines a linearized form of the Calderon problem for high-order polyharmonic operators, drawing inspiration from Calderon's foundational work. It establishes a uniqueness theorem for identifying up to gauge coefficients of a certain order by inverting a particular transform related to momentum rays.

Protoplanetary disks with irregular shapes provide a prime setting for the emergence of pressure traps. One major obstacle in the early planet formation process is the meter-sized hurdle, which severely restricts the growth timescale of planets. Several theories have been proposed to overcome this barrier, with pressure traps being a promising solution, allowing for the temporary suspension of planetesimal movement in specific disk regions where the pressure deviates from the general gradient. Despite their potential importance, the origins of pressure traps remain unclear, including their characteristic profiles. It is now understood that irregularly shaped disks are common in accretion disks, and we propose that such disks are responsible for the formation of pressure traps, which can aid in surmounting the meter-sized barrier. Our analysis explores the profile of pressure traps triggered by external torques and examines the implications for early planet formation in diverse environments, such as those surrounding binary stars and at the edges of disk gaps.

A comprehensive program for analyzing generalized parton distributions is introduced, utilizing a conformal moment expansion. The approach involves a universal parameterization strategy that effectively accommodates phenomenological parton distribution functions and lattice-derived generalized form factors. This parameterization can also be applied to direct lattice calculations of GPDs. Specifically, the analysis focuses on $t$-dependent parton distribution functions, which in the $\xi \to 0$ limit relate to generalized parton distributions. This strategy has the potential to be adapted for the $\xi \not = 0$ region and be used in conjunction with experimental data. An illustrative example featuring fitted generalized parton distributions is provided, highlighting quark transverse angular momentum densities and impact parameter space distributions within unpolarized and transversely polarized protons.

A key criterion in evaluating the compatibility of joint probability distributions with directed acyclic graphs is the d-separation criterion, which is based on conditional independences. This study focuses on developing a categorical framework for causal models and d-separation, leading to an abstract d-separation criterion. The proposed approach has significant advantages: it offers an intuitive criterion rooted in topological connections, and its implications extend beyond probability theory, encompassing deterministic and possibilistic networks. This enables a unified proof of the equivalence between local and global Markov properties and causal compatibility for various types of variables, including continuous, mixed, deterministic, and possibilistic.

Research into quantum phases of matter has been significantly enhanced by twisted multilayers of two-dimensional materials. The moire pattern resulting from the layers' relative twist creates long-wavelength effective potentials, which can cause electrons to localize. Although a wide variety of 2D materials exist, relatively few twisted heterostructures have been studied to date. In this work, we develop a first-principles continuum theory to examine the electronic bands in twisted Janus transition metal dichalcogenide homo- and hetero-bilayers. Our theory accounts for lattice relaxation, stack-dependent effective mass, and Rashba spin-orbit coupling. By generating and characterizing a large number of continuum models derived from DFT calculations, we find that moiré physics and emergent symmetries are influenced by the chemical composition, layer orientation, and twist angle. This results in the formation of unique electronic wavefunctions, including triangular, honeycomb, and Kagome networks. Furthermore, the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling, characteristic of these systems, can dominate the moiré bandwidth at small twist angles. This research enables the in-depth study of Janus twisted heterostructures, ultimately allowing for the discovery and control of novel electronic phenomena.

We explore the fundamental characteristics of the universe's earliest curvature through observations of dark matter substructures. By assuming a unique pattern in the universe's curvature at a specific scale, we simulate the development of the universe's large-scale structures, taking into account the uncertainties associated with how substructures interact with their surroundings. Our analysis reveals a more precise constraint on the curvature of the universe's early stages based on the number of small galaxies within our own galaxy and the patterns of stars observed in the galaxy's outer regions. This research yields a new limit on the amplitude of this unique curvature feature, suggesting a value of approximately 10^{-7} for a particular scale. Moreover, our findings indicate that this feature can amplify the signals of dark matter detection, potentially increasing their detectability by a factor of up to 10^4.

A retinal trait, encapsulating a specific aspect of a retinal image, can be condensed into a single numerical value, facilitating further analysis with statistical methods. Nevertheless, this simplification poses significant challenges due to the complexity of images. Consequently, existing methods to calculate retinal traits often involve intricate multi-step processes suitable only for high-quality images, resulting in substantial data loss. We contend that these pipelines can be approximated with a more straightforward, robust method. To address this, we propose Deep Approximation of Retinal Traits (DART), which uses a deep neural network to forecast the output of a complex pipeline on high-quality images based on synthetically degraded versions. We applied DART to retinal fractal dimension analysis and achieved exceptional correlation with existing results, even on severely degraded images. This suggests that our method has the potential to significantly reduce data loss in future research. Furthermore, our approach can efficiently process images at a rate of over 1,000 images per second, making it a promising tool for retinal analysis.

Fast-moving ejecta from binary neutron star mergers are expected to collide with the interstellar medium at relativistic speeds.  We have developed an analytical model for the synchrotron radiation generated by collisionless shocks in this scenario.  The model applies to ejecta with mass distributions characterized by a "shallow" power-law at low speeds and a "steep" power-law at high speeds.  Our model accurately reproduces the evolution of the radiation flux over time, including the period of deceleration.  This is a significant improvement over earlier models that overestimated the flux by a factor of ten.  This model will be useful for analyzing data from future observations of the non-thermal radiation from binary neutron star mergers, including the merger event GW170817, which may be visible for approximately 10,000 days.

Icicles grown from slightly contaminated water exhibit unique ripples. These ripples consistently display a similar wavelength and are thought to be a consequence of morphological instability. In an experiment using artificially grown icicles and impurities, such as fluorescent dye, we demonstrate that certain impurities get trapped within the icicle's interior. These impurities form inclusions that are organized into chevron patterns, mirroring the ripple formations. A distinct substructure consisting of curved shapes is observed within these chevrons. We also investigated the crystal grain structure of icicles, comparing samples with and without added impurities. Our findings provide a comprehensive analysis of growth patterns within icicles and discuss their significance in understanding the underlying mechanism behind ripple formation.

The significance of daily, informal conversations to both our mental and social development is being overlooked in favor of a narrow, one-dimensional understanding of quality conversations. Research focusing solely on interaction dynamics has often equated higher quality with reduced small talk, while studies examining the overall interaction experience have indirectly explored quality through separate concepts such as rapport and engagement. In this study, we address this gap by developing a comprehensive framework for conversation quality that incorporates the cooperative aspects of shared communication spaces. We employ a multi-faceted approach, creating and validating two measurement tools for perceived conversation quality at both the individual and group levels. By considering the aggregate impressions of external observers and analyzing the publicly available MatchNMingle dataset of spontaneous social interactions, we identify key behavioral features that contribute to perceived conversation quality, including smaller group sizes, equal opportunities for speaking, fewer interruptions, and synchronized physical coordination.

This work presents BRILLsson, a new binary neural network-based model for non-semantic speech applications that requires minimal data and computational resources.
The BRILLsson model is trained using a novel distillation process that leverages a large TRILLsson model with significantly reduced data input.
As a result, BRILLsson models can be as small as 2MB in size and operate at speeds below 8ms, making them ideal for use in low-power wearables.
We tested BRILLsson on multiple speech tasks and showed that despite its compact size and rapid processing, the model performs at a comparable level to its larger counterparts.

Researchers in fairness for machine learning have agreed on several key criteria that provide precise definitions of when an ML model is considered fair. Yet, these established criteria have significant drawbacks. We highlight four major limitations of these formal fairness metrics and propose an extension to performative prediction incorporating a distributionally robust optimization goal.

The possibility of primordial black holes (PBHs), created in the early universe, retaining electric charge up to the present day is explored. Calculations indicate that PBHs would initially have a non-zero charge resulting from both random variations and particle collisions in the early universe, although this charge may rapidly dissipate. However, it's found that magnetic fields produced by rotating black holes can prevent charge dissipation, regardless of PBH mass. Moreover, highly spinning, charged PBHs can generate magnetic fields capable of counteracting charge dissipation due to the Schwinger effect and Hawking emission for PBHs with masses greater than 1 kg. These mechanisms enable PBHs to retain their charge for extended periods. Later, it's concluded that charged dark matter haloes can bestow a net negative charge on PBHs. Calculations yield average charge to mass ratios of -10^-32 C/kg and -10^-22 C/kg for two windows of masses where PBHs can make up all dark matter. This charge is lower than the Schwinger limit, making dark matter slightly non-neutral. Considering initial charge, possible shielding against discharge, and late time negative charge accumulation, it's shown that PBHs of all masses could have a net charge, several orders of magnitude lower than the maximum limit for RN PBHs and even extremal Planck mass PBHs. The latter have the potential to be stable, charged relics, making up all dark matter in the universe.

Capturing the mass distribution of complex galaxy-scale gravitational lenses has become increasingly challenging, as high-resolution imaging data cannot be accurately represented by simple analytical models. To address this issue, we've developed a novel multiscale method using wavelets that effectively handles a broad range of spatial, mass, and morphological scales. This approach was tested using simulated Hubble Space Telescope imaging of various strong lens types, including localized dark matter, Gaussian random fields, and galaxy-scale multipoles. Our results demonstrate the method's ability to accurately recover these complex structures. This achievement is made possible by combining gradient-informed optimization with machine learning, which allows for simultaneous sampling of model parameters and their posterior distributions. Our framework integrates analytical, pixelated, and machine learning modeling paradigms into a single, modular system, ideal for fast analysis of large lens datasets. All methods are now available in the Herculens package.

This study investigates how the variation of the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$) with baryon chemical potential impacts hydrodynamic simulations qualitatively. The influence of this variable relationship has been largely unexamined in hydrodynamic simulations, with prior research often focusing solely on temperature dependence or assuming a constant effective viscosity. To address this gap, this work explores the effects of a generalized $\eta/s$ that depends on both temperature and baryon chemical potential within the SMASH-vHLLE hybrid approach. In an effort to minimize the impact of the equation of state used in the hydrodynamic model, the $\eta/s$ parameterization directly relates to the system's energy density and baryon number density. This parameterization is informed by transport coefficients in the hadronic phase and pQCD results, allowing for a nuanced understanding of the density dependence. This study examines the effect of density dependence on the system size, energy, and observables within the RHIC-BES energy range and compares the results with experimental data. The results indicate that a non-constant $\eta/s$ has a minimal impact on the elliptic flow, except in the early stages of the collision, and demonstrate the potential of the proposed parameterization as a proxy for the shear viscosity in the hadronic transport stage.

We examine the transverse momentum weighted Sivers asymmetries in reactions involving a transversely polarized proton target. This includes analyzing a weighted asymmetry in charged hadron production during semi-inclusive deeply inelastic scattering and another in the Drell-Yan process involving a pion-proton collision. Due to the integration of transverse momentum, these asymmetries can be expressed as a product of transverse-momentum dependent parton distribution and fragmentation functions. We have performed a numerical calculation using established parametrizations for these functions to predict weighted Sivers asymmetries in SIDIS and Drell-Yan processes at the COMPASS experiment's kinematics and compared them with existing data. Our calculation for SIDIS process asymmetry aligns with recent experimental measurements from COMPASS. However, the high uncertainty in current Drell-Yan data necessitates more precise experimental data to confirm the sign change property of the Sivers function and to constrain the Sivers function for sea quarks.

Helium-3 is now a crucial subject of research in fundamental physics, nuclear and atomic structure, magnetometry, metrology, chemistry, and medicine. Its nuclear magnetic resonance probes have the potential to become a new standard for absolute magnetometry. However, a high-accuracy value for the helium-3 nuclear magnetic moment is required, which has yet to be directly and accurately measured. In our investigation, we examined the ground-state hyperfine structure of helium-3 in a Penning trap, enabling us to directly measure its nuclear g-factor, zero-field hyperfine splitting, and electron g-factor. These results allowed us to determine the nuclear g-factor of the bare helium-3 nucleus. Our findings provide the first direct calibration for helium-3 NMR probes, achieving a significant improvement in precision compared to previous indirect measurements. The measured zero-field hyperfine splitting has also enabled us to precisely determine the Zemach radius of helium-3.

The accelerated failure time (AFT) model assumes a logarithmic relationship between failure times and covariates, offering a direct interpretation of covariate effects on failure times. In contrast to traditional survival models that focus on hazard functions, the AFT model is flexible and robust, making it a promising alternative to the Cox model for censored failure time data. However, AFT models often assume linear predictors, and limited research has been conducted on addressing nonlinearity in mean modeling. To address this, deep neural networks (DNNs) can be applied in AFT models, taking advantage of their ability to handle nonlinearity and complexity. By combining DNNs with a sub-sampling technique and a Gehan-type loss function, we propose a novel model called DeepR-AFT, which exhibits superior performance in simulations and real-world applications.

Gaia Data Release 3 has brought forth an extensive array of new data products for the scientific community, with astrophysical parameters playing a key role in this release. The parameters were generated by Apsis, part of the Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the astrophysical parameters in Gaia Data Release 3, including the methods used to create them. In Apsis, we utilized mean BP/RP and RVS spectra, astrometry, and photometry to derive a range of parameters, including classifications, probabilities, interstellar medium characteristics, distances, and extinction maps for vast numbers of sources, as well as redshifts for quasars and galaxies. We also applied unsupervised classification to analyze millions of outlier sources. The parameters cover a wide array of stellar properties, including temperatures, evolutionary stages, chemical abundances, and activity levels, for a substantial number of sources. This comprehensive database represents the most extensive and homogeneous collection of astrophysical parameters available to date, and it is based entirely on Gaia data.

This study investigates the concept of weak universality for the two-dimensional fractional nonlinear wave equation. It begins by identifying a key criterion that determines whether a sequence of high-degree potential Hamiltonians can converge to the fractional Φ2^4 as its invariant measures. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the corresponding wave dynamics of these sequences will converge to the renormalized cubic wave equation, provided that the fractional index remains below a certain threshold that is independent of the nonlinearity's degree. Notably, this extension generalizes the findings of Gubinelli-Koch-Oh (2018), which relied on local Cauchy theory with supercritical nonlinearities, to a scenario where such a theory is lacking.

Top Two algorithms, which were developed to improve upon Thompson sampling for multi-armed bandit models, specifically for parametric distributions, have achieved success by randomly choosing between a top-performing 'leader' arm and a contender 'challenger' arm to sample next. Although Top Two algorithms empirically outperform other methods, their theoretical guarantees of identifying the best arm have been limited to scenarios where the arm distributions are Gaussian with known variances. However, this paper provides a general analysis that reveals beneficial characteristics of the 'leader,' 'challenger,' and the (possibly non-Gaussian) distribution of the arms. Consequently, this analysis enables the derivation of theoretically validated Top Two algorithms for identifying the best arm under bounded distributions, and it demonstrates that the selection method inherited from Thompson sampling can be replaced with alternative approaches, such as choosing the empirical best arm.

We develop a relativistic theory to analyze the spin density matrices of vector mesons utilizing Kadanoff-Baym equations within the closed-time-path formalism. Our approach provides a robust foundation for calculating spin-related observables like the $\rho_{00}$ element. Specifically, we express $\rho_{00}$ for $\phi$ mesons as a product of momentum and space-time dependent factors. Notably, we find that at lower energies, $\rho_{00}$ is predominantly influenced by the $\phi$ fields that independently polarize strange quarks and antiquarks, analogous to the effects of electromagnetic fields. A key insight is that the $\phi$ meson wave function exhibits correlations between the fields responsible for quark and antiquark polarization. This correlation manifests as non-vanishing contributions to $\rho_{00}$ arising from squared fields, despite strong space-time fluctuations. By examining the fluctuations of strong force fields through $\rho_{00}$ in quarkonium vector mesons, we can gain insight into the fundamental properties of quantum chromodynamics.

To develop high-performing sequential recommenders that can adapt to different scenarios, researchers have introduced a range of sequence representation learning (SRL) techniques to model user behavior patterns. Most existing SRL methods rely heavily on item IDs to build sequence models, which can capture user preferences but struggle with cross-scenario applications due to their explicit reliance on IDs. To address this limitation, a novel universal sequence representation learning approach called UniSRec is proposed, utilizing item descriptions to generate transferable representations across multiple domains. This approach involves a lightweight item encoding architecture and two contrastive pre-training tasks to learn universal sequence representations. The pre-trained UniSRec model can then be effectively applied to new recommendation domains or platforms in an efficient manner, either inductively or transductively, and its performance is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets. The code and pre-trained model for UniSRec are available on GitHub for further reference.

The Graph Neural Network's capacity to integrate graph information has led to its extensive use in data analysis. Nevertheless, its expressive power has only been evaluated for tasks at the graph level, not at the node level, which includes node classification. In this paper, we investigate the expressive capabilities of GNNs for this classification task, a problem that can be viewed as function interpolation. Specifically, we have established a method to determine the number of weights and layers necessary for a GNN to approximate a band-limited function in d-dimensional space. The results reveal that GNNs require fewer weights to achieve the same approximation accuracy compared to fully connected neural networks. In fact, GNNs can approximate a discretized band-limited signal using only O((log ε^−1)^d) weights, achieved with O((log ε^−1)^d) training samples. This finding was made possible by drawing parallels between the GNN architecture and the classical sampling theorems, a novel approach in this area of study.

In various fields, sequential data often have varying lengths, with some sequences being exceptionally lengthy. As a critical tool in modeling, neural attention mechanisms should be able to capture long-range dependencies within these sequences. Unfortunately, many existing attention-based neural networks are restricted to short input sequences or require the use of chunking or padding to ensure a uniform input length. We propose a novel neural building block, referred to as ChordMixer, which enables the modeling of attention for sequences of diverse lengths. Each ChordMixer component comprises a position-wise transformation layer and an element-wise multilayer perceptron layer. By iteratively combining these blocks, a robust network architecture emerges that effectively blends input signals with target outputs. Our ChordMixer approach has been evaluated on the synthetic addition task, long-form document classification, and DNA sequence-based taxonomy categorization, resulting in significant performance improvements compared to other attention-based models.

To achieve domain generalization for unseen domains, it's essential to learn domain-invariant feature representations that capture an object's inherent characteristics. Recent studies on weakly supervised vision-language models have demonstrated their potential for semantic understanding by generalizing object traits across diverse domains. However, when multiple source domains are involved, the cost of annotating each image becomes prohibitively high, hindering the direct application of these models for optimal generalization. Inspired by this challenge, we investigate the potential of leveraging multimodal information from pre-trained networks to enhance domain generalization. To this end, we propose INDIGO, a straightforward method that combines the intrinsic multimodality in pre-trained models with visual modality to improve test-time generalization to unseen domains. We demonstrate INDIGO's effectiveness on various domain generalization settings and achieve state-of-the-art performance on unseen domains, providing a comprehensive analysis to deepen the understanding of INDIGO's mechanisms.

Current navigation systems heavily rely on standalone inertial sensors, particularly during periods of no external signal availability. During these intervals, the performance of these sensors degrades over time due to noise from instrumental sources, especially in low-cost consumer-grade inertial sensors. To counter this issue, model-based estimation techniques are often employed to reduce noise levels and enhance meaningful information, thereby improving the overall navigation solution. However, guaranteeing the optimality of these methods can be challenging due to variations in sensor performance resulting from manufacturing quality, process noise modeling, and calibration precision. Existing literature predominantly features model-based inertial denoising models, but recent studies suggest data-driven approaches, primarily for denoising gyroscope measurements. Accelerometer denoising tasks, however, present additional challenges due to the unknown gravity projection on the accelerometer axes. To address this, we introduce several learning-based approaches and compare their performance against prominent denoising algorithms, assessing noise removal efficiency followed by a stationary coarse alignment procedure. The benchmarking results obtained from field experiments reveal that learning-based models outperform traditional signal processing filtering techniques; the non-parametric kNN algorithm surpasses all state-of-the-art deep learning models examined; and denoising techniques can not only facilitate pure inertial signal reconstruction but also yield significant reductions in navigation-related errors, up to one order of magnitude.

We investigate the strong gravitational lensing effect surrounding rotating black holes in alternative gravity theories. By computing the deflection angle of strong gravitational lensing, we assess key observables including image locations, distances, magnification, and time discrepancies between relativistic images of rotating black holes across different theories. Our findings suggest that differences in image locations and distances between modified gravity and general relativity are more pronounced in the SgrA* black hole compared to M87*, whereas time discrepancies between modified gravity and general relativity are shorter in SgrA* than in M87*. By examining strong gravity regime observables, we can differentiate between modified gravity and general relativity. We also analyze the shadow observables of rotating black holes using the EHT's angular shadow radius measurements for supermassive black holes M87* and SgrA*. By applying these observations, we calculate the ranges for modified gravity parameters, establishing an upper limit constraint of $0.350\lesssim\alpha_{\rm up}\lesssim 0.485$ for M87* and $0.162 \lesssim \alpha_{\rm up} \lesssim 0.285$ for SgrA*, related to black hole spins. This constraint is the first obtained from EHT observations on the angular shadow radius, offering a tighter constraint compared to the one derived from the S2 star's orbital precession.

We investigate the multinomial coefficients and their recurrence relations within generalized quantum deformed algebras, and develop the $\mathcal{R}(p,q)$-deformed multinomial probability distribution and its negative counterpart. The recurrence relations are derived, and we identify specific instances from our general framework that correspond to known quantum algebras in the literature.

Following the discovery of superconductive twisted bilayer graphene, a new area of study known as twistronics emerged, revealing the intricate properties of moiré systems. Our research uncovers a surprising aspect in boron nitride twisted bilayers: for a specific moiré periodicity, five distinct stacking configurations are possible, preserving hexagonal symmetry. We introduce a new system to identify and label these stacking sequences and their respective twist angles in a bilayer system. Utilizing density functional theory, we analyze the evolution of the band structure in response to varying twist angles across the five boron nitride stacking sequences. Notably, our findings indicate an indirect gap across all twist angles and stacking configurations, as well as specific structural features common to each stacking sequence regardless of the twist angle.

Deep neural network interpretability methods often focus on how changes in the input affect the model's output, usually measured through gradients or modifications of them. A few methods also provide a model-agnostic perspective on what drives a prediction. We suggest and experimentally verify that considering the local shape of the model's parameter space relative to the input can lead to more accurate post-hoc explanations. To this end, we developed "geometrically-guided integrated gradients," an interpretability technique based on the gradient calculation along a straight line as in integrated gradient methods but now incorporating multiple scaled versions of the input to capture the optimal contribution of each input. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over traditional methods, and to improve confidence, we recommend combining it with a novel "model perturbation" test alongside the conventional "model randomization" check.

Fluorescence angiography, a technique for identifying optimal tissue perfusion, has shown impressive potential for minimizing anastomotic leaks during surgeries. Yet, its widespread adoption is hindered by the subjective nature of interpreting fluorescent signals, which leads to significant variability between different surgeons. To overcome this limitation, an AI-powered algorithm was developed to classify colonic tissue as perfused or not perfused based on intraoperative fluorescence angiography data.

A machine learning model based on Resnet architecture was trained using a dataset comprising fluorescence angiography videos from colorectal resections at a tertiary medical facility. Frames depicting fluorescent and non-fluorescent colon segments were utilized to train the classification model. Validation of the algorithm was conducted using frames from patients not included in the initial training set, both from the same equipment and different camera sources.

The performance metrics of the trained model revealed a 100% accuracy rate on the training set and an 80% accuracy rate on the validation set. Saliency maps were employed to analyze the model's output and a decision boundary was established based on the tissue classification results. 

A convolutional neural network was successfully trained and validated using a large dataset of frames from 7 patients and an independent dataset of frames from 14 patients, totaling 1790 and 24 frames respectively. 

Automated tissue classification using intraoperative fluorescence angiography has been achieved with high accuracy. This development enables surgeons to standardize the application of this technique, thereby reducing variability between surgeons. A user-friendly web-based app was created to facilitate the deployment of this algorithm.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) prove effective for identifying food items due to their ability to learn complex visual patterns. However, existing CNNs struggle with distorted images, which poses a significant challenge. Therefore, researchers developed a novel ensemble approach, referred to as a generalized specialist, that equips a model with two distinct skill sets: the ability to recognize pristine images and a specialized ability to classify images affected by a specific type of distortion. To achieve this, the generalized specialist approach combines data augmentation with a technique called RQMixUp, which generates synthetic images by randomly mixing clean and distorted images. This process allows the ensemble to learn from various distortion levels, with each model in the ensemble specializing in a specific area of distortion. The outputs from these diverse experts are then combined to improve classification accuracy, all without incurring additional costs. The proposed method is flexible and can be easily adapted to a wide range of supervised CNNs for transfer learning purposes. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the generalized specialist approach in improving the classification of distorted images while maintaining high performance on pristine images, as demonstrated through experiments using real-world food databases.

We introduce a computationally efficient technique to estimate Bayesian method predictive risks for various loss functions without excessive computational overhead. Our method leverages posterior covariance and yields predictors of Gibbs and plug-in generalization error. Additionally, we establish theoretical justifications for the proposed method, highlighting the relationships between the information criterion for wide applicability, Bayesian sensitivity analysis, and the infinitesimal jackknife approximation of Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation. Furthermore, the potential application of this method to private learning is also explored.

For certain differential operators defined by constant coefficients and positive-definite symbols in d-dimensional space, we examine a specific semigroup and its corresponding convolution kernel, which reveals unexpected large-time behavior that cannot be derived from basic scaling assumptions. Using a simple example, we develop a method to analyze the large-time asymptotics of this kernel and demonstrate the robustness of these results to higher-order perturbations, with applications to understanding convolution powers of certain functions on a complex Z-space lattice, marking the beginning of our research into this subject. However, deriving off-diagonal upper bounds for the convolution kernel remains an open challenge.

In the Heisenberg chain with a power-law exchange, we find that when the spin anisotropy reaches a specific threshold, the system demonstrates nearly ballistic spin transport along with persistent fermionic excitations up to exceptionally long periods, through an examination of spin domains, spin conductivity, and conserved operators' dynamics, effectively bridging two well-known models with purely ballistic transport.

A LieYRep pair, consisting of a Lie-Yamaguti algebra and its representation, is studied in this research, where the authors develop its cohomology theory, identify linear deformations using the second cohomology group, and define relative Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures. The paper investigates properties of these structures and finds that certain conditions lead to pairs of compatible relative Rota-Baxter operators. It also establishes an equivalence between r-matrix-Nijenhuis and Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures within Lie-Yamaguti algebras.

Modal logic's language can express first-order conditions on Kripke frames. 
Henrik Sahlqvist's classic finding shows a subset of modal formulas for which first-order equivalents can be found through an algorithmic approach. 
Researchers have expanded on this work to more complex modal languages. 
In this paper, we extend this concept to Linear-time Temporal Logic (LTL), a widely used language for temporal specifications, which adds temporal operators to basic modal logic. 
The increased complexity of LTL affects the class of formulas with first-order equivalents. 
Here, we identify a significant subset of LTL formulas built from modal operators, and prove that they correspond to first-order frame conditions.

Recovering 3D scene structures and camera poses using Structure-from-Motion is complicated by duplicate scene structures that appear visually similar, leading to incorrect camera and structure recoveries. To address this issue, existing studies often rely on external constraints or inference from two-view geometries and feature points. In contrast, this research leverages high-level scene information - specifically spatial context within local regions - to inform the reconstruction process. A new concept called track-community is introduced, where communities comprise groups of tracks that represent local scene segments. By using a community detection algorithm to segment the scene, potential ambiguities are identified and corrected by analyzing neighborhood tracks for pose consistency. The approach then reconstructs partial scenes within each segment and combines them using a novel cost function that considers 3D correspondences and relative camera poses. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in overcoming reconstruction failures caused by visually similar structures and merging partial reconstructions accurately.

To address dataset bias in deep learning, particularly in image classification, a new method has been developed to interactively guide a classifier's focus on specific image areas designated by users, reducing the impact of co-occurring biases and enhancing the model's transferability and interpretability. A key innovation of this system is its interactive design, allowing users to simply click on images to mark regions of interest. To further optimize the system's performance, an active learning strategy was introduced to significantly reduce the number of required annotations. The effectiveness of this system was demonstrated through both numerical analysis and user studies across multiple datasets, yielding superior results with reduced labor and costs compared to existing methods that rely on extensive polygon-based segmentation. The experiments confirmed that the proposed system is efficient, reasonable, and reliable, even in biased datasets.

We introduce Hyper-pool, an offline analytical algorithm for ride-pooling that maximizes the efficiency of shared transportation. Building on our previous ride-pooling algorithm ExMAS, we developed two new demand-side algorithms to further aggregate individual trip requests into compact and attractive shared rides. These algorithms generate stop-to-stop rides with a single pick-up and drop-off point optimal for all passengers and subsequently bundle these rides into hyper-pooled rides that closely resemble public transportation operations. Our approach uses a bottom-up framework, incrementally increasing the pooling level to maintain attractiveness at each aggregation stage. Hyper-pool produces the set of attractive pooled rides for a given travel demand, is publicly available, and suitable for large-scale demand datasets, opening new possibilities for ride-pooling optimization. Our Amsterdam case study demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness by pooling over 220 travelers into 40 compact hyper-pooled rides with an average occupancy of 5.8 passengers per vehicle.

To efficiently explore large numbers of candidate neural architectures and identify the most suitable one, researchers often use specific strategies to estimate their performance in a short amount of time. However, the effectiveness of these strategies varies depending on several factors including accuracy and query time. This research presents a new technique called EmProx Score, which shares similarities with Neural Architecture Optimization (NAO) in using an encoder-decoder framework to map candidate architectures to a continuous vector space. EmProx Score estimates the performance of candidates based on the proximity of their embedding vectors to those of well-performing architectures, using weighted k-Nearest Neighbors. The proposed method achieves comparable accuracy to the MLP-based performance predictor in NAO, but trains nearly nine times faster. Additionally, EmProx Score exhibits better or comparable accuracy to other existing strategies, while requiring significantly less training time - five to eighty times faster in some cases.

Recent studies in federated learning have discovered that utilizing large batches can accelerate convergence rates but incurs additional computational overhead in comparison to smaller batches. To mitigate this issue, a novel unified framework called FedAMD has been developed. FedAMD differentiates participant groups into anchor and miner groups based on time-varying probabilities. Participants in the anchor group compute their gradients using large batches, which serve as their objectives. Meanwhile, clients in the miner group perform multiple local updates using serial mini-batches, with their progress indirectly regulated by the overall goal derived from the average of the anchor clients' objectives. Consequently, the miner group achieves an update trajectory that closely approximates the global minimum. FedAMD has been found to converge at a rate of $O(1/\epsilon)$ for non-convex objectives when an anchor client is sampled with a constant probability. This is significantly more efficient than the state-of-the-art BVR-L-SGD, which converges at a rate of $O(1/\epsilon^{3/2})$. Moreover, FedAMD reduces the communication overhead to at least $O(1/\epsilon)$. The effectiveness of FedAMD has been empirically confirmed through real-world dataset evaluations, demonstrating its superiority over existing algorithms.

Current methods for evaluating the quality of natural language requirements rely heavily on factors such as passive voice and sentence length, which can indicate defects in the development process. Despite these efforts, the field of quality factors for textual requirements lacks a unified framework, hindering a thorough understanding of existing research and effective utilization of these factors. To bridge this gap, we propose an ontology for quality factors, which comprises a framework outlining key elements and a publicly accessible database. By applying a structured methodology to a comprehensive review of 105 primary studies, we establish a foundation for the ontology and accompanying web interface. Our contribution aims to facilitate collaboration among researchers in refining and updating this knowledge base, ultimately shaping a shared understanding of requirements quality factors and guiding future research in the field.

When examining the cascade decay $H\to Z^\ast(\to\tau^+\tau^-)+Z^\ast(\to\tau^+\tau^-)$ for identical particles and leptons, the mass impact is more pronounced by the gauge boson's off-shellness. Since $p_a^2$ and $p_b^2$ dictate the problem's scale, particularly within the range $4m_\tau^2\le p_a^2,p_b^2\le (m_H-2m_\tau)^2$, lepton mass effects become significant near the threshold of these off-shell decays. This study calculates the rates and decay distributions for single angles, and compares them with those from non-identical particle decays $H\to Z^\ast(\to e^+e^-)+Z^\ast(\to\mu^+\mu^-)$ where lepton masses are negligible.

Gaia Data Release 3 has introduced a wealth of new data products that can greatly benefit the astronomical community, particularly in determining the astrophysical characteristics of half a billion stars. This study showcases the high quality of these data products and demonstrates their potential applications in various astrophysical contexts. By integrating data from Gaia DR3 and cross-verifying results against external data and the Gaia catalogue itself, we have produced six uniform datasets of high-quality astrophysical parameters for stars across different regions of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Three of these samples span a wide range of characteristics, covering young, massive stars, FGKM-type stars, and ultra-compact dwarf galaxies. In addition, we have identified 15,740 genuine carbon stars, 5,863 solar-analogues, and provided the first comprehensive set of stellar parameters for the Spectro Photometric Standard Stars. The OBA sample is particularly useful for analyzing the rotation curve of the Milky Way, while the FGKM sample can be utilized to study known exoplanet systems. Furthermore, we used the properties of the FGKM stars to determine the ages of their unseen companions, and predicted the colors of the Sun in various passbands using the solar-analogue sample.

High-intensity electron beams used in FLASH radiotherapy are gaining significance in various preclinical cancer treatment trials, yet a real-time dose monitoring device remains absent due to the dose rate used. In this work, we have designed and developed a beam current transformer (BCT), starting with selecting the ferromagnetic component, shielding, and creating a front-end electronics circuit to optimize low-noise detection. Our BCT prototype measures a wide range of beam currents from 1.2 microamperes to 200 milliamps, possesses a rapid rise time of under 20 nanoseconds, and exhibits a minimal signal droop of less than 0.05% per microsecond. Initial on-site measurements are presented. Our ultimate goal is to merge the real-time BCT system with an ionisation chamber monitoring beam shape and position, thereby establishing a reliable dose monitoring system.

A novel method has been devised for single-channel partial wave analysis dependent on energy, which eliminates the need for creating and solving elaborate theoretical models of two-body reactions, instead leveraging fundamental principles of analyticity. Traditional methods to obtain energy-dependent two-body partial waves (multipoles) involved developing a theoretical model, solving it, and fitting free parameters to data before reconstructing partial waves from reaction amplitudes. By contrast, the new approach proposes decomposing partial waves in Laurent form, where the regular part is expanded in a series of a conformal variable known as Pietarinen expansion. Parameters (pole parameters and Pietarinen coefficients) are then adjusted to align with a comprehensive collection of observables for a particular reaction. Given the clear understanding of required partial wave singularities (poles and branch-points) for each reaction, the complexity of constructing theoretical models is sidestepped. This approach is exemplified by its application in the $K \Lambda$ photo-production process, which is supported by a substantial and confident dataset. Nevertheless, the involved formalism and numerous fitting parameters pose significant computational challenges that necessitate simplifications of the analytic structure of Laurent+Pietarinen expansion and the adoption of amplitude+partial wave analysis (AA/PWA) method.

Fermi J1544-0649 is a variable gamma-ray source first identified through its high-energy flares in 2017. Multi-spectral observations during this period revealed characteristics common in blazars, such as spectral energy distribution and variability. Outside of these flares, however, the source remains relatively quiescent in the gamma-ray band for nearly a decade, appearing as a typical galaxy. The detection of broad absorption lines has led researchers to further investigate the "misaligned blazar scenario". Through analysis of Very Long Baseline Array and East Asian VLBI Network data from 2018 to 2020, researchers identified four jet components originating from Fermi J1544-0649 and estimated a viewing angle between approximately 3.7 and 7.4 degrees. The range of this viewing angle suggests that Fermi J1544-0649 has an unusually low rate of gamma-ray emission, with the lower limit implying a blazar and the upper limit supporting the "misaligned blazar scenario". Follow-up multi-spectral observations have shown that the source has remained inactive in gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical frequencies since 2018, and a multi-messenger search has also detected a 3.1 standard deviation excess in neutrino emissions associated with this source.

Reducing machine learning's reliance on labeled data is crucial, which is where semi-supervised learning comes into play. It effectively utilizes spatial and semantic data structures in datasets such as images and language data with the aid of pre-trained models and data augmentation. However, this approach becomes impractical when data lacks inherent domain structures, rendering these methods ineffective. In such cases, simpler methods like pseudo-labeling can be applied without requiring domain knowledge but remain susceptible to noisy samples and arbitrary assignment thresholds that are often unknown. To address this limitation, we propose Confident Sinkhorn Allocation, a method that allocates confident labels and leverages optimal transport to determine the most effective label allocation. This novel approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in semi-supervised learning and is available for public access on GitHub.

We define the function $\zeta^k(s)$ as $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \tau_k(n) n^{-s}, \Re s > 1$ and derive three conditional results for the sum $\sum_{n\le X} \tau_3(n) \tau_3(n+h)$. These results are numerically verified and provide insight into the properties of this additive correlation sum. The first result proves the full main term for the case $h=1$ under an averaged level of distribution assumption for $\tau_3(n)$ in arithmetic progressions. The second derivation gives the leading term asymptotics for any composite shift $h$. The third result provides a complete expansion for the polynomial of the full main term for $h=1$ from the delta-method. We also refine Heath-Brown's result on the correlation of the usual divisor function and numerically analyze the error terms. The results support our approach, which uses elementary methods based on congruences and matches prior predictions by Conrey and Gonek, Ng and Thom, and heuristic probabilistic arguments by Tao. Our method can be applied to give the full main term with a power-saving error term for any correlation of the form $\sum_{n\le X} \tau_k(n) f(n+h)$, to any composite shift $h$, and for any arithmetic function $f(n)$.

We suggest a method to create photons from vacuum through time-varying manipulation of a quantum system, indirectly connected to the cavity field via a mediating quantum system. Specifically, we investigate the simplest scenario where an artificial two-level atom, referred to as a t-qubit, undergoes modulation while being linked to a stationary qubit, serving as the mediator. We discover that under resonant modulation conditions, it's feasible to generate entangled states with limited photons from the ground state, even if the t-qubit operates at a considerable detuning from both the mediator and the cavity, provided the t-qubit's frequencies are finely adjusted in relation to other system parameters. The accuracy of our approximate analytical findings is substantiated by numerical simulations, and we demonstrate that this phenomenon can persist despite typical dissipation mechanisms affecting the system.

There has been significant interest in quantized neural networks due to their efficiency during inference, which results in reduced space and computational requirements. Additionally, quantization is believed to serve as a form of regularization that improves model generalizability, but this notion has not been formally studied previously. In this paper, we view the binary weights of neural networks as stochastic variables and investigate how their distribution evolves across network layers. We introduce a quasi neural network to approximate this distribution propagation, which consists of a neural network with continuous parameters and smooth activation. By deriving the neural tangent kernel for this quasi network, we show that its eigenvalue decays exponentially, similar to the Gaussian kernel with randomized scale. This indicates that the feature space of binary weight neural networks is strictly contained within that of their real-valued counterparts. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed quasi network effectively approximates binary weight networks, and that the latter exhibit a lower generalization gap than real-valued networks, a phenomenon analogous to the difference between Gaussian and Laplace kernels.

In this research, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the production of doubly-charmed baryons in Z boson decay, based on nonrelativistic QCD factorization. Our study includes di-quark states and predicts a branching ratio for the Z boson decaying into a doubly-charmed baryon to be in the range of 10^-5, suggesting it can be experimentally measured. By comparing this to the yield of Lambda^+_c in Z decay, we estimate that the ratio of Z boson decay into doubly-charmed baryons to its decay into Lambda^+_c is approximately 0.85 x 10^-4 for the positive charge state and 1.70 x 10^-4 for the double positive charge state. These values are in contrast to SELEX measurements but in line with those reported by the LHCb and Belle collaborations.

A bipartite state in a system-ancilla configuration that can store all information about an unknown quantum channel acting on the system is considered faithful. The established connection between faithfulness of a state and the invertibility of its corresponding Jamiolkowski map, initially proved by D'Ariano and Presti, serves as a helpful characterization for process tomography with the aid of an ancilla. However, their initial proof had a flaw since it assumed that the operations in question are trace non-increasing, not necessarily quantum channels. This paper fills in the gaps of their proof and extends faithfulness to various types of quantum channels. Additionally, we introduce a broader notion called sensitivity, which represents a quantum state's propensity to be altered by any non-trivial action of a quantum channel. By examining the interrelation between faithfulness and sensitivity, we establish their properties for key classes of quantum channels, including unital channels, random unitary operations, and unitary operations. The results reveal that only two categories of quantum states are necessary for characterizing states that are faithful or sensitive to various subclasses of quantum channels. Specifically, we show that quantum process tomography and quantum correlations are related in such a way that only bipartite states lacking any local classical observables can detect the impact of unital channels.

As technology advances and people become more adept at exploiting it, the incidence of credit card fraud has been increasing, underscoring the need for a reliable method to identify these fraudulent activities. Machine learning algorithms, renowned for their ability to optimize prediction accuracy, seem particularly well-suited to this task. However, their performance may be compromised by an inherent limitation: the tendency to skew towards the majority class when datasets exhibit an imbalance between classes, such as the disproportionately small number of identified fraud cases in most credit card transaction data. To mitigate this issue, we employed a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to create a substantial number of authentic, synthetic examples of the minority class, thereby enriching the training dataset and enhancing the model's capacity for generalized prediction.

For two Hecke eigenforms in the Kohnen plus space of half-integral weight, denoted as $h_1$ and $h_2$, the Duke-Imamoglu-Ikeda lift of $h_1$ and $h_2$ are represented by $I_n(h_1)$ and $I_n(h_2)$, which are Siegel cusp forms associated with $Sp_n(\ZZ)$. The expression of the Rankin-Selberg convolution of $I_n(h_1)$ and $I_n(h_2)$ involves a certain Dirichlet series analogous to the triple convolution product of $h_1$, $h_2$, and the Cohen Eisenstein series $E_{n/2+1/2}$ of weight $n/2+1/2$. Our method is applied to investigate mass equidistribution for the Duke-Imamoglu-Ikeda lift, provided the Dirichlet series $D(s,h_1,h_1,E_{n/2+1/2})$ has a holomorphic extension.

We introduce an innovative approach to automatically calibrate tracked ultrasound probes using a custom-made phantom. The phantom features nine cones with varying heights, enabling key point identification through a convolutional neural network to accurately track the cones across multiple sweeps. RANSAC-based calibration is initially employed and then refined with image-based techniques to ensure robustness. Our design is easily replicable via 3D printing, outperforming current methodologies in numerous aspects. As the phantom does not necessitate a target on its own, user convenience is significantly enhanced. Moreover, the fully automatic method can be applied to new probes from various vendors, as evidenced by our experiments. Furthermore, our technique yields calibration results comparable to those obtained by domain experts.

This study examines the potential of the cosmic microwave background's (CMB)
E-mode polarization data to validate four CMB temperature data anomalies:
inadequate correlations at large angular scales, the alignment of the
quadrupole and octupole, point-parity asymmetry, and hemispherical power
asymmetry. Employing CMB simulations that mirror the noise levels of three
observatories: the Planck satellite, the Cosmology Large Angular Scale Surveyor
(CLASS), and the LiteBIRD satellite, we investigate how current and future
data constrain the anomalies in question. We discovered that the correlation
coefficients between temperature and E-mode estimators are less than $0.1$, with
the exception of point-parity asymmetry ($\rho=0.17$ for simulations without
cosmic variance), thereby confirming E-modes can serve as an independent check
on the anomalies. Compared to Planck's separated CMB data, the LiteBIRD survey
is expected to reduce errors on E-mode anomaly estimators by a factor of 3 to 26,
depending on the anomaly in question. The LiteBIRD survey would particularly
improve the precision of estimators for the quadrupole and octupole alignment,
although the extent of this improvement remains unclear due to large cosmic
variance. In comparison, CLASS would yield intermediate improvements, while
LiteBIRD's LiteBIRD survey would offer a much greater advantage in this regard.

The slow-roll parameter $\epsilon_H$ being smaller than $H^2/M_{\rm Pl}^2$ enables large enough quantum fluctuations of the inflaton after horizon crossing, allowing for eternal inflation to occur. Although insufficient to produce black holes in quasi-de Sitter space, these fluctuations can still generate sizeable density fluctuations in radiation as the number of degrees of freedom rapidly increases in time. We propose that a condition where radiation density fluctuations do not create black holes until the end of inflation is equivalent to the absence of eternal inflation. Furthermore, if radiation does not produce black holes, the information paradox is avoided when $\epsilon_H$ is above $10^{-7}(H^2/M_{\rm Pl}^2)$ and the time frame is under $10^4(M_{\rm Pl}/H^2)$. Even without an information paradox, a static observer cannot gather enough information, which is consistent with the concept of complementarity.

For any non-erasing morphism mapping one sequence to another, a map is established that transfers measures from one space to its image. This map, called the measure transfer map, is proven to be continuous and surjective and turns out to have an efficient method for computing its values on certain types of sequences. Furthermore, a key result states that when a certain property is satisfied for this morphism in a particular sequence space, the map is not only surjective but also injective. A specific characteristic defining this property involves the morphism preserving certain patterns within the sequence space and the map's ability to uniquely identify different sequence spaces.

We examine the fundamental structure of perturbative quantum field theory within the pure Yang-Mills framework established in [9] and demonstrate that the tree-level contributions are indeed free from anomalies. Furthermore, we will establish a more comprehensive expression for this invariance property.

A package manager plays a pivotal role in most technological frameworks, serving as a mediator to guarantee a reliable dependency package is installed, configured, or uninstalled from an application without any complications. Due to the vast array of technological frameworks in use, numerous package managers have been developed, each offering a unique set of features. Our recent study suggests that the features of package managers directly influence user experiences, yet it remains unclear what specific problems users encounter and what information is needed to resolve them.
