A systematic mapping study was conducted to gather 43 primary studies on RE for AI, analyzing the tools, techniques, and models used in real-world scenarios. The findings revealed several challenges and limitations of current RE practices when applied to AI systems. Notably, current methods are not adaptable enough for AI systems and require the development of new techniques and tools to support RE for AI. The majority of empirical studies focused on AI applications such as autonomous vehicles and managing data requirements, emphasizing the need for further research in areas like ethics, trust, and explainability.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is developing standards for secure cryptography that can withstand both classical and quantum computer attacks, replacing traditional encryption methods vulnerable to future quantum breaches. This document offers an in-depth examination and comparison of the BIKE QC-MDPC code-based post-quantum cryptographic key exchange (KEM) solutions, which are part of the NIST standardization process, evaluating their performance in software, hardware, and hybrid implementations and assessing the resource requirements for the hardware-based versions.

Following accusations of liberal bias on Twitter, Elon Musk's takeover led him to vow to revamp the platform's policies to promote free speech. Concerns arose that right-wing influencers might exploit this shift. This study utilizes data from a list of 138,000 Twitter users who secured verified accounts in November 2022. By analyzing nearly 5 million tweets from politically charged accounts, researchers discovered a notable rise in engagement following Musk's acquisition. However, this surge did not correlate with the subsequent verification of these accounts, which is instead attributed to a more supportive audience.

We examine the quantum gravity partition function that tallies the dimension
of a ball-shaped spatial region's Hilbert space, keeping its volume constant,
and calculate it using the leading-order approximation based on the system's most stable point.
The outcome is a value related to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, specifically the
area-based value associated with the surface boundary of the most stable point,
which holds true within the constraints of effective field theory provided that
the mild curvature issues near the ball boundary are effectively smoothed out
by incorporating higher-order curvature terms. This expands on a renowned
Gibbons-Hawking computation that applies to the special scenario where the
volume remains constant in the de Sitter spacetime's static patch, demonstrating
the holographic nature of quantum gravity in confined three-dimensional spaces.

We consider a totally real field, denoted by K, and a rational prime, denoted by r, where r is greater than or equal to 5. In this study, we utilize a modular approach initially presented by Freitas and Siksek to investigate non-trivial, primitive solutions of the equation x^r + y^r = z^p, where x, y, and z are elements of the ring of integers of K. These solutions have a signature of (r, r, p), with p being a varying prime. To adapt this modular method, we follow the work of Freitas, who constructed Frey curves over totally real subfields of K(ζr). When the field is the rational numbers, we find that for certain values of r and sufficiently large p, no non-trivial, primitive integer solutions exist for specific signatures when 2 divides z. For example, when r is equal to one of the primes 5, 7, 11, 13, 19, 23, 37, 47, 53, 59, 61, 67, 71, 79, 83, 101, 103, 107, 131, 139, or 149, and p is sufficiently large, there are no non-trivial, primitive solutions. Similar results hold for quadratic fields, such as the field of the square root of 2. For instance, for the signature (5, 5, p), (7, 7, p), (11, 11, p), or (13, 13, p) and sufficiently large p, no non-trivial, primitive solutions exist with the square root of 2 dividing z.

The advancement of deep neural networks has greatly enhanced representation learning in diverse fields, such as textual, graphical, and relational triple representations. This breakthrough has paved the way for novel relation extraction methods that transcend traditional text-centric approaches. Despite progress, researchers are still investigating the efficacy of incorporating multiple, heterogeneous domain information in unison, and models that can effectively leverage this information are anticipated to yield substantial contributions in tackling global challenges. This thesis investigates relation extraction of Drug-Drug Interactions (DDIs) as a case study and leverages heterogeneous domain information. Initially, a deep neural relation extraction model is developed, with its attention mechanism scrutinized. A method for merging drug molecular structure and drug description information with sentence-based input is proposed, demonstrating its effectiveness in relation extraction tasks. To further capitalize on the heterogeneous information, a diverse array of drug-related items are compiled from various databases, and a new knowledge graph (KG) is constructed. A link prediction task is conducted on the KG to obtain embedding representations of drugs encompassing the heterogeneous domain information. Ultimately, a method that integrates sentence-based information and the KG's heterogeneous data is proposed. The proposed model is trained and evaluated using a widely recognized dataset, showcasing that utilizing heterogeneous domain information significantly improves the efficacy of relation extraction from literature.

Human-AI collaboration in creative tasks is typically limited when the AI cannot reciprocate human input, hindering the potential for a truly collaborative experience. This study begins with an analysis of a comparative study involving 38 participants to examine the impact of AI feedback on user perceptions and interactions within collaborative systems, revealing enhanced engagement and experience with systems that facilitate two-way communication. Results suggest users perceive communicating AI as more dependable, personalized, and intelligent. Furthermore, findings indicate the necessity for identifying and addressing potential moral dilemmas arising from user interactions with a responsive co-creative AI, and to this end, the paper proposes utilizing participatory design fiction as a research method to explore the ethical implications of a communicative co-creative AI.

Soft robots have significant potential for manipulation tasks due to their ability to be flexible, non-threatening, and highly versatile. Yet, their limited workspace has restricted their capabilities in hemispherical workspaces. To address this issue, a supplementary soft prismatic actuator is incorporated into the design of a soft robotic arm. This actuator is comprised of pneumatic artificial muscles and a piston, enabling it to be back-driven. This innovation has expanded the arm's task space volume by 116%, enabling tasks that were previously unattainable with soft robots, such as picking and placing objects at various positions and retrieving items from containers. The integration of a prismatic joint with a soft robotic arm has substantially enhanced the usability of soft robots in object manipulation tasks. Furthermore, this advancement promotes the development of modular soft robotic systems suitable for human-centric environments and practical manipulation applications.

To utilize bosonic quanta in high-speed quantum processing, it's essential to rapidly cool down motional modes. Our research aims to overcome the limitations imposed by conventional cooling methods and explores an alternative approach using deep reinforcement learning to achieve this goal. This method has been successfully applied to accelerate the cooling process of a macroscopic sphere and can be adapted for more complex systems, including a tripartite opto-magno-mechanical system. Notably, our proposed approach is effective across various regimes, including those beyond the limits of traditional rotating wave approximation techniques. As a result, this technique offers a comprehensive toolkit for controlling and generating macroscopic quantum states in a timely and efficient manner, paving the way for quantum technologies.

Recently, the weighted numerical radius of a Hilbert space operator was introduced. This study delves into other attributes, utilizing this newly established numerical radius to derive several novel inequalities for both the weighted numerical radius and the numerical radius. It presents novel identities for the numerical radius, along with comparisons between the numerical radius and its real and imaginary components, as well as inequalities applicable to sectorial operators.

This article leverages specific properties of the transform $\mathscr{C}_{M,m}(A)$ to derive novel inequalities for a bounded linear operator $A$ within a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Specifically, we derive new relationships among the absolute values of $A$, its adjoint $A^*$, and its real and imaginary components $\mathfrak{R}A$ and $\mathfrak{I}A$. Additionally, we present extended numerical radius inequalities that surpass existing ones.

Our novel algorithm, EDS, is a direct monocular visual odometry that combines events and frames to estimate camera movement. By utilizing an event generation model, it accurately tracks camera motion during the interval between frames. EDS employs a direct probabilistic method to predict per-pixel brightness changes, which are then compared to observed events through a brightness increment error to estimate camera movement. This approach enables the recovery of a semi-dense 3D map via photometric bundle adjustment. Notably, EDS is the first method to apply a direct 6-DOF visual odometry using both events and frames, thus overcoming the limitations associated with changing appearances in indirect methods. Furthermore, for a given level of error performance, EDS can function at lower frame rates compared to existing frame-based visual odometry solutions, thereby facilitating the development of low-power motion-tracking applications where frame capture is triggered "on demand" and our method provides motion tracking in between. In addition, we make available our code and datasets to the public.

The ground state phase diagram of a dimerized spin-1/2 XX honeycomb model in a transverse magnetic field is already understood. However, the effects of removing this field are more complex. Without a magnetic field, two quantum states exist: the N\'eel phase and the dimerized phase. Introducing the magnetic field creates additional quantum states - the canted N\'eel and the paramagnetic phases. This paper uses the exact numerical techniques, Lanczos diagonalization and DMRG, to study the correlations between nearest-neighbour spins, particularly the concurrence, quantum discord, and the quantum entanglement among them. It demonstrates that quantum correlations accurately identify the critical points across the phase diagram, in line with existing knowledge. Additionally, although concurrence and quantum discord indicate short-ranged correlations, they are indicative of critical long-range entanglement. Furthermore, we observed a previously uninvestigated phenomenon, where the entanglement with the magnetic field is initially entangled around its saturation point.

Deep learning models for image reconstruction often produce a single image. Yet, the complexities of imaging tasks frequently render such point estimates unreliable or insufficient due to issues such as noise and model inaccuracy. In contrast, Bayesian methods treat both images and measurement data as random vectors, aiming to approximate the distribution of unknown variables. However, traditional Bayesian inference methods have their limitations, including excessive computational requirements. To overcome these challenges, a new method called C-Trumpets is proposed. C-Trumpets, a type of conditional injective flow, are specifically designed to tackle imaging problems and offer several advantages, such as reduced memory usage and lower training times. Furthermore, their architecture enables accurate approximation of point estimates and quantification of uncertainty in image restoration tasks.

The optimal neural architecture for a machine learning task heavily depends on various factors such as the dataset's complexity, and the available resources including processing speed, power consumption, and time limits. For tabular dataset problems, neural architecture search (NAS) has received insufficient attention. Conventional NAS methods for image datasets directly incorporate resource constraints into the reinforcement learning rewards, but this approach often yields suboptimal results when applied to tabular data. A novel NAS approach called TabNAS has been developed to effectively manage resource constraints for tabular datasets. TabNAS uses a reinforcement learning controller inspired by rejection sampling to immediately exclude architectures violating the constraints, eliminating unnecessary training. To adjust for this initial filtering step, TabNAS employs a Monte Carlo-based correction in its policy gradient updates. The proposed method has been shown to outperform previous methods on several tabular datasets, discovering superior models that meet the constraints.

The article enhances the triangle inequality for complex numbers by leveraging the Hermite-Hadamard inequality for convex functions. It further showcases the practical applications of this refinement to operator inequalities, incorporating numerical radius and operator mean inequalities.

To study the behavior of complex quantum systems under changing conditions, we've developed a simplified mathematical model, which allows us to analyze the system's response to time-dependent changes using straightforward calculations. By connecting this system to an external environment and using a specific mathematical framework, we've derived an equation that describes the system's evolution over time, leading to a state of equilibrium. Additionally, we've developed a method to calculate the correlations between the system's components and related these to the occupation of the system's energy levels. These results enable the analysis of quantum systems' dynamics under various external influences, facilitating a deeper understanding of the balance between the dissipation of energy and the creation of coherent states. This simplified model is ideal for investigating phenomena such as the nonequilibrium dynamics of quantum systems and the effects of temperature and driving forces on their behavior.

We develop a comprehensive, non-perturbative mathematical framework to describe the chaotic phase in quantum systems within the context of two-dimensional gravity. By utilizing a universe field theory, we derive a flavor-matrix theory description of the ergodic phase in holographic gravity, characterized by $\mathrm{U}(n|n)$ causal symmetry breaking and restoration. While JT gravity does not inherently possess causal symmetry, its universe field theory, the Kodaira-Spencer theory of gravity, does. We then demonstrate that the flavor-matrix theory can be derived from Kodaira-Spencer theory and its geometric significance can be understood through different D-brane vacua, ultimately revealing an open-closed string duality. This duality relates to the characteristic correlations in the quantum ergodic phase and provides a geometric interpretation.

When water droplets in clouds collide, they sometimes merge to form larger droplets that eventually become rain. However, this doesn't always happen due to the air resistance that can push droplets apart. To better understand why some droplets collide while others don't, scientists used advanced technology to closely track the movement of cloud droplets as they fall through calm air. By monitoring the positions and velocities of the droplets with unprecedented precision, researchers were able to pinpoint the moment when droplets would merge. They found that the key to determining whether droplets would merge was their acceleration towards each other, and developed a way to predict when this acceleration would exceed a certain threshold. By analyzing how droplets accelerate towards each other, scientists believe they may be able to develop a formula to predict the rate at which droplets collide and merge in turbulent clouds, ultimately shedding light on a long-standing mystery in atmospheric science.

Recent research has demonstrated that autoregressive language models can efficiently tackle a multitude of NLP tasks through zero- and few-shot learning techniques, offering new avenues for leveraging pre-trained models. This paper introduces two GPT-like models with 1.3 billion and 13 billion parameters, trained on a massive corpus of 60 languages from 25 linguistic families. We replicate the GPT-3 architecture using GPT-2 resources and incorporate a sparse attention mechanism, leveraging the Deepspeed and Megatron frameworks to optimize training and inference processes. The resultant models achieve performance on par with the XGLM models, while covering a broader language scope and expanding NLP possibilities for underserved languages in CIS countries and Russian-speaking nations. We detail our architecture design choices and elaborate on the data preparation pipeline, training multiple mini-models to determine the most suitable multilingual tokenization strategy. We assess model perplexity across all languages and evaluate its performance on a diverse range of multilingual tasks, including classification, generation, sequence labeling, and knowledge probing, utilizing zero-shot and few-shot learning methods. Additionally, we compare our classification results with the state-of-the-art XGLM model, and provide public access to our source code and the mGPT XL model.

We examine the efficiency of the recently introduced Local Polynomial Interpolation-based Gradient Descent method, specifically for the approximate solution of empirical risk minimization problems. This is done under the assumption of strongly convex and smooth loss functions with a known condition number, as well as a specific level of continuity with regard to the data. We identify that the computational cost associated with achieving a certain level of accuracy using LPI-GD scales with a particular factor related to the dimension and a given parameter, and we demonstrate that this factor can be significantly reduced under certain conditions. In contrast to more traditional methods, we find that LPI-GD offers improved efficiency in specific cases, and we propose and analyze accelerated versions of LPI-GD to further improve performance. Our experimental results confirm that these accelerated methods indeed outperform traditional alternatives under certain conditions.

A novel approach to particle filtering in complex systems is introduced, where the system's signal evolution is modeled using a stochastic differential equation (SDE). The new method involves discretizing the SDE, creating an efficient particle filtering process for the resulting discrete-time model. The proposed discretization scheme is designed to produce a sequence-dependent structure, allowing for improved performance in high-dimensional systems. Space-sequential particle filters, which leverage this structure, are developed and tested using simulations of a stochastic Lorenz 96 system with additive noise. Results show that these filters achieve consistent estimation accuracy with a manageable computational cost, even as the system's dimension increases. This paper also presents a general framework for discrete-time filtering in continuous-time systems, demonstrating that, given a weakly-convergent discretization scheme, the resulting discrete-time model's posterior laws converge to the original model's under a specific metric, with broad applicability beyond the specific numerical scheme and filters discussed.

Research suggests that supernova explosions and star winds are primary sources of large interstellar dust grains. Smaller grains are produced through the fragmentation of larger ones accelerated by random forces. To understand this process, a new numerical method was integrated into the astrophysical simulation software RAMSES. The method treats large dust grains as massive entities that experience drag and magnetic forces, and it underwent rigorous testing under various physical conditions to validate its accuracy. The results of decaying turbulence simulations showed that 1-2 micrometer grains can be significantly accelerated in cold interstellar medium conditions, both electrically charged and neutral, and that they are less likely to break apart due to their interaction with gas.
This document contains technical information about the Hybrid-AIM simulator, which was utilized in the research of Sharon and Stone (2017) and also by Parks-Young and Sharon in (2022).

We demonstrate the nonexistence of odd-dimensional, stable compact minimal immersions within the product of two complex projective spaces. Furthermore, we prove that the only stable compact minimal immersions in the product of a quaternionic projective space and any other Riemannian manifold are direct products of quaternionic projective subspaces with compact stable minimal immersions of the second manifold in the given Riemannian product. Additionally, we generalize results for immersions with lower dimensions or codimensions to arbitrary dimensions, establishing a similar result for immersions in the product of an octonionic projective plane and any other Riemannian manifold.

This paper constructs an anticyclotomic Euler system linked to the adjoint representation of elliptic modular forms adapted to an imaginary quadratic field $K$. It also connects this Euler system to a $p$-adic $L$-function, which stems from the work of Eischen-Wan and Eischen-Harris-Li-Skinner on $p$-adic $L$-functions for unitary groups. This connection yields novel instances of the Bloch-Kato conjecture in rank zero and a divisibility result for the Iwasawa main conjecture.

The goal of active mapping involves determining the most effective sequence of sensor views under budget constraints such as distance traveled. This study focuses on actively constructing occupancy grids with a range sensor like LiDAR or depth cameras. Current methods optimize information-theoretic metrics linking occupancy probabilities and sensor measurements, but they struggle due to the non-smooth nature of ray-tracing in grid representations. This makes the objective function non-differentiable, leading existing methods to search within a discrete space of potential paths. Our approach develops a differentiable approximation of the mutual information between grid maps and ray-based observations, enabling the use of gradient ascent optimization to search through the continuous space of possible sensor poses. Our gradient-based method produces more informative sensing paths while avoiding obstacles and collisions, and is demonstrated through experiments in simulated and real-world environments with 2-D and 3-D settings.

The goal of motion magnification techniques is to enhance and reveal subtle movements within video footage. There are two primary approaches, the Eulerian and Lagrangian methods, each offering distinct techniques for achieving this objective. The Eulerian approach amplifies motion implicitly by processing individual image pixels directly. In contrast, the Lagrangian approach employs optical flow techniques to extract and amplify pixel trajectories. Facial microexpressions, characterized by their rapid and localized nature, pose a significant challenge for detection. In this research, a novel method is proposed for amplifying local facial micromovements using the Lagrangian approach. This approach consists of three key contributions: Firstly, the recurrent all-pairs field transforms for optical flows deep learning model is fine-tuned using ground truth data from the variational dense inverse search algorithm applied to the CASME II video dataset, enabling efficient and accurate production of facial optical flows. Secondly, the proposed approach involves approximating the optical flow field by using sparse components in both space and time through double sparse decomposition, given that facial micromovements exhibit both local and temporal characteristics. Lastly, this decomposition is utilized to amplify micro-motions in specific facial regions by introducing a forward warping strategy that employs a triangular splitting of the image grid and barycentric interpolation of RGB vectors at the corners of the transformed triangles. The performance of this method is demonstrated through various examples, showcasing its efficacy.

Recent advancements in high-pressure synthesis methods have enabled the creation of (Pb,In)Te samples with higher indium concentrations. This has led to the discovery of lead-rich samples that exhibit enhanced superconducting transition temperatures compared to indium-rich compounds. This study aims to investigate the temperature-dependent properties of In$_{0.8}$Pb$_{0.2}$Te, a compound displaying a bulk superconducting onset at around 4.75 Kelvin. Our results indicate a typical BCS superconducting behavior, dismissing topologically nontrivial $A_{2u}$ pairing, but leaving the possibility of $A_{1u}$ pairing intact. Furthermore, critical field measurements below 1 Kelvin and other superconducting properties are presented in this study.

Co-creative processes involving humans and AI rely heavily on collaborative dynamics. Key factors influencing these interactions include communication styles, contribution types, and turn-taking strategies, which together form the foundation of effective co-creative systems. Despite the importance of these elements, research into interaction design within co-creativity remains relatively underdeveloped. Consequently, existing co-creative systems frequently overlook the role of interaction design. This research shifts the focus from AI capabilities to interaction design by introducing the Co-Creative Framework for Interaction (COFI), a comprehensive model that explores the vast possibilities of interaction design. With COFI, researchers can model, analyze, and compare the interaction dynamics of various co-creative systems. By applying COFI to a dataset of 92 co-creative systems, our analysis demonstrates its effectiveness in categorizing interaction models and reveals opportunities for redesign, enabling more effective human-AI collaboration.

A unified framework for mixed-space quantum representations in Condensed Matter Physics and Quantum Field Theory has been established. This unifying approach enables the expansion of quantum operators using a universal basis, the operator Y(u,v), which incorporates Hilbert spaces of position and momentum operators. The expansion coefficients are determined by the Fourier transform of the Wigner distribution function, a characteristic function. This framework allows for various unitary transformations, such as the Jordan-Wigner transformation, Holstein-Primakoff transformation, and Bogoliubov transformation, to be employed, facilitating calculations involving fermions, bosons, and spin systems. The Jordan-Schwinger transformation is also utilized to map matrix representations to bilinear expressions of creation and annihilation operators. It is demonstrated that the coherent states formulation of quantum physics is a specific instance of this unification, and a new QFT formulation based on Q-distribution of functional-field variables is proposed. Additionally, the unified framework is extended to nonequilibrium quantum transport physics, which involves non-Hermitian operators and time-reversal symmetry breaking, as discussed in the Appendix.

This study focuses on weighted Lp affine surface areas that arise in the context of the Lp Steiner formula in the Lp Brunn Minkowski theory. The research establishes that these areas represent valuations on convex bodies and demonstrates isoperimetric inequalities for them. It is found that the weighted Lp affine surface areas are connected to the f divergences of the cone measures of a convex body and its polar, specifically the Kullback-Leibler and Rényi divergences.

Manganese-based nitride antiperovskites with kagome lattices, like Mn$_3$NiN, display a triangular frustrated magnetic ordering that is sensitive to the symmetric and asymmetric interactions between Mn atoms. The non-collinear magnetic configuration is influenced by external factors such as applied epitaxial strain, which affects the electronic interactions. To understand this effect, we studied the impact of strain within the (111) plane while maintaining the magnetic and crystallographic symmetries. Our findings revealed a linear shift in the band structure energy and an increase/decrease of available states near the Fermi level with the applied strain. Compression strain reduced Mn-Mn distances but increased the separation between kagome lattices, linearly affecting available states. However, the anomalous Hall conductivity showed non-linear behavior, with $\sigma_{111}$ nearly vanishing under tensile strain and reaching a 26% increase with compression strain near -1.5%. This anomaly was linked to non-divergent Berry curvature within the kagome plane, increasing with compression and decreasing with expansion strain.

Unlocking the full potential of future cosmological surveys requires extracting valuable information from the complex structure formation processes in the universe. Despite the vast potential, analyzing observational data is hindered by the theoretical and computational intricacies involved. To overcome this hurdle, a set of novel summary statistics for cosmological matter fields have been developed, utilizing 3D wavelets to analyze the data. These statistics involve taking the spatial average of the 3D wavelet transform, raised to a specific power, and are known as invariant wavelet moments. The wavelets are specifically designed to be radially band-limited and separable on a spherical grid, coming in three distinct types. Through the Fisher forecast framework, it has been demonstrated that these summary statistics can achieve state-of-the-art results for parameter constraints on both the base ΛCDM parameters and the sum of neutrino masses. Furthermore, they have shown to significantly improve constraints, by a factor of 5 to 10, compared to the traditional power spectrum approach.

We derive limit theorems for the occurrence frequencies of fringe patterns in a randomly chosen ranked tree-child network, building upon the work of Bienvenu et al. (2022) for cherry patterns. For patterns of height one or two, our analysis reveals distinct behavior: either they emerge frequently, occur sporadically, or do not appear at all as the network size increases, leading us to hypothesize these outcomes as the sole possibilities.

New regulations have sparked an interest in machine unlearning, which involves deleting specific data points from a predictive model as if they never existed. This requirement may also arise from corrupted or adversarial data, or a user's changing privacy preferences. Models that don't require training, such as k-NN, can simply remove the relevant sample, but this approach is not suitable for more complex models that learn richer representations. Existing methods based on optimization suffer from scalability issues, particularly in large models. We propose using a new coefficient, L-CODEC, to identify the model parameters most closely related to individual samples. This approach avoids the need to invert a large matrix and can be applied to deep learning models and other vision applications. By utilizing Markov blanket selection, L-CODEC makes approximate unlearning possible in settings previously considered impractical, including models used for face recognition, person re-identification, and NLP.

The field of requirements engineering for machine learning lacks a strong foundation and thorough research, which leads to difficulties when developing ML-enabled systems. To improve the reliability of such systems, more focus on requirements engineering for ML is needed. Based on past studies and industry expertise, we have compiled a list of 45 considerations for designing ML systems, encompassing five key aspects: objectives, user experience, infrastructure, models, and data. Examples of these considerations include the system's execution and monitoring capabilities, as well as model transparency and reproducibility. We conducted a focus group with eight ML system developers to assess the importance and feasibility of our compiled list and gather feedback to refine it. Our research primarily contributes a set of verified and structured concerns, grouped by perspective, that can aid requirements engineers in specifying ML-enabled systems.

We examine the significance of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy within the frameworks of AdS/CFT and holographic quantum error correction, specifically through finite-dimensional models. In the context of operator algebra quantum error correction, a suitable extension of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy over finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras is introduced. It is demonstrated that bulk and boundary sandwiched relative Renyi entropies are equal if, and only if, bulk and boundary states are algebraically encoded, the Ryu-Takayanagi formula holds, relative entropies are equal, and subregion duality exists. This finding adds to a previous equivalence theorem between these concepts established in the paper arxiv:1607.03901. We then consider sandwiched Renyi relative entropy defined using modular operators and show it naturally applies to finite-dimensional models of holographic quantum error correction. Additionally, numerical computations of sandwiched Renyi relative entropies are performed for a simple holographic random tensor network, providing insights into corrections to the exact equality of bulk and boundary sandwiched relative Renyi entropy.

The development of massive galaxies in the local universe heavily relies on low-excitation radio galaxy feedback, yet the processes behind their evolution and the influence of active galactic nuclei on early galaxy development remain obscure. Using a sample of 10,481 low-excitation radio galaxies from the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey, a comprehensive study of the radio luminosity function of these galaxies is presented, showing relatively minor evolutionary changes. The low-excitation radio galaxies were classified based on whether their host galaxies were quiescent or actively star-forming, revealing that a prominent population of low-excitation radio galaxies resides in star-forming galaxies at high redshifts. In contrast, the presence of low-excitation radio galaxies in quiescent galaxies correlates with stellar mass, consistent with local universe measurements, and diminishes in space density as redshift increases. The quiescent low-excitation radio galaxy population dominated radio luminosity functions at low redshifts, but the characteristic luminosity of these galaxies increased with time. Meanwhile, the star-forming low-excitation radio galaxy population increased in space density at higher redshifts and eventually surpassed the quiescent population, hinting at a different fueling mechanism driven by cold gas supply present in star-forming galaxies.

This paper introduces the concepts of annular settling and output annular settling for nonlinear systems in general. We derive requirements for short-term stability, short-term boundedness with nonzero initial conditions, annular settling, and output annular settling for Persidskii systems with bounded input signals. The requirements are established through linear matrix inequality verification. A case study of recurrent neural networks demonstrates the practical value of these newly proposed concepts and requirements.

A precise measurement of a mechanical oscillator's or microwave field's shift in a specific direction within the phase space can be achieved using trapped ions or superconducting circuits, respectively, by linking the oscillator to auxiliary qubits. This coupling enables the transfer of the displacement information to the qubits, which can then be measured. However, determining a shift in an arbitrary direction in the phase space with certainty has not been explored in such oscillator-qubit systems. Our research proposes a novel setup combining oscillators and qubits to accurately measure phase space shifts in any direction, utilizing feasible interactions that go beyond the conventional approximation. We demonstrate that this hybrid setup outperforms existing methods, such as single-mode estimation schemes and a conventional interferometer, in terms of its quantum sensing capabilities. Moreover, the proposed method's sensitivity is independent of the oscillator's thermal energy, meaning it does not require cooling the oscillator before making the measurement. Furthermore, our study assesses the impact of qubit decoherence and oscillator thermalization, showing that the setup is robust and performs better than other benchmark methods even under large levels of these effects.

Designers face challenges in finding the perfect combination of design elements that meet specific goals. This optimization process is often difficult and time-consuming due to the complexity of the design task and the need for extensive testing. Computer algorithms can assist designers by generating potential solutions, but these methods require a detailed understanding of the design domain. On the other hand, "black box" methods, which can be applied to any design task, lack hands-on testing, limiting our understanding of their effectiveness for designers in real-world scenarios. This study investigated the use of Bayesian optimization as a tool to guide the design optimization process, helping designers decide which options to test next. In a comparative study involving novice designers, the optimizer proved to be a useful tool in exploring more design possibilities and achieving better results. However, participants felt a decrease in personal control and creativity when working with the optimizer. Despite lower mental effort, they felt less in control of their work, leading to the conclusion that human-in-the-loop optimization is most beneficial for novice designers where the need for personal control is less crucial.

To study graded Frobenius algebras through a ring theory lens, we define and examine the structure and representations of graded quasi-Frobenius rings, Frobenius rings, and their shifted counterparts. This involves revisiting fundamental concepts like graded simple Artinian rings, graded semisimple rings and deriving the graded counterparts of results related to the Jacobson radical and singular radical, which are connected to finiteness conditions and injectivity. Additionally, a key structure theorem is established for graded Frobenius and shifted Frobenius rings.

This thesis offers a range of optimization solutions tailored for various challenges in quantum information theory. We initiate with a proposed method for quantum state estimation, which relies on orthogonal projections across intersecting hyperplanes, identified through probability distributions and measurement operators. We evaluate its effectiveness, accounting for realistic errors, in terms of both runtime efficiency and fidelity accuracy. Next, a method for verifying quantum non-locality is introduced, which takes bipartite measurement frequencies as input to determine a Bell inequality with the maximum disparity between local hidden variable and quantum values. Finally, in addressing the quantum marginal problem, we develop an operator and a corresponding algorithm that, given a set of quantum marginals and eigenvalues, outputs a compatible density matrix if one exists.

We examine a flat FLRW model within the context of f(R,T) gravity, incorporating quadratic scalar curvature variations and a linear term of the stress-energy tensor's trace. Our model displays late-time Universe behavior characterized by accelerated expansion and ultimately ending in a big rip. Using the scale factor's parametrization, we formulate a model commencing with a point-like singularity of zero volume, infinite energy density, and infinite temperature. The model's present state exhibits accelerated expansion, mimics a Lambda CDM model at late times, and in the current era, it behaves as a quintessence dark energy model.

We explore the correlators of fields linked to an EPR pair of quarks in a super Yang-Mills theory through a holographic model, which is a string in an AdS space anchored at its endpoints on boundaries. Two scenarios are examined: one in which the string endpoints are stationary and another in which they uniformly accelerate in opposite directions. For both cases, the two-point correlators of the boundary field are derived exactly using linearized perturbations, revealing the all-time evolution of the correlators. When the string is accelerating, its worldsheet geometry has the causal structure of a two-sided AdS black hole with a wormhole, potentially realizing the ER=EPR conjecture. Causality significantly influences the dispersion relation of particles and the nature of the induced mutual interaction between them. If the worldsheet boundaries are causally disconnected, the induced effect from the field gives each particle dissipative dynamics, regardless of the particles' separation, with the induced coupling between them vanishing in late times following a power law. Conversely, if the endpoints are causally connected, the dispersion relation becomes non-dissipative in late times. This study also discusses the implications for entangled particle dynamics and the ER=EPR conjecture.

A cosmological model based on cubic $f(R)$-gravity was explored, treating nonlinear $f(R)$ terms as energy in curvature-inspired geometry. This resulted in an accelerating universe expansion, accompanied by anti-gravitating negative pressure. Various parameters were computed numerically and validated against the Hubble dataset and the Pantheon dataset, comprising 46 and 40 SNIa data points respectively. Analysis of dynamical parameters via plots revealed accelerating expansion in the present epoch, with the transition from deceleration to acceleration occurring at redshift $z_{tr}$ approximately equal to 0.694069, consistent with the $\Lambda$CDM model. Additionally, state finder analysis of the model confirmed its consistency with $\Lambda$CDM in late times.

A significant advancement in machinery fault diagnosis has been achieved through the application of machine learning methods, although a major constraint of these methods lies in their inability to provide transparent decision-making processes. This study presents a novel neural network architecture called the temporal logic neural network (TLNN), where the neural units are formulated using logical propositions. The TLNN structure can be represented as a weighted signal temporal logic formula, allowing for a formal interpretation and a more in-depth understanding of its operations. Furthermore, experiments using real-world datasets demonstrate the TLNN's ability to produce highly accurate fault diagnosis results with efficient computational processes, as well as providing insights into the decision-making process through its embedded formal language.

We examine how the principle of adiabaticity breaks down as a complex quantum system is cooled down from a thermally stable state towards a critical point, where distinct quantum phases meet. The system's excitation density, which serves as an indicator of the adiabaticity, is shown to adhere to universal scaling principles in terms of the cooling speed, the initial and final temperatures of the process, and is governed by specific critical exponents of the transition. Analytically, this is demonstrated for a specific model involving a quantum wire connected to heat baths, and it is argued that these findings hold under broader conditions. This research confirms that the properties of quantum phase transitions can be studied dynamically at finite temperatures without altering the system's control parameter.

We show that conventional analog transmission and filtering techniques can replace edge servers in distributed machine learning, allowing large networks with widespread user devices to operate without a centralized server. Additionally, we develop an algorithm enabling these devices to perform local processing without interruptions from global updates, thus maximizing their computing power. Convergence rates are calculated to evaluate the efficiency of the proposed methods, demonstrating that they can achieve server-based performance under Gaussian interference, but are hindered by heavy-tailed interference distributions. Our results indicate that parallelizing computation and communication significantly reduces overall processing time, particularly in systems with high latency. These findings are confirmed through extensive simulations.

This study focuses on generalized higher-order moment functions, which have a significant connection to well-known binomial functions that have been explored in various abstract frameworks. Building on our previous work on commutative groups, we now extend our investigation to the more abstract context of hypergroups. Specifically, we derive a characterization of generalized moment functions on a polynomial hypergroup by utilizing partial derivatives of a composition involving polynomial generators and an analytic function. Furthermore, we provide an explicit expression for the moment generating functions of rank two or less on the Tchebyshev hypergroup as a concrete example.

We introduce GraphMoE, a neural network-based method for learning generative models of random graphs, where a network is trained to capture the distribution of a particular type of random graph using a moment estimator. Graphlets, small subgraph counts, serve as the training features. By taking random noise as input, the network generates vector representations for nodes, which are then transformed into random graphs using a kernel function. The produced graphs are demonstrated to convincingly mimic real-world graph data from various domains, including chemistry, medicine, and social networks, and can even deceive discriminative neural networks that are typically skilled at distinguishing between different types of random graphs.

Single-task models have been successful in handling specific tasks, but their usefulness is limited when it comes to real-world applications that require multitasking and adaptability to changing domains. Recent advancements in instructional prompts have shown great potential in enhancing multi-task learning capabilities. Despite this, the impact of these prompts and multi-task learning on biomedical applications remains unexplored. To address this knowledge gap, this study delves into the effect of instructional prompts on multi-task learning in the biomedical domain. To this end, we introduce BoX, a collection of 32 biomedical instruction tasks across various categories. Leveraging this meta-dataset, we develop a unified model called In-BoXBART, which enables the simultaneous learning of multiple tasks from BoX without relying on task-specific modules. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to propose a unified model for the biomedical domain and utilize instructional prompts to achieve generalization across diverse biomedical tasks. Experimental findings reveal that our model outperforms single-task and multi-task baselines by substantial margins, demonstrating its effectiveness in few-shot learning scenarios as well. Notably, our analysis highlights significant room for improvement across tasks, indicating a promising area for future research.

We investigate the limiting behavior of the family of values $\frac{L'}{L}(1/2+\epsilon,\chi_D)$ as the fundamental discriminant $D$ varies, with a focus on the associated real character $\chi_D$ and the range $0<\epsilon<\frac12$. Additionally, we derive a rate of convergence for this family to its limiting distribution and apply this result to obtain an asymptotic estimate for small values of $\left|\frac{L'}{L}(1/2+\epsilon,\chi_D)\right|$.

Recent hyperspectral unmixing research has seen an increase in the use of deep learning, particularly with autoencoder architecture. We introduce a split architecture that employs pseudo-ground truth for abundances to guide the optimization of the unmixing network. Before the unmixing network, an approximation network is proposed to enhance the relationship between a pixel and its neighborhood, resulting in improved spatial correlation. This architecture, known as the Guided Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Hyperspectral Unmixing with Spatial Smoothness (GAUSS), utilizes one-hot encoded abundances generated through k-means to guide the unmixing network and eliminates the reliance on prior hyperspectral unmixing methods. To further modify this architecture, we experiment with two approaches: the first concatenates the unmixing and mixing networks to propagate gradients, while the second uses reliable abundance results from signal processing methods as pseudo-ground truth within the GAUSS framework. Our results from four datasets show that these architectures outperform or match existing hyperspectral unmixing algorithms from both deep learning and signal processing domains.

In the context of Celestial variables and four spacetime dimensions, we're investigating the 2-2 scattering process. We employ a specific approach called the crossing symmetric dispersion relation to transform the Celestial amplitudes into a set of crossing symmetric partial waves, which include spurious singularities in the Celestial variable. However, these singularities must be eliminated to ensure the theory remains local. By applying the locality constraints, we obtain closed-form expressions that enable us to establish novel bounds on the partial wave moments. This, in turn, allows us to assess the extent of low spin dominance in scalar theories. Additionally, we identify a form of positivity that appears to be prevalent in a wide range of theories, which we prove can only occur in theories characterized by spin-0 dominance. We then utilize techniques from Geometric Function Theory to analyze the crossing symmetric partial waves with the spurious singularities removed, known as Feynman blocks. These blocks exhibit unique properties in the Celestial variable, including typically real values. Using this insight, we derive non-projective bounds on the Wilson coefficients in terms of partial wave moments.

A novel approach to knowledge distillation has emerged, focusing on optimizing the performance of large-scale language models through advanced techniques such as Contrastive Learning, Intermediate Layer Distillation, Data Augmentation, and Adversarial Training. We propose a learning-based data augmentation method called CILDA, leveraging intermediate layer representations of the primary task for enhancing the quality of augmented samples via contrastive loss, and masked adversarial data augmentation. CILDA surpasses existing knowledge distillation methods on the GLUE benchmark and in out-of-domain evaluations.

An introduction to surreal numbers, specifically Cuesta-Conway numbers, as an extension of Cantor's ordinals reveals that these numbers can be straightforwardly defined from their basic form, involving exponentials indexed by ordinals. This foundation enables the straightforward derivation of addition, multiplication, and a total order relation, extending the properties of real numbers and ordinals. Constructing this class results in a series of real-closed fields, ultimately establishing the surreal numbers as a totally ordered, commutative, and real-closed field through a complete and well-established proof.

Reinforcement Learning's application in controlled text generation tasks, like unsupervised text style transfer, is hindered by the challenge of sparse rewards. These rewards are available only after the entire text is generated, leading to inefficient training and difficulty converging. Current reward-shaping strategies haven't made a significant impact, however, this work introduces a novel approach that provides continuous feedback in the form of dense rewards for each generated token. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through its application in unsupervised text style transfer. Compared to state-of-the-art systems, our style transfer system achieves a 21% improvement in human evaluation and 12% in automatic evaluation. Our approach outperforms existing reward shaping methods by 22% in human evaluation, and significantly reduces training time, achieving 2.5 times more efficient use of training samples and 7 times faster training.
This article aims to provide a definitive proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The particle in a box model employs a simplified classical Hamiltonian, H=p^2 (with reduced mass, 2m=1), and is confined within a limited spatial domain, -b<q<b, where b is a positive value. Due to its simplicity, this system has been thoroughly analyzed through canonical quantization. However, a crucial aspect of this model raises doubts about the prior results. Beyond highlighting the issue with conventional quantization, affine quantization yields an alternative quantization method, resulting in more intricate eigenfunctions and eigenvalues that are worthy of investigation.

Recent benchmark studies have highlighted a discrepancy between reported advancements in certain subfields of machine learning and actual progress.  This stagnation can be attributed to a lack of reproducibility in model comparison studies, which frequently overlook established causes of irreproducibility.  As a result, the findings in these studies often cannot be independently verified. The aim of this study is to comprehensively document the known causes of irreproducibility in machine learning. Through a literature review, we compile a taxonomy of sources of irreproducibility, discuss their implications, and propose three areas for further investigation.

Scientific breakthroughs often rely on understanding relationships within complex data, which deep learning can identify. However, its applications in science have been hindered due to the inability to grasp the underlying relationships it uncovers. The Information Bottleneck framework provides an analytical tool to break down the relationships into comprehensible approximations by finding a balance between their fidelity and complexity. By adapting this framework to work with multiple components of the input, a crucial modification is made, allowing for more in-depth understanding of the connections in complex systems. This distributed approach limits the interactions between system components, enabling deep learning to create meaningful approximations that don't rely on custom datasets or neural networks. When applied to complex systems, it illuminates key characteristics by controlling the information flow from individual components. The distributed Information Bottleneck technique showcases its potential in the field of physics and mathematics by deciphering the intricacies of complex systems, such as isolating crucial inputs in electronic circuits or identifying the patterns of material rearrangement in deformed glass structures. This novel framework provides much-needed clarity to deep learning applications and offers an innovative approach to studying the flow of information within systems.

The ability of NLP models to generalize across a range of unseen tasks when provided with detailed task instructions is explored through the introduction of Super-NaturalInstructions, a comprehensive benchmark of 1,616 diverse NLP tasks and their corresponding instructions, which encompasses 76 distinct task categories, such as classification, extraction, and text composition. Our dataset allows for rigorous evaluation of cross-task generalization by training models on a subset of tasks and assessing them on the remaining unseen ones. To address this challenge, we have developed Tk-Instruct, a transformer model designed to follow a wide variety of in-context instructions, outperforming existing instruction-following models such as InstructGPT by more than 9% on our benchmark despite being significantly smaller in size. Further investigation into generalization is conducted by analyzing its relationship with various scaling factors, including the number of observed tasks, instances per task, and model size, with the ultimate goal of advancing the development of more versatile NLP models.

Research on spin-orbit coupled states has led to significant interest in materials made of transition metals from the 4th and 5th periods of the periodic table, such as iridates and ruthenium trichloride, due to their ability to facilitate Kitaev interactions. By manipulating the balance between the interaction of the metal's spin with its orbital motion (spin-orbit interaction) and the effect of its environment (trigonal crystal field splitting) in Li2RhO3, researchers created a novel state by converting it into Ag3LiRh2O6. This change resulted in a greater influence from the trigonal distortion and reduced spin-orbit coupling in the resulting compound, which can be described using a specific expression derived from perturbation theory. This transformation is associated with a change from a 6 K spin-glass state in Li2RhO3 to a 94 K antiferromagnetic state in Ag3LiRh2O6. The emergence of these distinct magnetic properties opens a pathway to creating diverse magnetic phase diagrams by manipulating materials in this way.

Developing efficient solvers for time-dependent partial differential equations is crucial, particularly for achieving accuracy and stability. To tackle this challenge, we propose using graph neural networks to discover effective PDE solvers through a learning approach. First, we derive a method for representing PDE data in a way that remains consistent across different domains, drawing inspiration from established PDE solvers. Subsequently, we demonstrate how graphs can be employed to represent PDE data on complex, unstructured meshes and how message-passing graph neural networks can be utilized to encode governing equations, ultimately enabling the development of efficient and accurate solver schemes for linear and nonlinear PDEs. Moreover, our method yields solvers that are independent of the initial domain, thereby facilitating the application of trained solvers to a wide range of complex domains. Lastly, we explore the application of a recurrent graph neural network to find a temporal sequence of solutions to a PDE.

Single photon emitters are often diagnosed using a Hanbury Brown and Twiss intensity interferometer, consisting of a 50:50 beamsplitter and two time-correlated detectors. The intensity cross-correlation of photon arrivals between these detectors, measured as $g^{(2)}(\tau)$, typically exhibits a distinctive zero-dip at $\tau=0$ for a single photon emitter. A common criterion to detect these emitters is to observe a value of $g^{(2)}(0)<1/2$. This study applies stochastic methods to simulate the behavior of a single photon emitter under imperfect detection conditions. It reveals that single photon emitter identification can be compromised if the detectors have unequal detection efficiencies and if the detector noise surpasses half the emitter's true signal rate.

Our research introduces a camera system called the single-pixel imaging camera based on complementary detection and optimized Bernoulli modulation, referred to as CSPI camera, which greatly minimizes the impact of background light on SPI imaging technology. A numerical simulation indicates that when the probability of each coded pattern is set to 0.5, the CSPI camera can remain undisturbed, even in the presence of significant fluctuations in background light intensity, outshining the signal. Furthermore, our results show a comparison of reconstruction outcomes between SPI, differential SPI, and CSPI camera technology. This breakthrough CSPI camera technology is poised to accelerate the practical implementation of single-pixel imaging Lidar systems.

We examine a class of enriched, unfitted finite element methods, specifically Generalized Finite Element Methods (GFEM), for solving 1D elliptic interface problems characterized by discontinuous solutions. These include problems with implicit or Robin-type interface conditions. Developing GFEM poses significant challenges, particularly in constructing enrichment functions that accurately capture solution discontinuities without causing the condition number to rapidly increase. Building on the recently developed Stable Generalized Finite Element Method (SGFEM), which utilized a single enrichment function, we extended this method to arbitrary degree using two simple, discontinuous, one-sided enrichment functions. We demonstrated optimal convergence rates in the L^2 and broken H^1 norms, as well as at all nodes. Furthermore, we applied the enriched linear, quadratic, and cubic elements to a multi-layer wall model of drug-eluting stents, where both zero-flux jump and implicit concentration interface conditions are present, to verify the efficacy of the SGFEM.

The n-qubit stabilizer states are invariant under a subset of 2^n elements in the Pauli group and can be mapped using unitary transformations from the Clifford group, which consists of Hadamard, phase, and CNOT gates. A graph structure called the "reachability graphs" can be constructed to show how stabilizers are connected through these unitaries. At n ≤ 5, these graphs have been explicitly constructed. However, when only a subset of the Clifford gates is used, the graphs break into several complicated components. The entropic structure of the stabilizer states, which is formed by applying CNOT gates to two qubits, drives an examination of subgraphs created using Hadamard and CNOT gates on only two qubits. These two-qubit subgraphs can be embedded into more complex subgraphs at three and four qubits and it's argued that this is the maximum qubit number beyond which no additional types of subgraph emerge. Nonetheless, as qubit number increases, the entropic structures within these subgraphs become increasingly complicated, with some stabilizer states at four qubits having entropy vectors that do not conform to holographic entropy principles. This has implications for the transition from holographic to non-holographic states within these reachability graphs.

The inaugural MultiEarth 2022 Challenge is designed to tackle deforestation
monitoring in the Amazon rainforest under any weather conditions. As a common
platform for multimodal processing, the Challenge unites experts in Earth and
environmental science with those in multimodal representation learning to assess
the effectiveness of different methods in accurately estimating deforestation
levels under controlled conditions. This competition will be composed of three
sub-competitions: matrix completion, deforestation prediction, and image-to-image
translation. The accompanying paper outlines the Challenge's guidelines,
datasets, and assessment criteria for each sub-competition. Further information
about the Challenge can be found on its website at
https://sites.google.com/view/rainforest-challenge.

Recent studies have highlighted the significance of achieving equilibrium between conflicting objectives during model training (e.g., accuracy versus fairness, or different fairness metrics). This emphasis on balancing competing interests is a common aspect of multi-objective optimization problems where optimization techniques seek the most suitable trade-offs between multiple goals. This work introduces a differentiable metric to enable the direct optimization of fairness across groups during model training, specifically by balancing model accuracy across different groups. We present two framework models that are independent of specific architectures for learning Pareto optimal parameterizations over different groups of neural classification models. These frameworks are tested in hate speech detection tasks where earlier research demonstrated a lack of fairness across speakers from diverse English dialects. The experimental results of various convolutional, sequential, and transformer-based models show superior empirical accuracy-fairness trade-offs compared to existing work. Moreover, our approach enables the Pareto optimization process to achieve the best achievable trade-off between fairness and accuracy based on user-defined error tolerance thresholds for each dataset.

Graphene's electronic properties can be tailored through a process called intercalation. Furthermore, this method allows for the creation of thin layers with distinct properties that differ from their bulk counterparts, resulting from the effects of confinement. This study presents a layer of graphene with lead intercalation that exhibits a neutral charge with an exceptionally low carrier density of approximately 5.5 times ten to the ninth power square centimeters. By employing a technique called momentum microscopy, researchers have detected additional energy bands related to metallic lead at the interface with graphene. Low-energy electron diffraction revealed a distinct pattern, a Moiré superperiodicity of ten by ten, that cannot be found in existing band structure data. These findings demonstrate the confinement effects in layers of heavy elements and the potential for strong spin-orbit coupling effects, potentially even leading to superconductivity in a graphene-based system.

Conversational systems based on retrieval learn to rank potential responses by comparing their vector representations to the dialogue context. However, they are restricted when learning generalizable representations because they are trained using a single format for multi-turn dialogue. To improve this, a new framework incorporates modified versions of the dialogue context into the training process. Using a secondary objective based on contrastive learning, the model learns robust representations that remain unchanged under perturbations created through an augmentation technique. This framework combines effectively with established augmentation methods, outperforming existing ranking models based on BERT. Additionally, a novel data augmentation method, ConMix, is introduced, which introduces token-level perturbations through random mixing of tokens from other contexts within a batch. Our proposed method exceeds previous augmentation techniques and yields dialogue representations more resilient to common perturbations encountered during inference.

Imitation learning offers a viable alternative for robots to develop complex manipulation skills without relying on intricate reward systems or significant computational power. Nevertheless, current methods require sophisticated data collection systems and face challenges when generalizing beyond their training data. To mitigate these limitations, researchers can obtain additional data that better captures the full range of operating conditions. This work investigates the characteristics of supplementary demonstrations and their influence on performance. It specifically explores the effects of corrective and randomly selected additional demonstrations on teaching a five-fingered robot hand to complete a pick-and-place task. Our study reveals that corrective demonstrations outperform randomly selected demonstrations when the additional data is more representative of the full task environment, compared to the original training data. Conversely, when the original training data exceeds the supplementary data, the difference between corrective and randomly selected demonstrations becomes insignificant. These findings highlight the inherent trade-off between the effort required to collect corrective demonstrations and their benefits over randomly selected demonstrations. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that inexpensive computer vision sensors can be utilized to significantly reduce the cost of providing demonstrations for complex manipulation tasks.

This paper outlines the BLCU-ICALL system's performance in the 2022 SemEval Task 1, specifically in the Definition Modeling subtrack where it ranked 1st in Italian, 2nd in Spanish and Russian, and 3rd in English and French. To address this task, we designed a transformer-based framework for multitasking that combines different embedding architectures via cross-attention and utilizes a masking language model objective to capture gloss structure. Furthermore, our approach incorporates a straightforward yet efficient ensemble method to enhance robustness. The presented evaluation demonstrates the success of our approach, and the associated code can be accessed through https://github.com/blcuicall/SemEval2022-Task1-DM.

Open clusters play a crucial role in our understanding of star formation and evolution and serve as markers for tracing the characteristics of our Galaxy. Recent advancements in accurate stellar parallax measurements and proper motions have significantly improved the isolation of open clusters from the surrounding field. However, current studies based on optical wavelengths still face limitations in terms of completeness. To overcome these limitations, this research expands the open clusters' magnitude range by incorporating near-infrared data from the VVV survey, complementing existing Gaia information. A systematic analysis of 37 open clusters was conducted, using a combination of advanced statistical methods and machine learning algorithms to categorize the clusters based on their 8-dimensional characteristics. This process enabled the successful separation of clusters from field sources at near-infrared wavelengths, resulting in approximately 47% more member candidates on average, as confirmed by a membership probability of 0.9 or higher. This study represents the second installment of a larger series focused on providing a homogeneous near-infrared representation of open cluster sequences.

This survey chronicles advancements in approximating solutions to constraint satisfaction problems over the past decade, focusing on breakthroughs within the realm of streaming and sketching computational models. Following a review of relevant findings, we delve into detailed explanations of select proofs, shedding light on a pivotal dichotomy in sketching algorithms operating in subpolynomial space, particularly highlighting their limitations.

The Earth's and other planets' rotations respond differently to external gravitational forces, largely due to their unique internal structures. Notably, the existence of a specific mode in the fluid core known as the Free Core Nutation significantly amplifies forced nutations in a particular frequency range. A related mode, the Spin-Over Mode, refers to a free oscillation of the fluid core when it is rotating steadily. Using a model of a planet with a rigid outer layer and a fluid inner core, it is demonstrated that the Spin-Over Mode corresponds to the frequency at which external and internal torques balance, causing the outer layer to maintain a constant rotation. Internal friction at the boundary between the core and mantle causes the Free Core Nutation to lose energy and slightly alter its frequency. The effect of this alteration can be approximated as a decrease in the frequency of approximately one day for the Earth, resulting from the close proximity of the Free Core Nutation frequency to that of the Spin-Over Mode, which corresponds to a minimum in the magnitude of the nutation transfer function. Additionally, this closeness results in a slightly lower Quality factor for the resonance than that calculated using standard formulas. Finally, possible implications of this mechanism are explored for Mars, the Moon, and the long-term evolution of the Earth.

In the fields of materials and life sciences, infrared hyperspectral imaging offers significant advantages but, when applied to sub-diffraction nanoimaging, becomes a highly inefficient technique due to sequential data acquisition. We have successfully incorporated low-rank matrix reconstruction into atomic force microscopy-based infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) to enhance the efficiency of hyperspectral infrared nanoimaging. To evaluate this method, we utilized trypanosomatid unicellular parasites, specifically the Leishmania species, which are crucial in biological research, focusing on a 1300-1900 cm^-1 mid-infrared spectral window with a step width of 220 nm for precise imaging. By implementing hierarchical cluster analysis and selectively utilizing only 5% of the data from 134 x 50 x 148 AFM-IR measurements, we successfully reconstructed the full data set using low-rank matrix recovery, reducing the measurement time from over 14 hours to under 1 hour. Our findings demonstrate the substantial potential for boosting the practical use of hyperspectral nanoimaging in both academia and industry, particularly when handling nano- and bio-materials.

We've calculated the thermal photon emissivity of quark-gluon plasma at a temperature of 250 MeV using data from lattice QCD and spatially transverse vector correlators. Our analysis involved correlators from two types of fermions and we compared them to other theoretical models, finding a close match within 10%. We refined this comparison by examining the spectral functions of these correlators and made a more accurate comparison between the lattice QCD results and these models. Using this refined analysis, we've developed a model to calculate photon emissivity for different frequencies and temperatures. Our results for the differential photon emission rate at a specific temperature and photon momentum are more precise than previous calculations and we found a specific rate at a certain momentum to be 2.2 plus or minus 0.8 times 10 to the power of negative 3 GeV.

The discovery of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene has made flat bands in Dirac materials a prime candidate for achieving strong electronic correlations. We demonstrate that the symmetry group preserving the Dirac cone in such materials dictates whether the cone can be flattened through adjusting a limited number of parameters. By developing a criterion that accounts for a given symmetry group, we can determine the minimum number of parameters needed to eliminate the Dirac velocity. This criterion is applied to investigate band flattening in twisted bilayer graphene and three-dimensional topological insulator surface states. Following this examination, we identify the symmetries where the vanishing Dirac velocity corresponds to the emergence of perfectly flat bands. Our analysis enables the creation of additional model Hamiltonians exhibiting perfectly flat bands at specific points within the parameter space, including a simplified model of coupled 3D topological insulator surfaces and a quasicrystalline extension of the chiral model of TBG.

The control of nonlinear stochastic systems governed by differential equations is our focus, where we develop a new approach for path-wise control. We define a concept called stochastic relative degree and a coordinate transformation that simplifies the system dynamics into a stochastic normal form, enabling the design of a state-feedback control. However, this ideal control is impractical as it requires feedback from Brownian motion, which is not directly accessible. To address this limitation, we propose a hybrid control framework that uses state measurements to periodically compensate for the noise in the system dynamics. We show that this hybrid controller achieves the ideal control performance as the compensating period becomes infinitesimally small. Furthermore, we investigate asymptotic output tracking in both the ideal and practical control scenarios. Finally, our theoretical findings are demonstrated through a numerical example.

A previously inactive Oort cloud comet, C/2017 K2 (PANSTARRS), was observed to be active at distances beyond 20 astronomical units from the Sun, likely on its first passage through the inner solar system. Using the Hubble Space Telescope, researchers mapped the dust properties in the coma of the comet at a distance of 6.82 astronomical units from the Sun before water ice began to sublimate. This revealed a distinct color and polarization gradient in the coma, indicating a high concentration of micron-sized water ice grains near the nucleus. The radial intensity profiles from the data deviated significantly from those simulated for stable dust grains, supporting the presence of sublimating water ice grains in the inner coma. Further observations with the Palomar Hale Telescope confirmed the lack of micron-sized grains in the comet's tail but showed no clear color gradient in the JHKs colors. These findings were compared to observations of other Oort cloud comets and found to be consistent with a model of micron-sized water ice grains dominating the inner coma. A reevaluation of observations of comet C/2012 S1 (ISON) also revealed a reported polarimetric halo near the nucleus to be an observational artifact.

Quantum computing has the potential to greatly accelerate time-consuming calculations, 
such as efficiently resolving complex issues across numerous variables. In high-energy 
particle collisions, quantum-aided methods may significantly improve the grouping of 
particles into streams. This research compares the effectiveness of quantum annealing 
strategies in streamlining particle groupings by maximizing the "thrust" value in 
electron-positron collisions. Our findings show that quantum annealing achieves similar 
outcomes as precise classical methods and efficient classical approximations, provided 
the annealing parameters are properly optimized. Conversely, equivalent results can be 
achieved without optimization through the integration of quantum and classical computing.

We introduce cross-view transformers, a computationally efficient model that utilizes attention-based technology for multi-camera semantic segmentation of maps. By employing a cross-view attention mechanism that is sensitive to camera calibration, our model implicitly generates a universal map-view representation. Each camera view incorporates intrinsic and extrinsic positional information, allowing a transformer to infer mappings between different views without geometric modeling. Comprising convolutional image encoders and cross-view transformer layers, our architecture achieves real-time performance while delivering a state-of-the-art solution on the nuScenes dataset at four times the speed of prior models. The code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.

The intricate patterns of proteins inside cells play a vital role in crucial cellular processes like cell division and movement, involving dynamic shape changes. These changes in cell shape, in turn, impact the behavior of pattern-forming proteins, creating a complex interplay between cell shape and chemical dynamics. Although computational studies have explored this intricate dynamics, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
