The maximum size of intersecting subsets compared to the subgroup fixing any point is the group's intersection density.  A group has the Erdős-Ko-Rado property if its largest intersecting subset equals its point stabilizer.  This research focuses on permutation groups where the point stabilizer has prime order, particularly 2 and 3. These groups don't satisfy the Erdős-Ko-Rado property.  The paper also presents infinite families of groups where a point stabilizer of order 3 yields intersection densities of 4/3, or even arbitrarily large values.

To determine equilibrium emittances and damping times due to synchrotron radiation in coupled storage ring lattices, we calculate the synchrotron radiation's impact on the normal modes of the coupled motion. By accounting for off-axis distortions, our method evaluates the radiation's projections on the normal modes, providing efficient forward calculation formulae. These formulae have been integrated into the lattice design tool OPA, enabling interactive optimization and design.

A peculiar galaxy known as CSS J102913+404220, with the unusual feature of a nuclear optical outburst, has been studied in detail. Observations spanning a decade reveal that its mid-infrared flares, with an unusually high peak luminosity, were delayed by approximately two months. This luminosity is more than 10 times greater than any known supernovae explosion, suggesting the outburst could have been caused by a stellar tidal disruption event. The X-ray emission from this galaxy showed significant variability, initially increasing by a factor of over 30 before decreasing by a factor of 4 in a short period. Notably, the X-ray changes did not correspond to any variations in optical, UV, or mid-infrared bands. The unusual behavior is consistent with other highly accreting galaxies and could be attributed to changes in the absorber's covering factor as the galaxy accretes matter. Furthermore, an unusual enhancement in the flux of a particular emission line was observed about a decade after the initial outburst, a phenomenon never seen in other galaxies. This could be the result of gas clouds interacting with the galaxy's Broad Line Region.

Recent studies have shown that artificial models, such as OpenAI CLIP, exhibit language-biased image recognition. Similar to humans who experience "picture-word interference," the models display an influence of language on visual processing. By examining this bias, researchers can gain insight into how artificial models develop semantic understanding when jointly learning from language and vision. This study introduces new methods to evaluate language-biased models and assess their semantic representation capabilities. A word-embedded image benchmark task was created to test how words superimposed on images affect model classification accuracy, and the findings reveal that the CLIP model's image classification is distorted by words. However, the study also shows that the effect of the word embedding on the model's image classification is unrelated to the semantic relationship between the image and the embedded word.

In order to combat pandemics such as COVID-19, essential items including personal protection equipment are required to minimize transmission rates and safeguard individuals who interact with patients (referencing studies like those by Heymann and Shindo in 2020, and Klompas et al. in 2021). The escalating demand for these products rapidly exceeds local manufacturing capabilities as infection numbers grow (Ranney et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020), and disruptions in global supply chains can worsen resource scarcity due to factory closures or reduced transportation routes (McMahon et al., 2020). The COVID-19 outbreak initially saw a widespread emphasis on prioritizing local communities, with various regions, countries, and continents displaying this sentiment (Baldwin and Evenett, 2020). However, this paper proposes that a collaborative resource-sharing mechanism can significantly enhance the ability to respond to and manage epidemics by ensuring communities have access to necessary resources when needed, thereby potentially preventing local shortages and reducing total infected cases. Moreover, the success of this approach relies heavily on having a considerable time gap between the emergence of epidemics in different communities, suggesting that any global resource-sharing strategy must be coupled with measures aimed at slowing down the spread of infections between communities. Our research is a preliminary step in designing a resilient global supply chain framework capable of addressing future pandemics through proactive measures rather than relying on coincidental and unequal distribution of resources among communities.

To address the cold-start issue in CTR prediction, we introduce the Variational Embedding Learning Framework (VELF). VELF tackles the cold-start problem by mitigating overfitting resulting from sparse data, using two methods: 1) learning probabilistic representations, and 2) incorporating trainable and regularized prior information derived from rich side details of new users and ads. These approaches are integrated into a variational inference framework, enabling an end-to-end training process. Our framework, as demonstrated by comprehensive benchmark tests, and further confirmed by experiments that compared parameterized and regularized priors to fixed priors, yields superior performance.

A major hurdle for ongoing and future neutrino oscillation experiments using massive Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (LAr-TPCs) is differentiating neutrino interactions from cosmic-ray noise. Although rejecting this background is achievable through conventional cut-based methods, these methods often necessitate the preliminary use of computationally intensive reconstruction algorithms. This research proposes an alternative approach employing a 3D submanifold sparse convolutional network trained on low-level scintillation light signal information from LAr-TPC interactions. The technique is applied to example simulations from the ICARUS detector at Fermilab's SBN program, demonstrating a 76.3% reduction in cosmic background while maintaining over 98.9% efficiency in selecting neutrino interactions. Additionally, the research introduces a strategy for mitigating potential biases from imperfect simulations by leveraging Domain Adversarial Neural Networks (DANNs), which are trained on modified simulated samples and real data to enhance performance, resulting in improved neutrino interaction selection efficiency even in the presence of biases.

Researchers have shown significant interest in constructing LDPC codes from permutation matrices. A key challenge when working with these codes involves avoiding short cycles in the corresponding Tanner graph, essentially trying to maximize their girth. This paper introduces a framework to generate such codes, linking cycle criteria to number-theoretic principles involving Sidon sets. As a result, we develop LDPC code examples with specific girth values, and then expand these constructions to also produce irregular LDPC codes.

We categorize singularities at infinity in polynomials of degree three across three variables. This classification allows us to determine how the Milnor number changes as we transition from a special fiber to a generic fiber based on the singularity's classification. Additionally, our analysis is used to explore global fibrations in degree three polynomials and understand the topological structure of the fibers across distinct equivalence classes.

In a modified Bayesian framework, participants assess potential outcomes and restrictions beforehand. This type of model reflects a key aspect of modern online advertising where advertisers consider their projected returns over time and may undergo changes in their identity. We aim to address the incentive compatibility challenge within this Bayesian mechanism, providing a comprehensive description under minimal assumptions on the environment, and surprisingly discover that incentive compatible mechanisms can be fully defined by auto-bidding systems, widely implemented in the online advertising sector.

Araci et al. previously developed a p-adic analogue of the Haar distribution. Using this, they created the p-adic Volkenborn integral. This paper applies the Mahler expansion to continuous functions, providing a version of the Radon-Nikodym theorem for the p-adic distribution on Zp.

A network of decision-making agents utilizes a theoretical framework derived from quantum decision theory, where choices are influenced by the evaluation of utility, attractiveness, and available information, combining to determine the probability of selecting a particular alternative. This complex interplay between these factors leads to a non-linear decision-making process. Agents interact and exchange information in two primary forms: direct information exchanged between individual agents, and collectively created information within the social network. A shared information field among agents tends to stabilize the probabilities and mitigate abrupt changes in decision patterns. In the presence of short-term memory, agents' probabilities may fluctuate erratically, sometimes indefinitely, resulting in prolonged indecision. However, activating the information field can dampen or eliminate these oscillations, causing the probabilities to stabilize at fixed values. The model describes a phenomenon known as the dynamic disjunction effect.

M. Bhargava and P. Harron demonstrated that for specific cases of n, namely n equals three, four, or five, the distribution of ring shapes in degree n number fields of S_n, arranged in ascending order by discriminant, becomes uniform in the space of these ring shapes.  In place of ring shapes, we correlate grids to the number fields, retaining more of their characteristics. The space of grids forms a complex structure that overlays the space of shapes. Building on Bhargava and Harron's findings, we have proved that grids corresponding to rings of integers in S_n degree number fields are uniformly distributed across the grid space.

The Search-Oriented Conversational AI (SCAI) conference consistently showcases advancements in conversational search. SCAI's 2021 online event featured a task on conversational question answering, where teams used answer generation models. However, assessing the correctness of generated answers proved to be a significant challenge and area for research improvement. To address this, automatic evaluation was combined with crowdsourced experiments to evaluate answer plausibility and faithfulness. Consequently, the conversational QA dataset used for evaluation was enriched with additional correct answers produced by the participant systems during the shared task.

We have developed an implementation of the adaptive compression exchange (ACE) 
operator within the LAPW framework, enabling a low-rank representation of the 
Fock exchange without sacrificing total energy precision. Our findings confirm 
that ACE maintains its precision in non-relativistic calculations for all-electron 
systems using the PBE0 hybrid exchange-correlation functional. The calculated data 
for light atoms and molecules closely align with exact multi-resolution-analysis 
results, deviating by a few $\mu$Ha. In addition to ACE, high-energy local orbitals 
played a crucial role in achieving such high precision when incorporating Fock exchange. 
Utilizing this implementation, we have calculated PBE0 gaps in solids and compared 
them with other all-electron results.

NGC 1566 is identified as a changing look active galactic nucleus that repeatedly exhibits long-lasting X-ray outbursts. An increase in X-ray flux of approximately 24 times the historical minimum was observed in 2018. By analyzing pre-outburst, outburst, and post-outburst data, researchers have confirmed the discovery of a broad feature in the 5-7 keV band during the outburst period that is likely caused by relativistic iron K-alpha emission. This finding supports the hypothesis that X-rays originate in a corona above the accretion disk. Moreover, the response of narrow iron K-alpha emission to X-ray continuum variability occurred on a timescale as short as four months, suggesting the line-emitting region is small, similar in size to the optical broad line region. When compared to NGC 2992, NGC 1566 shows a greater variation rate of the iron K-alpha line relative to luminosity, which could be due to the presence of more gas or iron responsible for producing the line. The strength of the variable broad iron K-alpha line and soft X-ray excess emission appears to be correlated with the accretion rate, possibly due to a state transition associated with the changing-look phenomenon.

We examine a social learning framework in which at each point in time, agents randomly select one of their neighbors to obtain information from. Our findings demonstrate that under this reduced-communication protocol, agents ultimately arrive at the correct information and, notably, achieve an asymptotic convergence rate identical to that of conventional algorithms requiring more communication resources. Additionally, we develop large deviation estimates for log-belief ratios in a specific scenario where an agent replaces its existing belief with that of the selected neighbor.

More than two decades ago, Abadi et al. developed the Dependency Core Calculus as a versatile framework for examining dependencies within typed programming languages. Following this breakthrough, dependency analysis has delivered numerous practical advantages in the field of language design, including the capacity to facilitate users and compilers in enforcing security restrictions, and the elimination of redundant code among other applications. Our research proposes a novel expansion, the Dependent Dependency Calculus, which adapts this fundamental concept to a dependently-typed language context. By employing this calculus, we can monitor both runtime and compilation-time redundancy, thereby accelerating type verification and program execution.

We investigated the nonlocal dispersion compensation of broadband photon pairs transmitted over standard ITU-T G.652D fiber by measuring their precise temporal relationship. By adjusting the distance that the photon pairs traveled through the fiber, we successfully compensated for dispersion near perfection by closely maintaining the timing correlation between them at a level matching the resolution of our detection equipment. Experimental results showed that such high-quality dispersion compensation can be achieved even with relatively long segments of fiber (1km), which is feasible for real-world implementation. Ultimately, we maintained the photon timing correlation at a low level (51ps$\pm$21ps) across two 10km long stretches of metropolitan fiber with multiple sections.

For online food service platforms, reliable food reviews and suggestions have always been crucial. Nonetheless, evaluating and recommending food can be complicated due to diverse contexts and interpretations. This study employs various deep learning techniques to address challenges in sentiment analysis, automatic review categorization, and retrieval of food reviews. We are developing a web-based food review system at Nanyang Technological University, called NTU Food Hunter, which utilizes multiple deep learning methods to facilitate users in selecting food. Initially, we incorporate the BERT and LSTM deep learning models into the system for sentiment analysis of food reviews. Subsequently, a Part-of-Speech algorithm is developed to automatically extract adjective-noun pairs from the review content, using POS tagging and dependency parsing, for the purpose of generating review tags. Furthermore, a RankNet model is also trained to re-rank retrieval results and enhance the precision in our Solr-based food reviews search system. The experimental results demonstrate the potential of our proposed deep learning approaches for addressing real-world challenges.

We examine the sensitivity of split non-classical spin states with multiple characteristics, such as spin-squeezed and Dicke states, which are spread across several distinct modes that can be addressed individually. Mathematical formulas describing the spin-squeezing matrix of a set of states that can be achieved with current atomic experiments show how these states can enhance the precision of multi-parameter measurements and identify the best approaches to maximize this sensitivity. Furthermore, we investigate the entanglement between modes in these states by developing a test based on the spin-squeezing matrix for determining genuine entanglement among k components. Our findings demonstrate the benefits of mode entanglement for distributed sensing, and outline the most effective protocols for estimating multiple parameters using non-classical spin ensembles that are distributed across space.

We study the melting and undercooling behavior of gold nanoparticles, which are approximately 100 nm in radius, and suspended in a vacuum using a quadrupole ion trap. To observe these changes, the particles are heated with a laser and their properties are monitored through two primary methods. The first approach involves tracking the particle's mass loss during heating to estimate its temperature. The second method involves analyzing the differences in light scattering patterns that occur when the particle is in its liquid and solid states. By repeatedly heating the particles and varying their size, we investigate how particle size influences heating behavior and melting characteristics. Furthermore, we induce undercooling in these particles by using a series of laser pulses, and examine the degree of undercooling that occurs, comparing it to theoretical models.

We translated Emile Mathieu's paper "On the five-fold transitive function of 24
quantities" into English to facilitate our project involving the expression of $M_{23}$
in terms of additive functions on the finite field with 2^11 elements.

The task of network alignment involves identifying corresponding nodes between two networks, based on both structural properties and attribute information. Our investigation focuses on the existing network alignment methods which typically identify all node pairs simultaneously, and thus fail to utilize valuable information generated during the node matching process, which can lead to improved accuracy in subsequent correspondence discoveries. To address this issue, we propose Grad-Align, a novel network alignment method that gradually uncovers matching node pairs by leveraging early-stage correspondences with strong consistency. Specifically, Grad-Align initially generates node embeddings for both networks by utilizing graph neural networks in conjunction with our designed layer-wise reconstruction loss. This loss function effectively captures neighborhood structures at multiple levels. Subsequently, the method progressively aligns nodes by computing similarity metrics based on multi-layered embeddings and Tversky similarity, which accommodates differences in network scale. Furthermore, an edge augmentation module is incorporated into Grad-Align to strengthen structural consistency. Experimental evaluations on real-world and synthetic datasets reveal that Grad-Align consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art network alignment methods.

In populations, disparities in capital or resource allocation are notable phenomena. Understanding the sources of these disparities and potential remedies is of practical value. To investigate this issue, a model of interaction between agents in a network designed to mitigate wealth inequality is developed. To achieve the desired outcome of reduced inequality, we consider various interpretations of a game played within the network. The objective of this game is such that winning translates to a decrease in wealth disparities. The study explores the influence of different game interpretations on agent behavior and capital distribution, incorporating examples based on the capital-dependent Parrondo's paradox. The findings provide new insights into the dynamics of wealth inequality in society.

Recurrent recommender systems have proven to effectively capture temporal patterns in user behavior. However, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) struggle to identify long-term patterns due to limitations, causing RNN-based recommender systems to prioritize short-term user preferences over long-term interests. This phenomenon, known as recency bias, can have a negative impact on user satisfaction and overall system health. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel data augmentation technique called recency dropout, which enhances the robustness of recurrent recommender systems. We showcase the efficacy of recency dropout in a range of experiments, including simulations, offline evaluations, and real-world deployments on a large-scale commercial recommendation platform.

A long-standing problem in computer science is finding the minimum flow decomposition (MFD), where a flow is broken down into its simplest components. This is particularly relevant in bioinformatics, where solving MFD is crucial in RNA assembly tasks. However, existing algorithms are limited due to the NP-hard nature of the problem, forcing researchers to resort to heuristics or simplified versions. In RNA assembly tools, these limitations result in suboptimal solutions. Recently, a breakthrough has been made in creating a practical integer linear programming (ILP) formulation for MFD. This new approach can solve MFD instances in under 13 seconds, making it an efficient exact solver. Moreover, the ILP formulation can be easily adapted to accommodate various real-world scenarios, such as longer reads or error minimization, offering a promising solution to the tradeoff between complexity and tractability in RNA assembly. This advancement has the potential to become a fundamental component in future RNA assembly tools, overcoming current limitations.

Constructing a precise cosmic distance scale from a single vantage point in an irregular universe poses a challenge. To measure distances to distant Type Ia supernovae, nearby reference points must first be accurately determined. We've developed a framework that can accommodate a perturbed universe where minor irregularities exist on a flat spacetime background. This configuration results in an approximately 11% adjustment to the standard area distance calculations due to the surrounding universe's inhomogeneities. The primary contributor to this modification is the Weyl tensor's electric component, indicating a deformation of spacetime near the observer. Furthermore, we've explored the implications of this effect on Type Ia supernova absolute magnitudes in the Hubble flow. Our analysis reveals that this adjustment could simultaneously address the tensions between the supernova absolute magnitude and Hubble constants without requiring dark energy to manifest early or late in the universe's evolution.

This research explores a cosmological scenario where phantom energy dominates the universe with an equation of state parameter less than -1, and examines its long-term behavior. The author investigates the possibility of reaching a Big Rip singularity in the future, proposing that general relativity could prevent this event through the gravitational creation of particles, even in the absence of other particle-producing mechanisms. The model suggests that, in its distant future, the universe will have a constant, high Hubble rate and energy density, along with a low horizon entropy. Similar conditions existed at the universe's inception, potentially enabling the avoidance of the Big Rip singularity and guiding the universe toward a future inflationary phase, during which multiple new universes may emerge.

A gyroscope for detecting rotational movement is a crucial component in navigation systems, relying on precision. Recent interest has focused on using quantum technology to develop gyroscopes with greater accuracy than those limited by traditional noise constraints. Current quantum gyroscope designs are, however, severely hindered by decoherence, a phenomenon that defies precise measurement according to the no-go theorem of metrology. Our proposed quantum-optical-gyroscope scheme, utilizing two entangled optical fields as a quantum probe, circumvents this limitation by achieving the super-Heisenberg limit of sensitivity, even in noisy environments. Our analysis reveals that this optimal sensitivity can be attained when each optical field interacts harmoniously with its surroundings, paving the way for precise rotation sensing in realistic conditions.

A novel Boltzmann-Gibbs model is introduced, which characterizes local interactions within the energy functional through a spatial coupling function. The function utilizes smoothed derivatives, inspired by smoothed particle hydrodynamics theory, and is approximated by a second-degree polynomial of the Laplace operator. An explicit expression is derived for the Gaussian smoothing kernel, allowing the model to smoothly transition from discrete to continuous field representations, with connections established to Gaussian Markov random fields and the Matern field.

We revisit the concept of itinerant ferromagnetism in two and three-dimensional electron gases with any degree of spin-orbit splitting and intense electron-electron interaction. Our research reveals that the ferromagnetic quantum critical point is unstable at low temperatures due to resonant electron scattering near the Fermi surface. Unlike prior theoretical research, we demonstrate that these processes can't be completely eliminated even in the presence of varying spin-orbit splitting. A fully self-contained, non-linear treatment of electron-electron interactions near the phase transition reveals that these resonant processes consistently destabilize the ferromagnetic quantum critical point, resulting in a first-order phase transition. These processes can be identified by the non-analytical relationship between spin susceptibility and magnetic field, whether measured at a distance or near the phase transition.

In a multi-source status update system with varied source characteristics, a source-aware packet management policy has been implemented for an M/G/1/1 queueing model. The preemptive policy was designed to minimize age of information (AoI), where new packets from the same source override existing packets in the system. Moment generating functions (MGFs) have been derived for the AoI and peak AoI under this policy, as well as for source-agnostic preemptive and non-preemptive policies, which have previously only yielded average AoI and peak AoI results. Furthermore, MGFs were utilized to calculate average AoI and peak AoI for a two-source system under each policy. Numerical analysis indicates that service time distribution parameters significantly impact AoI performance: for heavy-tailed distributions, preemptive policies are superior, while light-tailed distributions benefit from non-preemptive policies, underscoring the importance of higher moments in understanding AoI dynamics.

Gaussian processes are valuable tools in machine learning and statistics for modeling continuous processes. By using known process values at a finite set of points, Gaussian processes can construct an interpolating surface for prediction and uncertainty assessment at other locations. However, this is not always feasible when information is given on the boundary of a domain, forming an infinite set of points. In this study, we develop a Gaussian process model based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces that combines both finite and uncountable information scenarios, by leveraging the connection between conditional expectations and orthogonal projections. This new model is explored in a statistical context, including numerical considerations and a proof-of-concept.

Deep learning-based liver segmentation continues to gain traction in clinical settings due to the rising prevalence of liver cancer. Despite the development of various medical image segmentation networks, accurately identifying liver lesions remains a persistent challenge. In response, this work proposes a hybrid model called SWTR-Unet, integrating convolutional and transformer-based architectures. The network, which incorporates a pre-trained ResNet and Unet-style decoder, was tested on real-world liver MRI data and the publicly available LiTS CT challenge. The results were compared against several top-performing models, and the SWTR-Unet achieved exceptional accuracy on both datasets. Specifically, the method demonstrated Dice similarity scores of 98% for liver and 81% for lesion segmentation on MRI data, and 97% and 79% respectively on CT data, outperforming all other networks tested. Furthermore, the results were comparable to those obtained through manual expert segmentation, underscoring the model's potential to streamline clinical workflows.

Recent studies have demonstrated the susceptibility of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks. Notably, the emergence of 3D adversarial attacks on point clouds has garnered significant attention, but existing approaches produce adversarial samples that have limited transferability and can be easily defended against. To address these shortcomings, this research proposes a novel point cloud attack strategy, AOF, which focuses on manipulating the low-frequency aspects of point clouds. AOF achieves this by integrating losses derived from both the point cloud and its low-frequency component to create more effective adversarial samples. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AOF substantially improves transferability compared to state-of-the-art attacks, while also being more resilient to current 3D defense methods. Moreover, AOF-generated adversarial point clouds exhibit more pronounced deformation than outliers compared to their clean counterparts.

The influence of nuclear structure on multiplicity ($N_{ch}$) and anisotropic flow ($v_{2}$ and $v_{3}$) is studied in the isobaric collisions of $^{96}_{44}$Ru + $^{96}_{44}$Ru and $^{96}_{40}$Zr + $^{96}_{40}$Zr at four energy levels using the string melting version of the AMPT model. Research findings indicate that, when compared to recent experimental data released by STAR collaboration, quadrupole deformation has a significant impact on $v_{2}$ in central collisions, while octupole deformation affects it in near-central collisions. The neutron skin effect is the main factor influencing these effects in mid-central collisions. These effects become more pronounced at lower energies.

We revisit the concept of importance weighted variational inference (IWVI), an innovative method for training latent variable models. IWVI leverages novel variational bounds, termed Monte Carlo objectives (MCOs), achieved by substituting uncomputable integrals with Monte Carlo approximations, often derived through simple importance sampling. Building on Burda, Grosse, and Salakhutdinov's 2016 findings that increasing the number of importance samples strengthens the bound's connection to the likelihood, we present a series of non-asymptotic results linking Monte Carlo estimate properties to MCO tightness. We challenge the assumption that reduced Monte Carlo variance results in better bounds and theoretically verify recent empirical findings indicating that negative correlation actually decreases the variational gap. Additionally, we extend the original monotonicity theorem to incorporate non-uniform weights. Our work applies several ideas and results from stochastic order theory.

We examine the behavior of a simple congestion game with two resources, where a vast number of agents employ a modified version of the Experience-Weighted Attraction algorithm. The dynamics are influenced by three parameters: the population's intensity of choice, a discount factor reflecting memory loss, and a parameter accounting for the asymmetry between the cost functions of the two resources. Our analysis reveals a wide range of bifurcation phenomena within this framework, where the dynamics transition from global convergence to equilibrium, limit cycles, or even chaotic behavior as the parameters change. We find that for any discount factor, a sufficiently large population intensity choice can lead to instability, with memory loss initially resulting in chaotic behavior, but giving way to predictable, periodic patterns as the discount factor increases. Our theoretical study is complemented by simulations and bifurcation diagrams that demonstrate the intricate complexity of population dynamics in this simple scenario.

Neural networks known as capsule networks have shown great promise in various computer vision tasks. Nonetheless, traditional capsule networks struggle to outperform state-of-the-art models on more complex datasets due to the significant computational and memory demands. To address this limitation, we introduce the Momentum Capsule Network (MoCapsNet), a novel architecture influenced by reversible residual building blocks used in Momentum ResNets. These reversible networks allow the reuse of activations in the forward pass during backpropagation, substantially reducing memory requirements. This paper explores the application of invertible residual building blocks to capsule networks and demonstrates that MoCapsNet surpasses baseline capsule networks on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with significantly less memory usage, while also providing open-source code at https://github.com/moejoe95/MoCapsNet.

To define continuity in the abstract, we need to first establish what it means for a set to be open in a given space, which involves a set of rules known as a topology. A topology is characterized by three fundamental principles that govern the properties of open sets within it. In this paper, we will explore the implications of altering one of these principles on the concept of a continuous function.

Solving the problem of finding the most cost-effective paths within a connected graph involves determining the minimum total cost for traversing the graph's edges. Typically, traditional methods cannot be applied when the costs of edges need to be adjusted in real-time according to specific requirements. However, it is now possible to represent path-finding problems as a neural network by mapping cost values to synaptic weights. This allows for the adaptation of weights through network learning mechanisms. Starting with an initial activity level, the network's activity propagation produces solutions equivalent to those generated by the Bellman Ford algorithm. Moreover, the neural network's computational complexity is comparable to Bellman Ford, and it can be shown that learning mechanisms, such as Hebbian learning, can adapt the weights to enhance the paths according to the task at hand. This novel approach is demonstrated through applications such as navigating around obstacles and following specific sequences of nodes, potentially enabling a new range of applications where path enhancement is seamlessly integrated with path finding.

The existence of the axion particle remains uncertain, but research suggests the axion field's potential in developing a localized theory of chiral gauge theory with both classical and quantum symmetry. Analogous non-Abelian axion fields have been introduced, enabling the creation of non-Abelian chiral gauge theories utilizing their unique properties. In these contexts, gauge symmetry is typically compromised, resulting in the mass acquisition of the gauge boson as it absorbs the non-physical axion particles.

We investigate four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ gauge theories that exhibit S-confining properties, which makes them equivalent to a Wess-Zumino model. S-confining theories with a simple gauge group have already been classified. We establish that all S-confining dualities in the list hold when matter fields transform according to rank-$1$ and/or rank-$2$ representations. Our argument is based solely on established S-confining dualities for $SU(N)$ with $N+1$ flavors and $Usp(2N)$ with $2N+4$ fundamental representations. To achieve this, we employ a step-by-step process involving a sequence of deconfinements and re-confinements, carefully considering the explicit superpotential at each stage.

In thermal equilibrium, we investigate the local and bipartite entanglement R\'enyi entropies of the free Fermi gas in a multi-dimensional space. We demonstrate that these entanglement entropies, for R\'enyi index $\gamma\leq1$, are positive for all temperatures above zero. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the entropies for large temperatures and large scaling parameters in two distinct scenarios - one where the chemical potential remains constant, and another where the particle density is held constant. This investigation completes the missing piece in our proof of temperature-dependent results for the free Fermi gas, which were initially established for $\gamma=1$.

The discrete Fourier transform holds great significance in photonic quantum information, however its scalability to high dimensions heavily relies on physical encoding methods, particularly in emerging platforms like frequency bins, where practical methods are still lacking. This letter demonstrates that d-point frequency-bin DFTs can be implemented using a three-component quantum frequency processor by adding a radio-frequency harmonic for each incremental increase in dimension d. Numerical simulations confirm a high gate fidelity and success probability, with these values experimentally verified for up to d = 10 dimensions. Our findings open doors for implementing high-dimensional frequency-bin protocols in quantum communication and networking applications.

This paper builds upon our prior research on spherical representations in the framework of operator algebras. We begin by exploring equivalent concepts to dimension groups using operator systems and their associated relatives. We then extend our analysis to the inductive limits of compact quantum groups, establishing a parallel to Olshanski's concept of spherical unitary representations in the context of quantum groups. Our findings also validate Ryosuke Sato's approach to quantum group representation theory at an asymptotic level.

The approximate solution of the Klein-Gordon equation for a real scalar field in a Kerr black hole's geometry, initially found by Detweiler, is commonly utilized in the study of black hole stability and axion-like particles. Our research verifies a previously overlooked $1/2$ factor in this solution, first discovered in a separate study. After correcting this result, we observed unexpected characteristics that question the effectiveness of a specific analytical strategy. We address this issue by incorporating the next-to-leading order contribution, which significantly reduces the percentage error of the basic solution, particularly for $r_g\mu$ values up to 0.35. In this range, the error is roughly 10% or less. The corrected solution is also notably more compact and easier to apply.

Natural language inference has become increasingly crucial for natural language understanding, which necessitates inferring the relationship between a pair of sentences (premise and hypothesis). To this end, many recent studies have employed contrastive learning by utilizing the relationship between sentence pairs from NLI datasets to obtain sentence representations. Notwithstanding, existing approaches primarily focus on comparisons at the sentence level. In this paper, we introduce a novel Pair-level Supervised Contrastive Learning approach, referred to as PairSCL. Our method leverages a cross attention module to acquire joint representations of the sentence pairs. A carefully crafted contrastive learning objective is designed to differentiate among the diverse classes of sentence pairs by attracting those within one class and repelling those from other classes. We evaluate the efficacy of PairSCL on two publicly accessible NLI datasets and observe that it outperforms other methods with an average improvement of 2.1% in terms of accuracy. Moreover, our proposed method surpasses the previous state-of-the-art approach on seven text classification transfer tasks.

Researchers at RHIC conducted the "isobar run" to compare $^{96}_{40}Zr$ and $^{96}_{44}Ru$ collisions to understand how nuclear properties influence the outcomes. However, the STAR data revealed unexpected differences between the two isotopes, leading to more pronounced effects than anticipated. Subsequent studies focused on quantifying the geometric differences, particularly in relation to specific observables. It is widely acknowledged that the observed discrepancies are linked to the isotopes' nuclear structure, particularly their lowest-energy states. However, a comprehensive connection between low-energy and high-energy nuclear physics remains unclear. In this study, I propose a theoretical link through thermal density matrices, considering nuclei at an elevated temperature to determine which excited states should be taken into account. Furthermore, I suggest employing a semiclassical "flucton" method at finite temperatures to calculate thermal density matrices.

We've developed a new probabilistic model for identifying noisy pattern repetitions in sparse binary data, building upon the Noisy-OR model used in disease and topic modelling. The model's capabilities are demonstrated through its application in extracting structure from retinal neuron recordings, and it has broader potential in discovering and modelling hidden patterns in binary data with noise. Specifically, in the context of spiking neural activity, the task involves attributing the firing of individual neurons to groups, known as "Cell Assemblies," which often synchronise their activity due to interactions or other factors. Our model identifies sparse patterns of activity in a set of binary variables representing cell assemblies, with each active assembly decreasing the likelihood of its constituent neurons being inactive. By learning the conditional probability kernels from data via expectation maximization, we infer the latent states and adjust the model parameters. We've validated the model using artificially generated spike trains, mimicking recorded retinal responses, as well as applied it to actual recordings of retinal ganglion cells during movie stimulation, revealing the underlying structure in the data.

We investigate a 3D ternary system, derived from the Nakazawa-Ohta density functional theory for triblock copolymers, which considers both interface energy and long-range interactions. Although binary systems in 2D and 3D, as well as ternary systems in 2D, have been extensively studied, there is limited knowledge on the ternary case in 3D. Specifically, it remains unclear whether minimal configurations consist of a finite number of components. In this research, we provide evidence that minimal configurations in the 3D ternary system have a limited number of components by proving that the upper bound depends solely on the total mass and interaction coefficients. However, the 3D structure of the system poses challenges in decoupling the long-range interactions from the perimeter term, making it difficult to determine the exact shape of minimal configurations, even for systems with small masses. This is largely due to the absence of a quantitative isoperimetric inequality in 3D with two mass constraints, complicating the creation of competitive minimal configurations.

A novel communication approach, task-oriented image semantic communication, prioritizes conveying meaning for artificial intelligence (AI) tasks over image quality. Yet, in autonomous driving applications, both image reconstruction quality and AI task performance are equally important to optimize. To address this, a task-oriented semantic communication scheme with semantic reconstruction (TOSC-SR) is proposed. TOSC-SR's primary objective is to minimize distortions at both pixel and semantic levels within a specified data rate, posing a new rate-distortion optimization challenge. A semantic distortion metric, quantified by mutual information between reconstructed images and task labels, is introduced. Subsequently, an analytical solution is derived to determine the optimal image mapping. For practical implementation, a variational approximation of mutual information is used to formulate an extended rate-distortion model applicable to multiple AI tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed TOSC-SR approach outperforms traditional and deep learning-based methods in image reconstruction, AI task performance, and multi-task generalization ability.

When applying Chebyshev's method to a given polynomial $p$, the degree of its resulting polynomial $C_p$ can be determined. For cubic polynomials, it's found that $C_p$ can have a degree of $4,6,$ or $7,$ and we investigate the dynamics of $C_p$ in each case. It has been established that if the cubic polynomial is either unicritical or non-generic, the connectedness of the Julia set of $C_p$ holds true. Furthermore, a family of rational maps, resulting from the application of Chebyshev's method to a non-unicritical and generic cubic polynomial, is parameterized by the multiplier of one of its extraneous fixed points. If we denote a member of this family with a specific multiplier $\lambda$ by $C_\lambda$, we've proven that the Julia set of $C_\lambda$ remains connected whenever $\lambda$ falls within the interval $[-1,1].$

Epilepsy ranks as the world's fourth most prevalent neurological condition, affecting individuals across all age groups. When standard treatments like medication and surgery fall short, Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) offers an alternative solution. To standardize this treatment and streamline its planning, a reliable algorithm is needed to automatically pinpoint the precise DBS target – the Anterior Nucleus of the Thalamus. This target is notoriously difficult to plan, making our comprehensive comparison of localization techniques all the more crucial. Our benchmarking study evaluates a range of methods, including traditional registration and advanced deep-learning-based approaches, such as heatmap matching and DSNT. Our results demonstrate that deep-learning methods, trained using pseudo labels, achieve comparable accuracy to human variability and far surpass traditional techniques in speed.

The dynamics of 2D truncated Airy waves and three-component solitons are studied within a system of two frequency components and their second-harmonic fields, connected by quadratic (chi^(2)) interactions. This system is representative of optical media that generate second harmonics and certain mixtures found in Bose-Einstein condensates. Besides maintaining stable solitons, the system also supports truncated-Airy-waves in a fundamental-frequency component, represented by exact, stable solutions, which differ from Airy waves seen in a similar, but degenerate, two-component system. Moreover, it is possible to introduce vorticity into the 2D Airy modes. We examine through simulations how two 2D Airy waves originating in distinct fundamental-frequency components, moving in opposite directions, interact via the second-harmonic field. The interaction results in the fusion of the input waves into a pair of narrow solitons, contrasting what is observed in a one-dimensional (1D) system where the waves split into numerous solitons. When two Airy waves carrying the same imprinted vorticities collide, they produce an additional pair of solitons, whereas opposite vorticities create a group of small-amplitude solitons ("debris") in the output. Slow-moving solitons interacting with a truncated Airy wave bounce back, whereas fast solitons are absorbed by it, with fast soliton collisions being quasi-elastic. Additionally, soliton collisions at different velocities result in either a single mode merger or elastic passage.

When subjected to mechanical stress, amorphous solids tend to undergo plastic deformation.
Studies have found that these plastic events in disordered particulate systems, which are usually of a quadrupolar nature, can dampen the elastic response. At high quadrupole densities, the gradients of their fields generate emergent dipole effects, leading to a shift in the mechanical behavior as seen in the displacement patterns.
This study investigates the phenomenon of screening in traditional glassy substances, comprised of point particles that interact via pairwise forces. Our analysis, encompassing both inverse power law forces and Lennard-Jones interactions, reveals that the elastic response can be significantly reduced in both scenarios, in line with the newly developed theory.
The extent of this departure from classical elasticity is quantified using a proposed new metric that is shown to correlate with the amount of energy dissipated during plastic deformation.

A specific type of branching program is a natural model for read-once linear branching programs where queries are in the form of $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear equations and each path's queries are unique. Two variations of this model, weakly and strongly read-once branching programs, are examined. These models generalize standard read-once branching programs and parity decision trees. 

Key findings are:

  - Average-case difficulty. Pseudo-random functions called directional affine extractors are developed and shown to be difficult to solve on average for strongly read-once branching programs. An explicit construction of these functions with good parameters is provided. This strengthens a previous result on parity decision trees. These functions are a stronger version of well-known affine extractors and may be of independent interest.
  - Proof complexity. The $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ proof system, an extension of resolution that uses linear queries, is also studied. It's shown that a linear branching program for solving a search problem corresponds to a refutation of a CNF in this system, and vice versa.

A proposed framework for designing approximation algorithms using Lyapunov functions comprises two stages. Initially, inputting a Lyapunov function generates a continuous-time approximation algorithm with a guaranteed level of accuracy. The second phase transforms this continuous algorithm into a discrete-time algorithm with an equivalent accuracy, as well as a provable execution time. A unique aspect of this framework is its flexibility, allowing the parametric form of the Lyapunov function to be determined after the first phase through optimization. Several advantages of using Lyapunov functions include the unification of existing algorithms, provision of a guideline for developing and analyzing new algorithms, and offering fresh perspectives for enhancing existing methods. Various submodular maximization problems are employed as case studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework.

A collection of sets meets the Helly property, if all subgroups sharing a common intersection also have an intersection. A graph is classified as Helly if the sets of its maximal complete subgraphs follow the Helly property. This study establishes that for k-regular graphs with n vertices where n is greater than a certain threshold 3k + sqrt(2k^2-k), the complementary graph does not possess the Helly characteristic. Additionally, the investigation explores whether Hellyness and the convergence of the clique graph operator share equivalent properties for k-regular graph complements, especially when k has a small value.

We re-examine the problem of a Noether current linked to local scale symmetry or equivalently Weyl symmetry, which vanishes identically. Utilizing the second Noether theorem for a local symmetry, we demonstrate that in four-dimensional Riemannian geometry, the Noether current associated with Weyl symmetry typically vanishes within any gravitational theories that are Weyl invariant. We further clarify the reason for this: Weyl transformations are non-dynamical because they lack a derivative term of the transformation parameter, unlike conventional gauge transformations. Additionally, we apply this finding to a quantum theory of general Weyl invariant gravity, leading to the derivation of currents associated with choral symmetry, which is rooted in $IOSp(10|10)$ supersymmetry.

Autonomous driving relies heavily on precise 3-D object detection, which has been efficiently achieved through point cloud-based methods due to their accurate depth information. Building upon existing datasets like KITTI, the nuScenes dataset, developed by NuTonomy, offers a significant expansion in terms of size, sensor modalities, categories, and annotations. Nevertheless, this dataset faces a severe class imbalance issue. A study on Class-balanced Grouping and Sampling presents an augmentation and sampling approach to resolve this imbalance but its localization precision is hindered by the loss of spatial details in downscaled feature maps. In response, we propose to enhance the performance of the CBGS model by incorporating an auxiliary network that leverages the structural details of 3D point clouds, ultimately boosting the localization accuracy. This auxiliary network is optimally trained with two distinct point-level supervisions – foreground segmentation and center estimation – without adding extra computation during inference, as it can be detached during testing.

Our Aegis Combat System implementation utilizes command and control principles. 
Key components include missile guidance and tracking functionalities. 
A simplified Aegis model will be developed to explore these aspects further. 
In this simplified model, a small car will autonomously mimic the movement of a remote-controlled car. 
The model consists of three main components: a control unit and two small vehicles. 
Through this simulation, the team can illustrate how real-world command and control concepts function, specifically command issuance, communication protocols, and sensor data integration.

Decision-making theories, including Fuzzy-Trace Theory (FTT), propose that individuals rely on a text's essential meaning, its core message, when making decisions. We introduce GisPy, an open-source Python tool designed to quantify the Gist Inference Score (GIS) of text. Our evaluations on benchmark datasets from news and scientific texts show that GisPy's scores effectively differentiate between documents with low and high levels of gist content. The GisPy tool is accessible to the public via: https://github.com/phosseini/GisPy.

In weakly supervised text classification, pseudo-label quality significantly impacts performance, but these labels are inherently noisy and unreliable. Identifying the most reliable pseudo-labels can greatly improve performance. Selecting samples based on their neural classifier's softmax scores is a simplistic approach but it is inefficient and unstable due to overconfident predictions from mis-calibrated models. Inspired by research on deep learning memorization patterns, we developed the LOPS method which considers the order in which samples were learned. We propose that earlier-learned samples have a higher likelihood of being mis-annotated, thus suggesting they be prioritized for removal. Our LOPS approach can be easily integrated into various weakly-supervised text classification methods to enhance performance as demonstrated through extensive testing on multiple real-world datasets.

For numerous reasons such as establishing trust and diagnosing model inaccuracies, it is desirable to assess an explanation's reliability. Our work, centered on the natural language inference task, introduces a novel method called Faithfulness-through-Counterfactuals, which creates hypothetical scenarios to test the consistency of a model's predictions with its provided logic. Unlike existing techniques, this method doesn't necessitate training a separate verification model. We verify the effectiveness of automatically generating counterfactual hypotheses using the few-shot learning paradigm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed measure can distinguish between human and model agreement or disagreement on newly introduced hypothetical scenarios. Finally, a sensitivity analysis confirms that our metric responds appropriately to explanations lacking reliability.

Our investigation focuses on how the angular momentum of guided photons transfers to a two-level atom with a quadrupole transition near an optical nanofiber. The generation of an axial orbital torque on the atom from the driving field is determined by the quadrupole transition's internal-state selection rules and angular momentum conservation. The torque depends on the photon's angular momentum, the change in the atom's internal angular momentum, and the quadrupole-transition Rabi frequency. We performed numerical calculations for the torques between specific hyperfine-structure levels of a $^{87}$Rb atom. Our results indicate that the absolute value of the torque is higher for the higher-order mode HE$_{21}$ compared to the fundamental mode HE$_{11}$, except in a specific case where the torque for HE$_{21}$ is zero.

In our initial investigation, we analyzed the combination of the isoscalar pseudoscalar meson $\eta$ and the pseudoscalar glueball $G$ within the framework of $N_f=2$ QCD at the pion mass $m_\pi\approx 350$ MeV. Our research determined the mass of the $\eta$ to be $m_\eta=714.1(5.4)$ MeV, allowing us to estimate its $SU(3)$ equivalent at $\sim 935$ MeV via the Witten-Veneziano relation. Utilizing a large-scale gauge simulation, we found the energy and mixing angle of the $\eta-G$ interaction to be $|x|=107(14)$ MeV and $|\theta|=3.47(46)^\circ$ based on $\eta-G$ correlators derived through the distillation method. Additionally, we verified that $m_\eta$ can be accurately deduced from $\eta-\eta_c$ correlators, where $\eta_c$ is the pseudoscalar charmonium. We concluded that the interaction between the $\eta$ and the glueball is extremely small, and the QCD $U_A(1)$ anomaly primarily accounts for the mass of the $\eta$.

This paper explores how goal-oriented dialogue systems can assist users in achieving specific objectives. However, the effectiveness of these systems in the eyes of their users is largely unexamined. We address this knowledge gap by developing computational metrics to gauge the helpfulness of these systems. By defining a dialogue response as valuable if it's relevant, logical, useful, and informative, we gather human feedback on response helpfulness and train a model to autonomously evaluate the helpfulness of dialogue responses. Furthermore, we propose assessing the fairness of dialogue systems by considering how helpful they are across different types of user inquiries. Experiments involving leading dialogue systems under various information-seeking contexts show that existing systems often perform better when responding to queries about advanced concepts from developed nations than those from less-developed regions, highlighting underlying fairness concerns with current goal-oriented dialogue systems.

Over the past few years, research on learned representations of point clouds has been gaining momentum, building on the concept of 3D shapes. Although existing representations have become more expressive, most still struggle to accurately reconstruct point sets. To address this limitation, a novel sampling model, dubbed 'Spotlights,' was developed to represent 3D shapes using a compact array of depth values. This model mimics the configuration of cameras placed evenly around a sphere, where each virtual camera projects light rays through sample points on a small concentric cap to detect intersections with the surrounding object. As a result, the structured point cloud is defined implicitly as a function of depth. A comprehensive geometric analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of this new sampling scheme in the context of point cloud completion. Experimental results showed that our method outperforms state-of-the-art completion methods in terms of accuracy, consistency, and computational efficiency, also yielding superior performance on the downstream point cloud registration task.

Recent research has highlighted the potential for large language models to leak personal information through memorization of their training data, particularly during the pre-training phase. However, little is known about the privacy risks associated with the fine-tuning phase, where different methods (like fine-tuning the full model or specific components) could have varying levels of vulnerability to data exposure. As the 'pre-train and fine-tune' approach becomes more widespread, there's growing concern about the potential consequences of fine-tuning methods on data privacy. This study investigates how different fine-tuning techniques fare against membership inference and extraction attacks, revealing significant differences in their susceptibility. The findings show that fine-tuning the model head is particularly vulnerable to these attacks, whereas using smaller adapters appears to be less susceptible.

A new family of techniques, characterized by lightweight fine-tuning methods,
permits parameter-efficient transfer learning by making targeted adjustments
to a small subset of parameters while leaving pre-trained language model
parameters intact. Despite its effectiveness, there has been no research on
how knowledge of downstream fine-tuning approaches should inform pre-training.
This study demonstrates that choosing the right fine-tuning method prior to
pre-training can significantly enhance the performance of parameter-efficient
fine-tuning. By utilizing meta-learning through modified MAML, we adapt
pre-trained models for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, achieving up to 1.7
points of improvement in cross-lingual NER fine-tuning tasks. Our experiments
show that the specific adjustments made to MAML are key to achieving these
gains.

The High Intensity Proton Accelerator (HIPA) at Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI) produces a 590 MeV continuous-wave proton beam with 1.42 MW power capacity, then it transfers this beam over a 120 meter long channel towards surface muon production stations before depositing remaining power at SINQ. In the High Intensity Muon Beamline (HIMB) study, a modified target will enhance muon production but managing proton beam losses is essential; a novel approach utilizes combined temperature and beam measurements to predict losses using Monte Carlo simulations for improved understanding of power deposition.

In 1984, Gauduchon analyzed a functional involving the squared norm of his torsion one-form on a compact Hermitian manifold. He derived the associated Euler-Lagrange equation, revealing that in 2-dimensional space, only torsion-free critical metrics are valid. This note builds upon his work by proving the same principle applicable in higher dimensions. Moreover, this study also explores the squared norm of the full Chern torsion, with concrete examples demonstrating the existence of critical points that are not Kählerian.

We investigate the influence of eccentricity on the precision of gravitational wave parameter estimation for binary neutron star systems. Using signals with low eccentricity simulated for advanced LIGO sensitivity, we utilize the Bayesian method based on a circular waveform model to determine how estimated parameters deviate from their actual values, focusing on intrinsic properties like chirp mass, symmetric mass ratio, and tidal deformability. By comparing our results with those obtained from the analytical Fisher-Cutler-Vallisneri method, we establish valid criteria for the FCV approach. Applying the FCV method and considering a realistic distribution of binary neutron star sources across the m1-m2-e0 space, we compute measurement errors and systematic biases, as well as their generalized distributions within a specified range of eccentricity. Our findings show that biases for all three parameters increase with higher eccentricity values, with this increase being more pronounced for larger eccentricities. We discover that biases are largely dependent on the eccentricity and only weakly dependent on the masses of the binary neutron stars, leading to a narrow band in the e0-bias plane. We provide examples to illustrate our results, including the bimodality of posteriors, and demonstrate the importance of including eccentricity in parameter estimation to avoid incorrect predictions of the neutron star equation of state.

The task of Visual dialog, or VisDial, involves responding to a series of image-based questions, taking into account the conversation history. Current methods for training VisDial models focus solely on labeled VisDial data or utilize pre-trained models on similar vision-and-language datasets. This research proposes a semi-supervised learning technique called Generative Self-Training, GST, which utilizes unlabeled web images to significantly expand the available training data. GST first selects relevant images, generates simulated conversations about them using text generation techniques, and then trains the model on these generated conversations combined with the original VisDial data, thereby scaling up the training data by a factor of up to 10 (1.2M to 12.9M). To enhance the model's training robustness, this research introduces a data selection method based on perplexity and a multimodal consistency regularization approach. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on VisDial v1.0 and v0.9 datasets and demonstrates substantial performance gains in low-data scenarios, with improvements of up to 9.35 points in terms of NDCG.

To combat noise in hard-to-access data qubits, a spectator qubit is employed to detect and compensate for disturbances, given its increased sensitivity. This qubit is frequently measured, and its results are sporadically used to rectify errors in the data qubits. A Bayesian strategy combining complex linear maps has been developed for the dephasing phenomenon caused by random telegraph noise, leading to an optimal adaptive protocol for measurement and control. As a result, the decoherence rate can be effectively reduced, with its suppression rate proportional to the sensitivity of the spectator qubit, thereby confirming the effectiveness of this approach in suitable conditions.

Text generation systems often produce inaccurate content, but for Data-to-Text (D2T) applications, it's crucial to ensure the facts in generated text are accurate. Our proposed framework, R2D2, tackles unfaithful text generation by training a model to both generate text and evaluate its faithfulness. To make this process more efficient, we suggest methods for creating unfaithful sentences and propose additional metrics to assess a system's entity recognition capabilities. Our results demonstrate that R2D2 effectively reduces inaccurate text generation, setting a new standard on several benchmarks, including FeTaQA, LogicNLG, and ToTTo, with notable improvements.

This thesis aims to investigate and examine potential attack pathways on the Iota 2.0 protocol, focusing on the Distributed Ledger Technologies' existing vulnerabilities and assessing their relevance to the Iota 2.0 framework. A targeted attack against the ledger's integrity is proposed and dissected within a network configuration featuring nodes running a full version of the Iota protocol.

A significant limitation in researching image captioning in many languages has been the absence of high-quality evaluation datasets. This study introduces the Crossmodal-3600 dataset, a comprehensive collection of 3600 images from diverse geographical regions, each with 36 language captions written by humans. These images are chosen to represent areas where the 36 languages are spoken and are annotated with captions that exhibit consistent style across all languages, ensuring that the captions were not directly translated. Our dataset serves as a new benchmark for evaluating and selecting image captioning models that operate across multiple languages and shows improved alignment with human evaluations when used as a standard for automated assessment metrics.

This paper presents FLEURS, a novel benchmark for evaluating universal speech representations in a few-shot learning setting, encompassing 102 languages and a 12-hour speech dataset per language. FLEURS is built upon the machine translation benchmark FLoRes-101 and is applicable to various speech tasks such as Automatic Speech Recognition, Speech Language Identification, and Retrieval. We provide initial performance metrics for FLEURS using pre-trained multilingual models like mSLAM, aiming to expand speech technology capabilities in underrepresented languages and stimulate low-resource speech understanding research.

We establish the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of the following Cauchy problem \begin{equation}\label{ab eqn} \begin{cases}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(t,x)=\psi(t,i\nabla)u(t,x)+f(t,x),\quad
&(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d,\\ u(0,x)=0,\quad & x\in\mathbb{R}^d
\end{cases} \end{equation} within weighted Lp-spaces, using time-measurable pseudo-differential operators. Specifically, we identify conditions on the symbol $\psi(t,\xi)$ to ensure the problem's well-posedness in these weighted Lp-spaces. The smoothness of the symbol with respect to $\xi$ is characterized by a property of the weight. We demonstrate that a solution u satisfies the inequalities: 
$\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x) |^p (t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt \leq N\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x)|^p (t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt,$
and 
$\int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x) |^p |x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt \leq N\int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x) |^p |x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt$, under certain conditions on the parameters p,q, alpha, alpha1, and alpha2, and where $\gamma$ is the order of the operator $\psi(t,i\nabla)$.

The advancement of event extraction has been hampered by the scarcity and imbalance of data. In this research, we introduce a self-training with gradient guidance (STGG) framework which involves (1) an initial training phase using existing event annotations followed by its application to large unlabeled corpora to predict new event mentions, and (2) a scoring model that assesses the correctness of event predictions based on the AMR graph. The predicted events along with their correctness scores are then utilized as pseudo labels to refine the event extraction model, and the gradients of this model are guided by the correctness scores. Experiments on ACE05-E, ACE05-E+, and ERE-EN datasets demonstrate STGG's effectiveness, achieving up to a 1.9 point increase in F-score over the base model. Furthermore, our analysis reveals STGG's versatility, enabling its application to various event extraction models and outperforming them when combined with extensive unlabeled data, even without the high-quality AMR annotations.

The cartoon domain has gained significant traction in recent times. Despite previous efforts to apply portrait stylization to this domain, they have struggled to address the critical challenges involved, such as needing a vast library of training images and an inability to effectively handle abstract cartoon facial structures. Recently, researchers have employed layer swapping techniques for stylization, requiring a minimal amount of training data; however, its usage remains limited as it still inherits the underlying problems. In this paper, we introduce a new method called Cross-domain Style mixing, which combines the latent codes from two different domains to achieve stylization of faces across multiple cartoon characters at varying levels of abstraction using a single generator.

Multilingual question-answering systems that rely on document retrieval may struggle with inconsistencies when processing documents in various languages, as they can provide a model with differing information about the same topic. To investigate how language influences these systems, we examine the behavior of open-domain multilingual models, specifically the impact of retrieval bias. Our analysis involves evaluating multiple retriever models and their responses to the same questions in different languages on two multilingual question-answering datasets, TyDi QA and XOR-TyDi QA, with a focus on whether cultural differences and social biases manifest through varying document content.

We introduce a new resampling-based technique for developing an asymptotically accurate statistical test that evaluates any group of hypotheses concerning coefficients within high-dimensional linear regression. This method can be seamlessly integrated into multiple testing procedures to enable reliable statements about relevant predictor variables. Our approach constructs individual hypothesis test statistics by utilizing data partitioning and a variable selection strategy, and then combines these test statistics to create a subset test. This resulting procedure boasts exceptional adaptability, as it permits various selection techniques and multiple aggregation functions. We present the method in two variants: an exact formulation and an approximate variant that necessitates reduced memory usage and shorter computation time, thereby facilitating scalability to high-dimensional scenarios. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations and an analysis of real gene expression data.

Current machine translation models face difficulties with complex inputs like distorted information and less common phrases. Various studies have tackled this robustness issue by recognizing specific noise patterns and adjusting models to excel at handling them. A significant but understudied problem involves subtle, nuanced differences that maintain the intended meaning in the target language. We define and explore this phenomenon as Natural Asemantic Variation and analyze its impact on machine translation robustness. Our results show that standard translation models are unsuccessful when dealing with Natural Asemantic Variation, however, we demonstrate that fine-tuning these models with human-introduced variations enhances performance. Furthermore, our findings indicate that robustness to Natural Asemantic Variation can be effectively applied across languages, and artificially created distortions can replicate some but not all benefits of naturally generated variations.

Mathematical techniques such as discrete integration, gradient descent optimization, and state estimation are generally confined to Euclidean spaces due to their reliance on linear algebra. However, this article outlines a way to adapt these methods for use with non-Euclidean state vectors, particularly those involving rotational and translational movements of rigid bodies. To achieve this, the article delves into the mathematical properties of the SO(3) and SE(3) Lie groups, focusing on various representations, their tangent spaces, perturbation analysis, and the specific Jacobian definitions necessary for implementing the previously mentioned calculus methods.

Given certain Hilbert modules over bounded symmetric domains of rank $r$, we can break down their "eigenbundle" (localization bundle), yielding complex-analytic fibre spaces with a stratified structure of length $r+1$. The structure of these fibres is explained in terms of Kähler geometry as sections of line bundles over flag manifolds, and their metric embedding can be precisely determined through the derivatives of reproducing kernel functions. Key illustrations of this phenomenon include the determinantal ideals characterised by specific vanishing conditions along the distinct strata resulting from the stratification.

We investigate the challenge of generating text from large pre-trained language models that meet specific requirements while remaining coherent and maintaining their accuracy in downstream applications. Our solution, MuCoLa, allows users to impose arbitrary constraints on the model, which are then incorporated into a unified energy function along with the model's inherent probability. By utilizing a novel non-autoregressive sampling technique, MuCoLa initializes text with noise and applies iterative refinement using stochastic optimization to converge on desired outputs. We demonstrate the efficacy of MuCoLa in scenarios involving both strict and flexible constraints, achieving notable advancements over comparable methods in terms of avoiding toxicity, managing sentiment, and incorporating target keywords into generated text.

In the realm of Android malware detection, machine learning (ML) techniques have gained prominence as a potential solution, giving rise to various proposals incorporating diverse algorithms and feature sets, which often exhibit remarkable detection capabilities. Nevertheless, these proposals are often hindered by the absence of a standard evaluation framework and the lack of reproducibility, making it challenging to compare their performance. In this paper, we undertake a comprehensive analysis of ten notable research works on Android malware detection, utilizing a common evaluation framework to facilitate comparison. Through extensive experimentation, we identify five critical factors - duplicated samples, label attribution, class imbalance, evasion techniques, and app evolution - that significantly impact the performance of trained ML models if not carefully considered. Our findings reveal that the studied ML-based detectors have been evaluated unrealistically, thereby contributing to the optimistic published results. Furthermore, our research underscores the necessity of crafting realistic experimental scenarios that take into account these factors, aiming to foster the development of more effective ML-based Android malware detection solutions.

Modern natural language processing systems primarily rely on large language models. These models exhibit exceptional accuracy and robustness but are hindered by their substantial computational demands, leading to slow and expensive inference. Recent research has aimed to alleviate this burden by employing techniques such as structured and unstructured pruning, quantization, and distillation to accelerate inference and reduce model size. This study focuses on exploring the transferability of models pruned with gradual unstructured magnitude pruning across domains and tasks. The experiment reveals that models pruned during pretraining with general domain masked language models can successfully adapt to new domains and tasks without the need for exhaustive hyperparameter tuning or tailored approaches. Specifically, we show that our general sparse model can be transformed into a specialized model by fine-tuning the compressed architecture on a specific domain's text, as demonstrated by our Sparse*BERT becoming SparseBioBERT after pretraining on unstructured biomedical text. Furthermore, SparseBioBERT achieves comparable quality to BioBERT while using only 10% of its parameters.

The edges of cells play a significant role in detecting external signals and navigating their environment through the process of spreading and movement. Recent studies suggest that the edges of these cells wrap around fibers found outside the cell, but the mechanisms behind this wrapping process are not well understood.
