To address this, we have conducted a comprehensive study combining theoretical models and experimental observations of how cell protrusions coil around fibers of different shapes. Our theoretical framework describes how specific proteins within the cell membrane drive protrusions, and identifies key factors influencing the direction in which the edges of the protrusions curve around fibers. According to our model, cells tend to curve their edges when interacting with round fibers, but stop doing so when encountering flat or elliptical fibers. These predictions are supported by detailed observations using advanced microscopy techniques that allow for precise examination of cell behavior on suspended fibers of varying sizes.

Deep learning models for cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) face challenges due to the scarcity of expert-generated labels and the inherent complexity of the data. Self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) has been shown to enhance performance in medical imaging tasks. However, it is uncertain how effectively pre-trained representations capture the primary organ of interest as opposed to irrelevant surrounding tissues. In this research, we investigate the optimal approach to incorporating anatomical prior knowledge into SSCL training. Specifically, we examine the use of a segmentation network to explicitly identify the heart in CMR images, followed by SSCL pretraining on multiple diagnostic tasks. Our findings suggest that leveraging prior anatomical knowledge can significantly improve downstream diagnostic performance. Moreover, pre-training with in-domain data generally improves performance and results in human-like saliency, as compared to end-to-end training and ImageNet pre-trained networks. Nevertheless, introducing anatomical knowledge to pre-training does not significantly contribute to the outcome.

This research analyzed the impact of repulsive nucleon-nucleon interactions stemming from the Pauli exclusion principle on the half-lives of heavy even-even nuclei within the Z range of 84 to 92. By incorporating the Pauli exclusion principle into our analysis, we adjusted the nucleon-nucleon interactions based on the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition and also used it as a correction term in the double-folding formalism. Specifically, we evaluated the kinetic energy variation at the overlap points between the alpha and daughter nuclei. Our results indicate that the standard deviation of calculated half-lives compared to experimental data decreased from 0.340 to 0.309 when incorporating the kinetic energy contribution estimated using the extended Thomas-Fermi approach. This suggests that associating the kinetic energy contribution with the double-folding formalism yields more accurate alpha decay half-lives.

Using the continuum Skyrme Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory formulated with the Green's function method, the exotic properties of neutron-rich Ca, Ni, Zr, and Sn isotopes are explored. The experimental separation energies are accurately reproduced, with predictions of shorter drip lines made using one-neutron separation energies as compared to two-neutron separation energies. The neutron pairing energies are found to be significantly lower in odd-$A$ nuclei than in their even-even neighbors, due to the lack of pairing energy contribution from unpaired odd neutrons. By examining the single-particle structures and density distributions of these isotopes, the presence of halo structures is predicted. This is characterized by sharp increases in rms radii and highly diffuse density distributions. The orbitals with low angular momenta near the Fermi surface are identified as the main contributors to the extended density and large rms radii. The occupation numbers of neutrons above the Fermi surface, in the continuum, exhibit behaviors consistent with those of the pairing energy, supporting the crucial role of pairing correlations in the formation of halos.

The DeGroot-style opinion formation model assumes ongoing interactions within a social network. It struggles to account for agents that temporarily connect with those within the network. Real-world entities like businesses often find themselves in this scenario, where they aim to influence a large audience but are restricted by time. To address this limitation, we've developed a DeGroot model variation enabling external agents to interact with the network for a specified duration. By studying and simulating this variant, we gain insights on optimising an external agent's influence in opinion formation.

As networked control systems expand and interactions between separate components become increasingly complex, concerns about network resilience have grown in significance. A new research area focusing on applying graph theory to redefine traditional system and control concepts has gained attention. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of using graph-theoretic techniques to analyze networked control system resilience. We discuss various decentralized algorithms operating on networked systems and assess their robustness against malicious actions by examining their network structures. Furthermore, we describe methods to measure attack impacts and reframe system-theoretic concepts of resilience from a graph-theoretic perspective to minimize attack effects. Additionally, we explore various security-related challenges in networked control systems and utilize graph theory as an analytical tool. Finally, we highlight potential avenues for future research in this field.

The intricate vacuum fields present in QCD serve as the base for matter, and this presentation uses advanced visualization tools to dissect their microscopic composition. Centre vortices, found within these ground-state fields, hold particular significance, and we are currently working to understand how dynamical fermions in QCD's vacuum modify the centre-vortex configuration. The influence of these fermions is considerable and offers fresh perspectives on the role of centre vortices in the confinement of particles and the breaking of chiral symmetry within QCD.

In crowded ion environments, steric repulsion between ions and solvent molecules becomes crucial, and the conventional Poisson-Boltzmann equation needs to be revised. We examine the steady-state limit of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations with steric effects by assuming that such effects transform the equations into a Poisson-Boltzmann type equation with steric effects (PB-steric equation), incorporating a parameter that accounts for the ion and solvent radii. This model reduces to the conventional PB equation when the parameter is zero, but increases as the parameter increases, representing stronger steric repulsion. We study the limiting case where the parameter goes to infinity and show that the PB-steric equation has a unique solution that converges to the solution of a modified PB equation under specific boundary conditions. Our findings suggest that the limiting equation is a form of modified PB equation that is equivalent to previously established models.

Recent advancements in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) heavily rely on deep neural networks, which pose an interpretability challenge for experts. While previous studies on interpretable reinforcement learning achieved promising results with decision tree-based policies in the single-agent setting, a gap exists for the multi-agent scenario. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first algorithms for extracting interpretable decision-tree policies from MARL-trained neural networks. Building on VIPER, a single-agent interpretable RL method, our first algorithm, IVIPER, is adapted for MARL environments and demonstrates the capability to learn high-quality decision trees for each agent. To better capture the inter-agents coordination, a centralized algorithm, MAVIPER, is developed, which grows each agent's decision tree while considering the predicted behaviors of the other agents. MAVIPER's use of resampling allows it to focus on critical states affecting its interactions with other agents. Our experiments show that both IVIPER and MAVIPER outperform baseline models, with MAVIPER-trained agents exhibiting better coordination on three MARL environments.

The complex reasoning processes of neural language models are notoriously difficult to interpret. Researchers have made progress in automatically generating machine rationales to understand these models, but the impact of using these rationales to improve model performance is still underexplored. A specific technique called explanation regularization (ER) aims to enhance model generalization by aligning machine and human rationales. Current studies mostly evaluate ER models' in-distribution generalization, while overlooking their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization capabilities. Furthermore, the influence of ER criteria and training instances with human rationales on model performance remains unclear. In response, a novel protocol called ER-TEST has been proposed to evaluate ER models' OOD generalization across multiple dimensions. By utilizing ER-TEST, researchers can investigate the most effective ER criteria for OOD settings, the impact of training instances with human rationales, and whether ER can be effective even with limited and distantly-supervised human rationales. ER-TEST allows for a comprehensive analysis of these questions by considering a diverse range of tasks and datasets. Through ER-TEST, researchers have found that ER has minimal impact on in-distribution performance but can significantly improve out-of-distribution performance. Additionally, the study shows that the best ER criterion varies depending on the task, and ER can still yield benefits in OOD performance even with scarce or distantly-supervised human rationales.

A significant problem in reinforcement learning is defining tasks in a way that is both understandable and verifiable. To overcome this issue, a common technique involves specifying tasks using reward machines – finite state machines that outline the task to be solved. We present a skill machine representation that can be directly learned from these reward machines and encodes the solution to such tasks. Our approach involves a framework where an agent first learns a set of fundamental skills in a setting without rewards and then uses these skills combined with the learned skill machine to create composite behaviors defined by any regular language, such as temporal logics. This allows the agent to map complex logical task specifications to near-optimal behaviors with zero additional learning. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness in both a tabular and high-dimensional video game environment where an agent faces various long-horizon tasks. The results indicate the agent can meet extremely complex task requirements while achieving near-optimal performance with no further learning. Furthermore, we show that the performance of skill machines can be enhanced using regular offline reinforcement learning algorithms when optimal behaviors are the primary goal.

We investigate concentration phenomena for discrete-time random dynamical systems, specifically in the context of an unbounded state space. A functional approach is devised to establish exponential concentration inequalities for such systems. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the presence of an exponential-type Lyapunov function not only ensures stability in these systems but also leads to exponential concentration inequalities when sampling from their stationary distribution, leveraging the transport-entropy inequality. This research has notable implications in reinforcement learning and control, enabling exponential concentration inequalities even for unbounded observables without requiring assumptions of reversibility or complete knowledge of the random dynamical system, as typically necessary in concentration inequalities for statistical mechanics and Markov diffusion processes.

The circuitry world revolves around three fundamental elements - capacitors, resistors, and inductors, which are defined by their relationships to voltage, current, charge, and flux. However, the introduction of the memristor, proposed by Leon Chua in 1971, challenged this concept by suggesting a fourth fundamental element that relates flux to charge. This theoretical concept was practically realized in 2008 by researchers at HP Labs who presented a model for a physical memristor and its advantages, including variable resistance, flexibility, and compatibility with CMOS technology. The memristor exhibits distinct characteristics for different applications, resulting in the development of various models. As a result, devices based on memristors have numerous applications, such as memory, logic, and neuromorphic systems. To facilitate the analysis of circuit behavior and the development of memristor-based applications, a computer model of the memristor is essential. In this paper, the simulation of various VerilogA memristor models is presented, using sinusoidal inputs and verifying their outputs under different window functions, to analyze the circuit behavior of these models.

In Federated Learning, user data privacy is a significant concern and ViT models have a particular vulnerability to privacy leaks when subjected to specific types of attacks. We've discovered that a feature that accelerates training in ViTs, by learning spatial patterns in input data, actually poses a major risk to user privacy. By understanding this weakness, researchers have found a way to protect user data by making the model position-insensitive, but removing the related component from the model may actually make it more susceptible to attacks. To resolve this conflict, a novel technique called Masked Jigsaw Puzzle has been developed to protect user data from being compromised. This method is straightforward to implement and can be easily integrated into existing ViT models. Experimental results show that MJP not only enhances model performance but also significantly boosts the model's ability to protect user data from privacy leaks. The full implementation is available at https://github.com/yhlleo/MJP.

Current research on Entity Linking often relies on the assumption that reference knowledge bases are comprehensive, allowing for seamless linking of all mentions. However, this assumption rarely holds true in reality, as knowledge bases are frequently incomplete and new concepts continually emerge. This paper addresses this limitation by developing the Unknown Entity Discovery and Indexing (EDIN) benchmark, where entities lacking descriptions in knowledge bases and labeled mentions must be integrated into a conventional entity linking system. By comparing EDIN to zero-shot entity linking, we gain insight into the unique challenges it presents. Leveraging dense-retrieval based entity linking, we propose the end-to-end EDIN pipeline that detects, groups, and indexes mentions of unknown entities within context. Experimental results demonstrate that unifying information from multiple mentions via a single entity embedding outperforms indexing individual mentions independently.

Recent advancements in neural attention models have achieved notable improvements in various natural language processing tasks. However, their applicability to long text summarization is hindered by the self-attention module's memory complexity, which increases quadratically with input length. Rather than designing more efficient attention modules, we explore the possibility of models with limited context outperforming memory-efficient models that maintain a global context. To this end, we apply our model to individual units, such as pages, which contain locally grouped input segments during both encoding and decoding. We conducted experiments on three levels of text summarization, ranging from sentence-level to document-level locality. Our results demonstrate that our model exceeds the performance of strong baselines utilizing efficient attention modules, and our analysis offers deeper insights into our locality-driven modeling approach.

State-of-the-art performance has been achieved in Natural Language Processing (NLP) by Large Language Models (LMs). Yet, the escalating cost, time, and environmental impact of continually developing and enlarging these models are becoming significant concerns. To address this challenge, researchers are investigating alternative approaches to improving model performance. One promising method involves transforming complex data into forms that more effectively exploit a model's existing capabilities, thereby rendering challenging questions more manageable. This involves determining whether humans can break down intricate queries into simpler, more easily solvable components that leverage a model's strengths. Our research has yielded encouraging results, revealing that question decomposition can notably enhance model performance, for instance, by as much as 24% for GPT3 and 29% for RoBERTa-SQuAD in combination with a symbolic calculator. Moreover, our approach offers an innovative way to involve people in NLP research and presents a potential alternative route to developing large-scale LMs. The code and data for our study are available at https://github.com/Pruthvi98/QuestionDecomposition

Surveys play a crucial role in informing policy, decision-making, and social understanding. Nevertheless, conducting large-scale surveys to generate accurate subpopulation data can be both costly and time-consuming. A promising solution lies in Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP), which enables reliable subpopulation estimates from smaller survey datasets. Although graphical representations have become a staple in communicating and analyzing MRP results, there is a scarcity of research on optimal visualization strategies for this field. This study addresses this knowledge gap by conducting a systematic literature review to examine the current practices of MRP visualization. To further illustrate the implications of current visualization methods, we apply MRP to analyze the Trump vote share in the 2016 U.S. presidential election using the Cooperative Congressional Election Study (CCES) data. Our findings indicate that current practices often overlook the significance of uncertainty in survey inference. Furthermore, we demonstrate how incorporating uncertainty into visualization can facilitate a deeper understanding of model performance and specification effects. Building on these insights, we propose a novel visualization strategy that takes into account the bias-variance trade-off when evaluating MRP models.

As technology advances with smaller nodes and more complex processor clusters used in high-risk areas, faults triggered by radiation during operation are a significant concern, affecting design choices. This study proposes an innovative approach for dynamic error resilience in core architecture by integrating a new On-Demand Redundancy Grouping method into an open-source RISC-V processor system. This allows the cluster to seamlessly transition between high-performance operation as six individual cores and fault-tolerant operation as two combined cores without incurring significant overhead. The added redundancy unit takes up a remarkably small portion of the processor's area, causing negligible timing delays and outperforming commercial alternatives in recovery times by 2.5 times. Moreover, when redundancy is unnecessary, this approach enables the redundant cores to handle separate computations, leading to a 2.96-fold increase in efficiency for specific tasks.

Calculating the similarity between text data terms and their meaning is crucial for various applications, such as knowledge acquisition, personal recommendation, and natural language processing. The development and use of ontologies over the past few years have provided a structured knowledge base for information systems, which has led to the advancement of semantic similarity calculation from these ontologies. This can be complemented with other methods depending on the specific context. This paper aims to present and implement an approach to calculate semantic similarity using ontologies in the context of a recommender system.

A conditional set generation approach learns how to map an input sequence of tokens to a set. Applications of set generation, such as identifying entities and categorizing emotions in dialogue, can be effectively tackled using sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models. However, these models often overlook the inherent characteristics of sets - order invariance and size - by treating them as sequences instead. A new algorithm has been developed to sample informative set orders from the vast label ordering possibilities, thus addressing this issue. This proposed method combines the estimation of set cardinality with the generation of a set by prepending its size and utilizing the autoregressive factorization technique used in Seq2Seq models. It acts as a data augmentation tool that can be integrated with any Seq2Seq model, enabling them to capture the signals of order invariance and size without requiring extra annotations. The model demonstrates its efficacy by yielding an average relative improvement of 20% on four benchmark datasets using different models: BART, T5, and GPT-3. A publicly available implementation of the method, known as SETAUG, can be found at: https://setgen.structgen.com.

Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) have excelled in various image generation tasks by gradually reversing the diffusion process of the data distribution back to a Gaussian distribution. This reversal process, which generates a high-quality image from noise, is extremely inefficient, often requiring hundreds to thousands of steps in practice. To address this issue, this work proposes a strategy called Early-Stopped DDPM (ES-DDPM), which accelerates the process by stopping the diffusion earlier, when the noise is still non-Gaussian, and leveraging a pre-trained generative model to efficiently generate images. By combining the two approaches, ES-DDPM significantly reduces the number of required denoising steps and produces images of higher quality, outperforming both vanilla DDPM and the pre-trained model. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate the promising acceleration effect and improved performance of ES-DDPM over baseline methods, while also offering several attractive properties, including orthogonality with existing acceleration techniques and simultaneous control over global semantic and local pixel-level aspects of image generation.

Recent applications of Deep Neural Networks to hyperspectral image classification have been successful, yet the majority of previous studies employed general deep architectures without considering the unique structure of hyperspectral images, including physical noise generation. As a result, these models are unable to produce effective features, thus hindering their classification performance. To address this limitation, we designed a novel deep learning framework incorporating a noise-oriented module and denoising mechanism specifically tailored for hyperspectral image classification. Firstly, we modeled the spectral signatures of hyperspectral images using a physical noise model, highlighting their high intraclass variance and class overlap. We then developed a noise-oriented module to capture and a denoising framework to remove such noise. Ultimately, the proposed CNN architecture with these modules yields discriminative features and achieves high classification accuracy. Our experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. The code and implementations of the proposed and comparative methods can be accessed via the repository at https://github.com/shendu-sw/noise-physical-framework.

To mitigate noise in isolated qubits with minimal measurements, researchers can employ an auxiliary noise probe and correct only when necessary. A theoretical study, inspired by solid-state qubits, examines dephasing noise from two-state fluctuations and introduces a spectator qubit to aid noise reduction. By analyzing the effectiveness of various measurement and control strategies in a regime where noise mitigation is optimal, the study begins with the Greedy algorithm, which focuses on maximizing qubit coherence at each step. The results show that this algorithm is effective and can be approximated by a simpler method with just a few parameters. This led to the development of a one-parameter algorithmic family that significantly reduces qubit decoherence rates, particularly in scenarios with high noise sensitivity. By fine-tuning this algorithm, the study found that the Map-based Optimized Adaptive Algorithm for Asymptotic Regime outperforms the Greedy approach, particularly in high-noise sensitivity environments.

The phrase "nobody is safe until everybody is safe" underscores the interconnected world's vulnerability to pandemics, such as COVID-19, which necessitates a unified global response. To model and explore various vaccination strategies during the ongoing pandemic, we developed a model simulating a virus's spread across interconnected communities. Starting with susceptible populations and considering a susceptible-vaccinated-infected-recovered model for unvaccinated ("Bronze"), moderately vaccinated ("Silver"), and well-vaccinated ("Gold") communities, we found that the "Bronze" community drives an increase in infections in the "Silver" and "Gold" communities, highlighting the adverse effect of non-vaccination on vaccinated communities. In network scenarios, coupling strength and network density significantly influence the spread of a virus, particularly between different communities. Our analysis in Barabasi-Albert networks showed that moderately and well-vaccinated communities ("Silver" and "Gold") experienced lower infections compared to unvaccinated communities ("Bronze"). Notably, even a small number of unvaccinated communities can trigger an increase in infections among vaccinated communities. When examining various network structures, including dense Erdos-Renyi, sparse Watts-Strogatz, and Barabasi-Albert networks, we discovered that communities in dense networks reached a disease-free state more quickly, whereas communities in sparse networks struggled to eradicate the virus.

In this theoretical study, we investigated the $D\bar{D}K$ three-body system using the fixed center approximation of Faddeev equations, taking into account the chiral unitary interactions between $D$ and $K$, and $D$ and $\bar{D}$ mesons. We examined the $K$ meson scattering off a cluster of $D\bar{D}$, considering the possibility of forming a scalar meson $X(3720)$. Due to the strong $DK$ interaction, which dynamically generates the scalar $D^*_{s0}(2317)$ meson, our calculations reveal a resonance in the three-body $K$-$(D\bar{D})_{X(3720)}$ scattering amplitude, indicating the formation of a $D\bar{D}K$ bound state. Our findings align with earlier theoretical predictions of a new excited hidden charm $K$ meson, specifically $K_{c\bar{c}}(4180)$, with $I(J^P) = \frac{1}{2}(0^-)$ and a predicted mass around $4180$ MeV. These results are expected to inspire experimental searches to validate the existence of this meson.

In this research, we focus on a dynamic resource allocation problem where T sequential resources must be divided among n fixed agents who have additive utilities drawn from a known probability distribution. Agents' resource allocations are made immediately and cannot be changed. Most previous studies on dynamic resource allocation have aimed to maximize the overall well-being of agents, potentially leading to unfair allocations where a few agents receive most of the resources while others go without. In this paper, we explore a different approach by focusing on the fair allocation of resources to all agents, balancing efficiency and fairness in the allocation process. We first develop a fluid-based policy based on a deterministic model of the problem and show it achieves a level of regret comparable to the square root of the total time T, measured against the optimal allocation that can be achieved with perfect knowledge of utilities in advance. We then introduce a new policy called Backward Infrequent Re-solving with Thresholding, which limits the number of times the fluid problem is re-solved to O(log log T) and demonstrates a significantly lower regret of O(1) against the optimal allocation, regardless of the total time T and initial resource distribution. Additionally, we present simulation results demonstrating the improved performance of the new policy compared to previous approaches.

As autonomous systems become more capable, concerns over safety grow more pressing,
particularly in unstructured environments. To mitigate these risks, this research introduces
a safety feature that identifies and responds to destabilizing influences from external sources.
This safety layer operates independently, complementing existing nominal control systems such as
position tracking or wrench management. When instability is imminent, the system restricts power flow
to prevent adverse consequences. This method leverages the Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE) to gauge
the rate of change in the system's dynamics, signaling potential dangers. By continuously computing this
metric, hazardous system behavior can be quickly detected and addressed. By integrating the LLE with
Control Barrier Functions, the system can enforce limits on power consumption, ensuring a jerk-controlled
system remains stable. The proposed architecture has been successfully tested on an Omnidirectional Micro
Aerial Vehicle in various flight scenarios.

We examine the classic problem of distributing a divisible and heterogeneous resource, like a cake, among a group of agents with the goal of achieving fairness. This study introduces a variation of the problem where agents are connected on a network. Each agent compares their portion of the cake only to the portions received by their neighbors. Given a network, the objective is to quickly identify a fair distribution where every agent prefers their portion to that of any of their neighbors. Currently, the most efficient algorithm for this problem has a high time complexity. This research makes significant contributions by finding a simpler network structure - a tree-like network with two levels of connections - where a fair distribution can be efficiently calculated using a query-based approach. This approach involves dividing a cake into portions to ensure a fair distribution among agents on such networks with an average time complexity of O(n^3 log n). For a specific case of this network structure, the task can be completed in O(n^2) steps. Additionally, this study demonstrates the minimum number of steps required to determine a fair distribution in certain network configurations.

Current methods for conducting cybersecurity threat and risk analysis automate some, but not all, aspects of the process, requiring experts to make critical decisions based on their individual judgment. In practice, teams of specialists manually analyze software systems through group brainstorming sessions, leaving room for potential bias and unequal representation of different viewpoints, particularly from underrepresented groups such as women in the field. Despite the importance of understanding non-technical threats, the impact of diversity on technical risk analysis has not been thoroughly researched. This paper aims to establish an experimental framework for examining the key factors influencing diversity in risk analysis.

This research tackles the issue of mobility in massive multiple-input multiple-output systems, leading to substantial performance losses in 5G mobile networks. We present a new channel prediction approach called multi-dimensional matrix pencil (MDMP), which estimates channel paths by utilizing the angular-frequency-domain and angular-time-domain characteristics of wideband channels. MDMP also introduces a novel path pairing technique to pair delay and Doppler frequencies, leveraging the super-resolution capabilities of angle estimation. Our method can handle the realistic constraint of time-varying path delays resulting from user movements, an aspect previously unaddressed in the literature. We theoretically demonstrate that, even with only two arbitrary channel samples, the prediction error converges to zero as the number of base station antennas increases, under the condition of time-varying path delays. Additionally, we derive a lower-bound for the number of base station antennas required to achieve a satisfactory performance. Simulation results under the 3GPP industrial channel model confirm that the proposed MDMP method closely approaches the performance of a stationary scenario even at velocities of 120 km/h and a significant latency of 16 ms for channel state information.

To personalize human-agent interactions, we consider behavior style as a key factor and develop an efficient machine learning approach that generates gestures based on prosodic features, text, and speaker style. Our zero-shot multimodal style transfer model uses data from the PATS database to synthesize gestures of unseen speakers during training. We view style as an inherent aspect of communication, influencing the expressiveness of speech content conveyed through multimodal signals and text. Our approach disentangles content and style, allowing for direct inference of style embeddings even for speakers not part of the training data. The model has three objectives: generating source speaker gestures based on two audio and text modalities, conditioning these gestures on target speaker style embeddings, and transferring zero-shot style transfer of unseen speakers without retraining. Our system comprises a style encoder network and a sequence-to-sequence synthesis network that learn speaker style embeddings and generate gestures conditioned on these embeddings. Evaluations demonstrate our model's ability to synthesize gestures of source speakers and transfer target speaker style knowledge in a zero-shot setting, converting 2D gestures to 3D poses for animation production. We validate our approach through objective and subjective evaluations, comparing it to a baseline model.

Given a finite group G with the identity element 'e' and a non-trivial subgroup H, we define a generalized non-coprime graph GAmma_{G,H} where G excluding 'e' forms the vertices, and two distinct vertices 'a' and 'b' are connected if their orders share a common factor other than 1 and at least one of 'a' or 'b' belongs to H. In this paper, we investigate the graph theoretical properties of such generalized non-coprime graphs for cyclic groups, specifically characterizing the conditions for these graphs to belong to particular classes such as stars, paths, cycles, and others. We then extend our analysis to nilpotent groups and observe that this does not yield any new results, however we provide an example contrasting with this observation for a certain class of groups where all elements have prime power order.

A compartmental model of COVID-19 based on nonlinear partial differential equations continuously tracks the spread of the infection across various locations over time. However, refining spatial resolution, incorporating extra model compartments, and categorizing them based on medical significance increases the number of unknown variables to millions. To tackle these complex high-fidelity models, a highly efficient parallel solver is used, which combines domain decomposition and algebraic multigrid preconditioners to ensure the solver's scalability and performance. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a five-compartment COVID-19 model that simulates the spread of the infection over Southern Ontario. Using the proposed solver, it is possible to predict infections three months in advance for a system of 92 million in just 7 hours, thereby significantly reducing the time needed for traditional solvers, which could take months to process.

Researchers Dorigoni, Green, and Wen proposed a groundbreaking formula for an integrated correlator of four superconformal primary operators in N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, which we have extensively examined in the large N limit. Our analysis reveals that their formula can be re-expressed as the sum of contributions from (p,q)-strings, with these contributions unified by a single function through SL(2,ℤ) duality. The large order behavior of this function allows us to uncover non-perturbative large N corrections, which can be interpreted as D3-brane instantons within the holographically dual type IIB string theory. An alternative approach yields the same result through the solution of a Laplace-difference equation for the integrated correlator.

Determining the physical properties of massive star-forming clouds requires highly sensitive and high-resolution observations. We are interested in quantifying the accuracy with which observations can inform our understanding of these clouds. Specifically, we examine the potential of the Next Generation VLA interferometer. To this end, we utilize magnetohydrodynamic simulations of star formation and focus on a filamentary structure resembling an infrared-dark cloud. We create synthetic ngVLA observations of spectral lines, and then analyze the column density, gas temperature, and motion of the simulated cloud. These results are compared to those of ideal and real observations. Even at a distance of 4 kiloparsecs, the ngVLA can achieve resolutions of 0.01 parsecs in its most compact configuration. This allows the mapping of cloud kinematics and structure down to sub-arcsecond scales for abundant molecules. Reliable column density maps can be obtained for entire clouds, such as the 15 by 40 arcsecond cloud we studied, without additional data. However, high frequencies result in a loss of large-scale emission, complicating the interpretation of cloud kinematics. The ngVLA's line observations accurately track cloud motion, but are limited by the line-of-sight confusion that affects the interpretation of optically thick lines. The interferometer will provide accurate information on the small-scale structure and physical properties of clouds in high-mass star-forming regions, although complementary single-dish observations are still necessary for estimates of the total column density and large-scale motion.

To achieve ultra-reliable low-latency communications with high security and efficiency, a joint optimization problem is investigated for downlink transmissions involving multiple users and potential eavesdroppers in a finite blocklength environment. A multi-objective optimization framework is formulated to maximize a combined secrecy rate and minimize the maximum error probability and information leakage rate simultaneously. However, the optimization problem is complex due to the presence of back-off factors, non-convexity, and intertwined variables. To overcome these challenges, an alternating optimization approach is employed, splitting the problem into two stages: secure precoder design and error probability and information leakage rate minimization. In the initial stage, an optimal lower bound of the secrecy rate is derived and used to determine local solutions for the precoders via a power iteration-based method. In the second stage, a weighted-sum approach is adopted and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions are formulated in terms of the error probabilities and leakage rates for a given precoder configuration. Simulation results validate the proposed optimization algorithm.

To quantify entanglement entropy between two spacetime regions of a static black hole, separated by its horizon, we analyze the Schwarzschild black hole and then generalize to more complex black holes, such as charged Reissner-Nordstrom and Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes, as well as those within more general F(R) gravity. Entanglement entropy is computed via the replica trick by determining the explicit metric for the replica spacetime corresponding to each black hole type. This analysis yields entanglement entropy consistent with the Bekenstein-Hawking area law for static, spherically-symmetric black holes.

Deep learning models have achieved exceptional performance across numerous tasks, including image classification, speech recognition, and natural language processing. However, these models are highly susceptible to a significant vulnerability: adversarial attacks. By subtly modifying input images, these attacks render them imperceptible yet induce drastically different classifications from the model. This research delves into the efficacy of two types of attacks – projected gradient descent (PGD) and Adaptive Mask Segmentation Attack (ASMA) – on a specific image segmentation model, DeepLabV3, with two different network architectures: MobileNetV3 and ResNet50. Notably, the results indicate that while PGD consistently altered the segmentation outcome, ASMA's effectiveness was compromised when targeting multiple classification categories. Nonetheless, the presence of such attacks exposes all image classification deep learning networks to potential exploitation.

This research introduces a high-performance and dynamic system for real-time
supply landscape analysis in online auctions. The system's discovery process is
influenced by the predictive uncertainty of click-through rate models, and it is
tailored to operate within high-volume, low-response-time settings. Through live
experiments, our study confirms that leveraging model uncertainty during the
discovery phase has a beneficial effect on both model performance and key
business metrics.

A longstanding issue in computational biology is to find equilibrium between the quality and quantity of data, and the complexity of models. Various analytical tools such as identifiability analysis and information criteria have been designed to address this balance, but they can still fail to bridge the gap between available data and the detailed information required in complex mathematical models to answer crucial biological questions. In many cases, only straightforward models such as logistic and Gompertz growth models can be reliably estimated from standard measurements. To gain insights from intricate models that incorporate pivotal biological processes, researchers study the mapping relationships between non-identifiable parameters in the complex model and identifiable parameters in a simpler model. This enables an extra layer of interpretation between the set of non-identifiable parameters and the model's fit to the observed data. We showcase our approach by examining a series of mathematical models of tumour growth and show how our geometric method can predict which parameters cannot be reliably determined from the data, identify specific combinations of these parameters that relate to particular data features, and ultimately reveal additional insights from complex models.

In the context of heavy element nucleosynthesis, understanding photon strength functions is crucial, and their relationship to photoabsorption cross sections enables researchers to experimentally constrain these functions by analyzing the photo-response of atomic nuclei. The goal of this research is to determine the photo-response of $^{66}$Zn in a specific energy range and investigate the contribution of the elastic decay channel back to the ground state. To achieve this, a detailed analysis of electric and magnetic dipole transitions is also conducted. The researchers conducted nuclear resonance fluorescence experiments at the High Intensity $\gamma$-ray Source using a quasi-monoenergetic photon beam and two High Purity Germanium detectors for subsequent $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy. By leveraging the monoenergetic characteristics of the photon beam, the team was able to extract full photoabsorption cross sections from the data. The analysis also revealed the average contribution of electric and magnetic dipole strengths and the average branching ratio back to the ground state. The findings indicate that the photoabsorption cross sections in this study are lower than those obtained from a previous experiment that utilized bremsstrahlung on $^{66}$Zn. This discrepancy is attributed to the underestimation of the branching ratio in statistical-model calculations compared to the results from this analysis, which may explain the higher cross sections observed in the bremsstrahlung data.

Object localization with coarse annotations like image categories poses significant challenges. Current approaches using deep networks mainly rely on class activation maps, which tend to focus on specific regions rather than the entire object. Moreover, recent transformer-based techniques often prioritize background elements, making it harder to identify the complete object. To address these issues, a re-attention mechanism, termed the Token Refinement Transformer (TRT), is introduced, which leverages object-level semantics for accurate localization. TRT incorporates a novel module, the Token Priority Scoring Module (TPSM), to filter out background noise and concentrate on the target object. Furthermore, the class activation map is used as a semantically informed input to confine the attention map to the target object. Comprehensive experiments conducted on two benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in comparison to existing approaches using image category annotations.

Robustness issues associated with graph neural networks (GNNs) pose a significant challenge as these models are susceptible to noise and adversarial attacks in input data. Developing methods that can effectively defend against such threats is crucial for their practical application. The current GNN defense techniques are often computationally expensive and not scalable. This paper introduces a universal framework, Weighted Laplacian GNN (RWL-GNN), which combines Weighted Graph Laplacian learning with GNN architecture. By leveraging the positive semi-definiteness property of Laplacian matrices, RWL-GNN formulates an optimization framework that eliminates adversarial or noisy edges and weights the connections within the graph appropriately. A case study utilizing the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) architecture demonstrates the efficacy of RWL-GNN in achieving both high accuracy and computational efficiency. Notably, the proposed framework is adaptable to various existing GNN architectures. The results of simulations using benchmark datasets confirm the effectiveness of RWL-GNN, and the accompanying code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Bharat-Runwal/RWL-GNN.

To ensure the autonomous racecar makes informed decisions during racing, accurately predicting the paths of its surrounding opponents is crucial. However, utilizing deep neural networks, which are complex and lack transparency, can be a hindrance in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving. In this research, we present a structured framework for predicting the movements of competitor vehicles using deep neural networks, resulting in constrained and reliable output trajectories. This framework enables the provision of quality assurances for the predictions. We compared the model's performance with an LSTM-based encoder-decoder architecture, utilizing data from high-fidelity Hardware-in-the-Loop simulations, and found it outperforms the baseline in terms of prediction accuracy while maintaining the quality guarantees. Consequently, our model demonstrates its potential for robust real-world implementation. Moreover, the proposed model was successfully deployed on the Technical University of Munich's racecar during the 2021 Indy Autonomous Challenge, and the associated code is freely available on GitHub.

Galaxies are commonly divided into two distinct categories based on their star formation and structure, with disk-shaped galaxies forming new stars and spherical galaxies no longer forming new stars. However, a recent study of 4574 galaxies in the local universe has revealed that the classification of galaxies into two categories may be overly simplistic. At the same time, fixed stellar mass, the galaxies show no bimodal distribution and the rotation speed of fast rotators is a combination of at least two populations: disk galaxies and intermediate systems. Disk galaxies are not only more massive, but also more numerous, making up the majority of the star-forming population, while the non-star-forming population is composed of multiple types of galaxies. Notably, passive disks, which represent about 30% of the non-star-forming population, play a crucial role in understanding the process of quenching, or the reduction of star formation, in galaxies. The results suggest that the majority of galaxies in the local universe are disk-shaped and that a significant portion of them lose some of their rotation support after quenching. Spherical galaxies, while present, do not represent the final stage of galaxy evolution for the majority of galaxies.

Tractable density models called normalizing flows can efficiently approximate intricate distributions such as those in physical systems. But existing training methods for these flows have drawbacks including getting stuck in local modes, needing expensive simulations, or employing loss functions with high variability. We resolve these issues by incorporating annealed importance sampling into flows, and we optimize the mass-covering $\alpha$-divergence with a value of 2 to reduce importance weight variability. This results in our novel Flow AIS Bootstrap method, which uses annealed importance sampling to generate samples where the flow is weak, thereby discovering new modes. When applied to complex targets, our method effectively approximates them where others struggle. Moreover, to our knowledge, we are the first to learn a molecule's Boltzmann distribution solely from an unnormalized target without access to simulated samples, outperforming training with maximum likelihood on such samples while using 100 times fewer target evaluations: our reweighted samples yield nearly identical, unbiased dihedral angle histograms to the truth.

Capturing the complexities of user behavior is a fundamental aspect of contemporary e-commerce, which is often achieved by simultaneously optimizing click-through and conversion predictions. However, existing approaches frequently neglect two crucial factors influencing user behavior: for each item list, the user's behavior on any item is not solely determined by the item itself but also by the user's past actions on other items in the sequence; (i) contextual dependence and (ii) varying time intervals, where users tend to click frequently but make purchases infrequently. To address this limitation, we propose the Hierarchical rEcurrent Ranking On the Entire Space (HEROES) model, a multi-scale network that integrates contextual information to estimate user behavior at different time scales. By introducing a hierarchical framework, HEROES separates user engagement and satisfaction behaviors, learning a suitable time scale for each to capture dynamic user patterns. The proposed model also utilizes the Hawkes process to create a novel recurrent unit, incorporating items' features and the excitation or discouragement from past behaviors. Furthermore, HEROES can be extended to build fair ranking systems by combining survival analysis techniques. Our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, as evidenced by experiments on three large-scale industrial datasets.

The Lightning Network has rapidly expanded in recent years and now serves as the primary scaling solution for the Bitcoin blockchain. Its security is contingent upon nodes' ability to settle balances by confirming a transaction on the Bitcoin blockchain within a predetermined time frame. This inherent constraint makes the LN susceptible to attacks aiming to increase blockchain congestion and prevent protocol execution. We investigate the vulnerability of the LN to mass exit attacks from a small coalition of malicious nodes. We analyze two attack types: a zombie attack where unresponsive nodes lock funds for an extended period, and a mass double-spend attack where nodes attempt to steal funds by submitting multiple closing transactions using outdated protocol states. Our simulations under historically-plausible congestion conditions demonstrate that both attacks can be carried out by a small coalition, assuming mild statistical assumptions about channel balances. To support our findings, we formulate the problem of identifying the worst-case coalition of adversarial nodes as a graph cut problem and justify our results with the LN's scale-free topology.

A photometric search has been conducted to discover new cataclysmic variable stars with the objective of identifying potential AR~Scorpii-type binary system candidates. We targeted GAIA sources that are likely linked to unidentified X-ray sources and analyzed the light curves obtained from the Zwicky Transient Facility, Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, and Lulin One-meter Telescope in Taiwan. This led to the investigation of eight potential CV candidates, out of which six are newly identified. Two other sources had been previously identified as CVs but were left unexplored. Furthermore, two eclipsing systems were associated with unidentified XMM-Newton or Swift sources and a polar candidate linked to an unidentified ASKA source was found promising. Two polar candidates appear to be situated in the period gap of CVs, whereas the remaining six candidates exhibit orbital periods shorter than the period gap. Despite failing to identify promising AR~Scorpii-type binary system candidates, our research suggests that surveys may have overlooked CV systems with X-ray emission that do not frequently exhibit outbursts.

Most studies of layered turbulent flows, which assume that temperature and velocity gradients align perfectly, need to be revised. In this research, we examine the impact of these misalignments on the behavior of turbulent flows, using both theoretical models and complex simulations. Our findings reveal that turbulent flows exhibit characteristics from two previously distinct types of instabilities when their gradients are not aligned. Furthermore, the misaligned gradients lead to uneven mixing patterns that combine elements of upwelling and erosion, ultimately reorganizing the gradients themselves. Our results also indicate that the misalignment significantly reduces the influence of certain parameters on turbulent flows, with important implications for understanding ocean currents.

Recent advancements in unpaired image denoising have shown considerable progress.
However, existing methods heavily rely on assumptions about noise characteristics,
which are often impractical. A more robust approach can be achieved by focusing
on the structural aspects of the denoising problem rather than noise statistics.
Motivated by this idea, we introduce a self-supervised denoising method that
operates without pairing and leverages spatial degradation followed by refined
estimation under regularization. This novel approach significantly outperforms
previous methods and consistently delivers reliable results across diverse data sets.

The integrin receptor protein plays a crucial role in remodeling the actin network and attaching the cell membrane to the extracellular matrix through complex mechanical processes. At integrin-rich regions, the clustering of lipids and lipid-bound proteins necessary for certain endocytic processes is facilitated. To explore this phenomenon, we've developed a simple yet accurate mathematical model that considers the interaction between integrin's on/off states and membrane dynamics. This model allows us to derive an analytical equation for membrane deformation, velocity, and lipid clustering, revealing that these processes evolve in a non-linear fashion. Furthermore, our findings show how membrane properties and stochastic shuttling timescales influence these complex behaviors.

Researchers have developed numerical solutions for Einstein's constraint equations, working with intricately shaped, three-dimensional structures that have unique geometric properties. Two types of solutions were derived – one straightforward and the other more complex – on examples of manifolds from specific geometric classes. These constant mean curvature solutions also satisfy the Yamabe problem, which reconfigures a space to achieve a uniform curvature.

The concept of homophily can be quantified within network frameworks, describing how "similar connections are made". A network is considered homophilic when the groups or classes it is divided into form denser subgraphs than would be expected by chance. This idea is tied to a 'random coloring model' where the observed class sizes are seen as outcomes of random partitioning. A network's homophilicity is established when the probability of achieving such class sizes by chance is below a certain threshold, known as significance level $\alpha$. However, approximating this probability is a challenging problem, so we use a bound derived from Cantelli's inequality to measure homophily. To make this feasible, we derive a formula for the covariance matrix of subgraph sizes under the random coloring model, which surprisingly depends only on the network's degree distribution and the class partition's type. This allows us to create a practical index for measuring homophily, which is a useful tool for analyzing network behavior.

The Fabbri-Russo model represents a broad framework of two-dimensional dilaton gravity, which can encompass various specific gravity theories characterized by the parameter "$n$". The Russo-Susskind-Thorlacius model fits the case of $n=1$. In this context, we analyze Page curves and the concept of entanglement islands within eternal and evaporating black holes. Notably, the emergence of islands leads to a deceleration of the rise in entanglement entropy of radiation after the Page time, adhering to the principle of unitarity. For eternal black holes, the fine-grained entropy reaches a saturation value equivalent to twice the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, whereas for evaporating black holes, it converges to zero. The parameter "$n$" significantly influences the Page curve at very early times but is a minor factor in the large distance limit, resulting in "$n$"-independent Page curve shapes. We also explore the connection between islands and firewalls, demonstrating that islands are a more suitable solution to the quantum entanglement-monogamy problem. Lastly, we discuss how gravity/ensemble duality might resolve the state conundrum caused by the island formula.

The temporal point process (TPP) model is commonly used to model asynchronous event sequences with timestamps, conditioned on historical impacts, using probabilistic models. However, previous works focused on maximizing likelihood have unsatisfactory predictive performance, resulting in large gaps between model-generated timestamps and actual observations. Recently, deep generative models have excelled in image generation tasks, generating high-quality samples. Despite this, there's a gap in exploring generative models in the context of event occurrence modeling for TPP. To address this, a unified generative framework for neural temporal point process (GNTPP) is proposed to investigate feasibility and effectiveness and improve predictive performance. Additionally, an adaptive reweighting term is introduced to measure historical impacts based on event types and time intervals in attentive models. Extensive experiments demonstrate the predictive capability of GNTPP with generative probabilistic decoders and the benefits of the revised attention. This work is the first to adapt generative models in a complete unified framework, exploring their effectiveness in TPP. The codebase is made available to facilitate future research in Neural TPPs.

In vehicular networks, Federated edge learning technology presents a promising solution to balance computation workload reduction and user data privacy. Within this framework, vehicles send their data to edge servers, where local models are updated without compromising sensitive information. Nevertheless, the cache queue's finite capacity and time-varying wireless channels between servers and vehicles create challenges in choosing the optimal number of vehicles to ensure stable edge server cache queues and optimal learning accuracy. Furthermore, selecting vehicles with varying resource levels impacts the total training data volume, thereby influencing model precision. To address this, a novel vehicle selection method is proposed, considering the statuses of all vehicles within an edge server's coverage area, with the aim of maximizing learning accuracy while maintaining cache queue stability. Simulation experiments validate the efficacy of this approach, demonstrating its superiority over existing benchmarks.
